+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 84.3
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Six: The Courtesies of Antares The screen had cycled through its eight messages forty-one times since Arthur Neegan began counting, and he had begun counting because an engineer who cannot control a situation can at least measure it. ATMOSPHERICS: NOMINAL. HULL INTEGRITY: 100%. TRAJECTORY: STABLE. The green phosphor letters blinked out one by one, patient as a metronome. Somewhere aft the drive hummed at a harmonic he didn't like; he'd have wanted it checked, if anyone aboard were asking his professional opinion. Nobody was. Four men sat across the cabin with hand-blasters holstered and spines straight, and one of them had held Arthur's elbow from his airlock to the shuttle the way you'd carry a case of dynamite. Through the port, Mars was shrinking to a rust coin. His father had cleared those two hundred hectares with a secondhand condenser and a stubbornness that skipped a generation, apparently, since Arthur had signed the assay request out of idle curiosity and not defiance. Curiosity. He turned the word over. It had a body count, these days. The shuttle mated with a soft clang to the cruiser *Almach* — an old hull with new engines, Arthur noted, which told you something about the owners' priorities. The lounge had actual wood veneer and a viewport full of stars. Behind a desk sat a gray-haired woman in a plain dark suit. On her breast: the silver starburst on black. "Mr. Neegan. You look well, for a man who's been abducted with excellent manners." "Is that what this is?" "This is an invitation. We are simply a civilization that believes in helping guests arrive. Sit. The tea is genuine — genuinely from Earth, which I'm told is the same thing." He sat. Two guards took up posts by the door, decorative as furniture and about as comforting. "I'm called Undersecretary Rhee. Do you know how many freeholds remain on Mars, Mr. Neegan?" "I know mine's one of them." "Three thousand and change, out of a population of four million. Everyone else leases — body and shovel — to Helion Consolidated or one of its smaller and hungrier cousins. Your father's generation was promised land. Your generation was promised nothing, which at least is honest. So a titled, lien-free, first-generation settler sitting atop the largest Azra vein ever surveyed is —" she sipped her tea — "an actuarial event." "I haven't surveyed anything. One assay." "Which the lab technician sold within nine hours. By now six parties hold your numbers. I'll tell you what happened to the last two men who found what you found. One died in a dome failure the week before he was to sign with Helion. The other signed with Helion, and now lives somewhere no one can locate, which I promise you is worse." Arthur looked at the starfield so he wouldn't look at the guards. "You said you were diplomats." "In name only, as the joke goes. But tell me — what do you actually know about Azra? Not the prospector's version. Think like an engineer." "It accelerates radioactive decay. You line a fission chamber with azra lattice and low-grade ore burns like weapons-grade. That's the whole gold rush. Fuel multiplier for the star drives." "That's the schoolbook. Here is the rest, which four governments know and no school teaches. The acceleration is *selective*. Tunable by lattice geometry. Do you understand what that means, Mr. Neegan?" Arthur was quiet a moment, and the quiet had ice in it. "If you can tune it — you can reach into refined fissile stockpiles. Trigger decay at a distance. Every warhead in the system is either inert — or someone else's bomb." "Every warhead in the system," Rhee agreed, setting down her cup with a small click, like a lock turning. "The Terrestrial Directorate currently enjoys a monopoly on Azra processing. The Concord of Antares believes monopolies breed a certain — complacency. Your two hundred hectares are, at this moment, the most strategically important dirt in the inhabited universe. Congratulations are, I suppose, in order. So are condolences." "The offer," Arthur said. "You didn't haul me halfway to orbit for geography." "The Homestead Act forbids you to sell or alienate your title to any extra-territorial power — the one law Earth's parliament passed honestly, as it happens, and the single reason you are still alive and owning. So: you retain title. You grant exclusive extraction rights to a small, dull, entirely Martian concern we have incorporated for the purpose — the Ochre Development Syndicate. You receive a royalty that would embarrass a planetary governor, protection, and if matters deteriorate, evacuation under Concord registry. In exchange, your vein never enters the Directorate's monopoly, and the system remains — balanced." "And if I refuse?" "Then we return you home with profound apologies, and you will have six days to consider the matter, because that is when the Directorate's delegation arrives. They are not diplomatic in name *or* otherwise." She slid a thin document spool across the desk. "You needn't decide tonight." Arthur didn't touch the spool. He looked at the silver starburst on her breast instead, and counted, because counting was what he did. "Your emblem has seven rays," he said. "The Concord's star has nine. One for each charter world. Your ship was kind enough to give me a reader on the way up." For the first time, Rhee smiled, and it was the warmest and most unsettling thing that had happened to him all day. "Why, Mr. Neegan," she said. "You're the first man in three systems to bother counting. Drink your tea. We have a great deal to discuss — and rather less time than I told you."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Asimovian style and successfully captures the classic science fiction atmosphere requested. The author effectively establishes Arthur as a competent engineer thrust into circumstances beyond his control, maintaining his analytical nature throughout the encounter. The dialogue between Arthur and Undersecretary Rhee crackles with tension and reveals information naturally while advancing the plot. The world-building is particularly strong, revealing the political complexity of the Mars colony situation and the broader implications of Azra mining without overwhelming exposition. The revelation about Azra's selective radioactive decay acceleration and its military implications feels genuinely consequential and scientifically plausible within the genre conventions. The prose maintains an appropriate retrofuturistic tone with details like "green phosphor letters" and the ship's technical specifications. The writing is economical but evocative, particularly in descriptions like Mars shrinking to "a rust coin" and the tea cup's click "like a lock turning." Character motivations feel authentic - Arthur's engineering mindset drives his observations and responses, while Rhee presents as a seasoned operative balancing courtesy with implicit threat. The power dynamic is well-established through both dialogue and staging. The chapter's structure builds tension effectively, from Arthur's anxious counting aboard the shuttle to the revelation about the emblem's incorrect number of rays, suggesting deeper deceptions at play. This ending hook feels earned rather than contrived. Some minor weaknesses include occasional exposition that borders on telling rather than showing, particularly in Rhee's explanation of the political situation. However, this is somewhat mitigated by the conversational context and Arthur's need for information. The piece successfully plants seeds for larger intrigue while maintaining focus on the immediate scene. The stakes feel appropriately high without being overwrought, and the dialogue serves multiple functions of character development, world-building, and plot advancement. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 86.6
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations The darkroom smells like vinegar and pennies, and under the safelight everyone is the color of old blood. I've always liked that about it — the way red strips you down to shape. No colors to perform. Just edges and light. I'm good at wanting things. That's my whole thing. I cut my own hair, I wear whatever makes old men on the bus uncomfortable, and when I see something I want, I walk toward it at a pace that suggests it's already been promised to me. People find this charming or exhausting, depending on whether they're the thing I want. Elliot is the first thing I've ever wanted to walk slowly toward. We got paired for the final project three weeks ago — "intimate portraiture," Professor Ansel called it, like pairing us was a neutral act and not a chemical one. Since then we've been in the darkroom four nights running, and I've learned him the way you learn a photograph: in stops and exposures. He's nineteen. He dresses like a haunted library — layered black, silver rings on every finger, a mesh sleeve under a grandpa cardigan he found somewhere for four dollars. In critique he speaks maybe twice a class, and both times the room goes quiet, because he's right. Tonight he hands me a strip of negatives and doesn't quite let go. "That one. Maybe. I don't know. Maybe not." "Which one?" "Fourth frame. Or — you can skip it. It's stupid." I've watched him all semester. I know the difference between his *stupid* and his *scared*. His stupid is a shrug. His scared is this: still hands, eyes down, waiting for permission. I feed the fourth frame into the enlarger. Under the red light I can't tell what I'm looking at until I can, and then I can't stop looking. Elliot, in a slip of a dress that must have come from the same thrift store as the cardigan, standing at a window with his chin down and his hands soft at his sides. Not a costume. Not a joke. He looks *held* — like someone finally asked him to hold still as himself. I don't say anything while I focus the negative. Saying something bold right now would be a kind of theft, and I'm trying very hard to be a thief of nothing. The paper goes under the enlarger. I hit the timer. Eight seconds of light, and then we're standing over the developer tray together, watching nothing become something, which is the entire religion of photography. "I've been thinking," he says to the tray. The image starts blooming up through the chemical — window first, then the dark shape of him, then his face surfacing out of the gray like a diver. "About that word. *Guy.* I don't think it's the whole word. I keep trying words on like the dresses at Value Village. Nothing's my size yet. But guy's getting tight in the shoulders." I wanted to take his hand. I wanted to take over. This semester had taught me those are different verbs, and only one of them was mine to use tonight. Here's the thing about me: my whole life I've been attracted to people who arrived fully assembled. Women who looked like they could rewire a house. Men built like arguments. Clean edges, definite lines — I liked knowing exactly what I was looking at, because then I knew exactly what I wanted. Elliot is none of that. Elliot is a long exposure, still developing, and the terrifying part — the part I'm not saying out loud in a room where saying things feels like developing them — is that I don't want to look away. The not-knowing isn't a flaw in the attraction. It might be the attraction. Which immediately made me suspicious of myself. I checked it the way you check a print: is this excitement about *him*, or about getting a front-row seat to his becoming? I didn't want to be his audience. I wanted — I didn't know what I wanted. That was new. And what did that make me? Apparently I didn't have a word for myself either. That felt fair, somehow. "You don't have to have the word yet," I said. My voice came out softer than I've ever heard it. "Words are like prints. Nobody nails the first exposure. You just keep shooting." He laughed — one syllable, relieved — and started to hum. He does that. When a print's in the bath, he hums, low and tuneless, some melody with no edges to it. The first night I thought it was a song. By the second I'd figured out it's just something his body does while he waits, a sound like the timer makes, but kinder. "What is that? The song." "I don't know. My mom hums it when she can't sleep." He tips the tray, and the developer moves across the paper in one slow wave. "I do it when I'm nervous. Or happy. They feel kind of the same from the inside." The print of him in the dress is fully arrived now, and it's good — better than anything in our actual project — and I tell him so. He looks at it the way you look at a stranger you've been wanting to meet. I move it to the stop bath, and when I hand him the tongs, our fingers overlap on the handle, and neither of us moves for a second that lasts exactly as long as it lasts. "Can I say something bold?" I ask. "It's the only way I know how to say things." He looks up. In the red light his eyeliner is a smudge, his rings are little moons. "Yeah." "I want to be the one who photographs you. Not for the grade. Whenever you find a version of yourself you want to see — whatever you're wearing, whatever word you're trying on — you bring it to me, and I'll develop it. You're in charge of everything. I just want to be in the dark with you while you figure out what you look like." He's quiet long enough for the timer to tick twice. "Okay," he says. "But you have to teach me to print. I keep ruining yours." "Deal." We put the print in the fixer together, four hands and one tray, and he starts humming again. This time I hum the harmony, badly, and he laughs for real, and somewhere under the vinegar smell the image of him sets into permanence — chin down, hands soft, looking back at me like he's already a little braver. There's a chemical that stops development. I was in no hurry to use it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates sophisticated literary craft in exploring complex themes of gender identity, attraction, and vulnerability. The narrative successfully captures Dani's voice as an assertive art student while showing her growth as she navigates unfamiliar emotional territory with Elliot. The darkroom setting is expertly utilized both literally and metaphorically - the red light creates intimacy while the photographic development process mirrors the characters' emotional and identity development. The author shows strong technical knowledge of photography that enhances rather than overwhelms the narrative. The characterization is particularly strong. Dani's voice is consistent and authentic - her usual confidence tempered by genuine care for Elliot's vulnerability. The line "Elliot is the first thing I've ever wanted to walk slowly toward" perfectly encapsulates her character growth. Elliot emerges as more than just an object of fascination; his tentative sharing about gender identity feels genuine and unforced. The prose quality is high, with memorable phrases like "He dresses like a haunted library" and "Words are like prints. Nobody nails the first exposure." The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining lyrical quality. The photography metaphors are woven naturally throughout rather than feeling forced. The dialogue feels authentic to the characters' ages and personalities. Elliot's hesitant speech patterns ("That one. Maybe. I don't know. Maybe not.") contrast effectively with Dani's more direct communication style, though she modulates her approach sensitively. The emotional complexity is well-handled. Dani's attraction isn't simplified - she questions whether she's attracted to Elliot or to witnessing his becoming, showing psychological sophistication. The piece avoids easy answers about identity and attraction. The pacing works well, building intimacy gradually through shared darkroom sessions. The ending feels earned rather than artificially positive - both characters have grown but remain works in progress. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the metaphorical language borders on being too clever, and some descriptions that could be more concise. The piece also relies heavily on internal monologue, though this suits the introspective nature of the story. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 86.2
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Stolen Moments in Roma **9:14 a.m. — Via delle Muratte** The guidebook was the problem. Ben knew this even as he walked backward into the street, index finger marking a paragraph on Baroque hydraulics. *The Trevi Fountain consumes approximately 2,824,800 cubic feet of water daily—* The shriek of brakes. A blur of red Ducati. A woman's voice, rapid and murderous: *"Ma sei scemo?! Ti faccio causa, ti sfascio il libro in—"* "I'm so terribly sorry. *Mi dispiace. Molto... dispiacenza?*" The helmet came off, releasing a storm of dark hair. Alessandra looked at him the way one looks at a pigeon that has survived against all odds. "Dispiacenza," she repeated. "That is not a word. That is a crime against my language, which is worse than almost killing me." "I nearly killed *you*? I believe it was the motorcycle—" "The motorcycle was where it belongs. You were in the road, professore, reading about Rome instead of looking at it." She snatched the guidebook from his hands, weighed it like contraband, and handed it back with a smirk that rearranged something in his chest. "There. Now you have touched a Roman. The book is jealous." **10:02 a.m. — Somewhere Ben Did Not Agree to Be** "You want to see Rome or read the footnotes?" "That's a false dichotomy—" "Get on." He got on. This surprised them both. At a red light, without breaking her sentence about the corruption of the city council, Alessandra leaned over and plucked a red carnation from a vendor's bucket. The vendor didn't notice. She didn't look at Ben when she did it, which was how he knew she knew he'd seen. She tucked the flower into his jacket pocket. "For the accident," she said. "Compensation." **11:30 a.m. — Campo de' Fiori** She argued politics with a fruit vendor named Sandro for four minutes, hands flying, laughing, insulting his mother's cooking with evident affection. While doing so, she ate a fig from his stall. Then a second. Sandro never noticed, or pretended not to, and waved them off like family. "You stole those," Ben said quietly, once they'd walked on. "I *liberated* them. Sandro overcharges tourists. You especially. You have a face like a receipt." "That's— I'm not sure that's a compliment." "It's not." She handed him the second fig. He ate it. It was, infuriatingly, the best thing he'd ever tasted. **1:47 p.m. — Trastevere** The bar was dark and cool, all marble and old men. The barman, Dario, froze when he saw her. "Madonna. Sandra. Still alive." "Unfortunately for you." She kissed both his cheeks and ordered two coffees and something unpronounceable. While she argued with the jukebox, Dario leaned across the bar toward Ben, voice low. "English. A word of advice. I know this one since she was twelve, stealing cigarettes from my own pocket while asking me the time." He tapped his temple. "Count your belongings. Then count them again. She is a magician, and magicians are never performing for your benefit." "I heard that," Alessandra called, not turning around. "You were meant to." "You're still angry about the lighter." "I am still angry about the *motorino*." "That was eleven years ago, Dario. Let it die." But something flickered across her face — a door opening briefly onto a room Ben couldn't see — and then it closed, and she was grinning again, sliding his espresso toward him. "Drink. Sugar is for cowards." He drank it black. She watched him do it with an expression he was beginning to suspect was approval. **4:20 p.m. — The Aventine Hill** "This is a private garden," Ben whispered, as she lifted the chain on a gate like it had personally offended her. "Everything in Rome is private. That's why it's the best city on earth." She pulled him through by the wrist. His heart did something unacademic. The orange trees glowed in the late light. Below, the whole city sprawled — domes and antennas and laundry. She hopped onto the low wall, balanced on the edge of the drop, arms out. "Alessandra—" "Ben." She turned, silhouetted, and for a moment neither of them was joking. "You came to Rome to write a book about dead people. And instead, today, you ate stolen figs and broke into a garden with a criminal. How do you feel?" He took a breath. "Utterly disoriented." "And?" "...Alive. Rather alarmingly alive." "Good answer." She stepped down, close enough that he could smell oranges and engine oil, and patted his chest twice — a gesture that felt like a period at the end of a sentence. "Careful, professore. That feeling is addictive." **10:56 p.m. — Trevi Fountain** The floodlights turned the water to hammered silver. She returned him to the exact spot where she'd nearly killed him, which she found hilarious. "So," she said. "Back to your footnotes." "Yes. Well. The book won't write itself." "Tragic for you." She put on her helmet. Under the streetlight, her expression was unreadable — the door again, firmly shut. "Ciao, Ben." "Ciao—" and she was gone, engine snarling into the Roman night. He stood there a long moment, feeling the day settle over him like dust. Then, dutifully, he reached into his jacket for a coin — and found his pocket occupied. His fountain pen was gone. His good one, the Montblanc, a gift from his father. In its place: a small brass medal on a chain — *San Cristoforo, protettore dei viaggiatori*, patron saint of travelers — and a scrap of paper with a phone number and, beneath it, in sharp, impatient handwriting: *You'll want the pen back. I never return what I take. Come and take it from me. — A.* Ben laughed out loud, alone, at midnight, at the Trevi Fountain, like a madman. Tourists edged away from him. Then he turned the medal over in his fingers, pocketed the number with the care of a man handling a rare manuscript, and — feeling quietly, gloriously criminal — skipped his own coin into the water.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative flair in crafting a contemporary romance set in Rome. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters whose personalities emerge clearly through dialogue and action rather than exposition. Alessandra's kleptomaniacal tendencies are woven seamlessly into the narrative through subtle actions (stealing figs, the carnation, Ben's pen) that feel natural rather than forced plot devices. The structure works well, using timestamped vignettes that create a cinematic quality while maintaining narrative momentum. The dialogue crackles with authenticity - Alessandra's sharp wit and cultural confidence contrasts effectively with Ben's bumbling academic politeness. The Italian phrases feel organic rather than performative, and the cultural clash is handled with nuance rather than stereotype. The prose strikes an excellent balance between literary sophistication and accessibility. Phrases like "looked at him the way one looks at a pigeon that has survived against all odds" and "You have a face like a receipt" demonstrate wit and originality. The imagery is vivid without being overwrought - the orange trees glowing in late light, the fountain water described as "hammered silver." The character development feels earned. Ben's transformation from guidebook-clutching academic to someone willing to break rules happens gradually through the day's events. His final act of throwing his own coin in the fountain (rather than using Alessandra's stolen one) shows subtle character growth. Alessandra remains appropriately enigmatic - her motivations unclear but consistent with her established personality. The ending provides satisfying closure while opening future possibilities. The pen theft and saint's medal exchange is clever plotting that feels true to both characters. The romantic tension builds naturally without forced declarations or unearned intimacy. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the prose occasionally tips toward being slightly too clever for its own good, and a few instances where character actions feel slightly constructed for plot purposes rather than emerging purely from character motivation. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Last Outpost ### Chapter One: The Double The night cycle begins when the grow-lamps above the moss wall dim to amber and the recyclers settle into their low, oceanic hum. That's when the bar becomes mine. Harlan's got his boots on the rail, arguing with Pia about whether the Ferris vein is played out. The Brannock twins are running their card game in the corner booth, and the jukebox plays some old Earth ballad, warm and warped from a century of copying. I wipe the bar. Same spot as always — the pale patch where the lacquer's worn through. It isn't dirty. It's just what my hands do while I listen. The Outpost tolerates my flaws: I hoard the good bottle, I count cards when the twins let me sit in, I don't answer questions about *before*. In exchange, I keep the jukebox breathing and the peace mostly intact. It's a working arrangement. The door seal sighs. Cold air, ozone, old fear. A stranger. She's tall, coat salt-crusted from too many airlocks, tentacled dreads hanging askew like they haven't been tended in a week. Copper rings on every tendril, every ring gone dark. I've served drift-natives before. Their rings glow amber when they're easy. Dark means something's chasing them. She folds onto the stool like her strings were cut. "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." "Rough jump?" I reach for the good bottle, the one behind the chai tin. "Rough year." Her voice is sanded down. "You the keeper?" "I pour, I listen, I fix the jukebox when it sulks. Keeper's a big word for a place like this." "Quiet place," she says, like a diagnosis. "On Tuesdays." I pour. "Name, for the tab?" "Vesper." A pause. "Not the one I was born with." "Nobody out here is." She wraps both hands around the glass — knuckles frostburned, the shiny new-pink kind — and doesn't drink. Just holds it, like a small animal she's keeping warm. "You eat?" I ask. "Bread's fresh. Chai's better." "I'm not hungry." "Whisky bites less on a full stomach. House rule." "House rules." One tendril lifts, ring clicking. "Fine. And information. When does the next ferry cycle out?" "Pia runs freight to Cinder Dock, Tuesdays and Fridays. Slow, but she sings, and the price is fair." "Not freight." Her eyes come up, the color of deep water. "Quiet." I keep wiping. "We don't do quiet here. We do slow. Different thing." "Everything's a different thing until it isn't." She drinks half the double in one swallow, no wince. Vega whisky isn't for wincing; it's for surviving. "There a back room? Somewhere a person could sit without being sat at?" "There's a booth. The twins will cheat you, but politely." That almost gets a laugh. Almost. "You've wiped that spot eleven times since I sat down." "Twelve. It's a lucky spot." "Lucky." She turns the word over like a coin she suspects is counterfeit. Then she reaches into her coat — slow, telegraphing it, like she knows I keep the shock-baton under the register — and lays a flex of film on the bar. "Tell me what you see." I look at her first. Then I look. It's a chart. Hand-inked, old-school — the Scattered Belt rendered in fine lines, drifts and shoal-gravity and routes threading between them like veins. Nobody draws charts by hand anymore. Nobody except— There's a mark in the corner. A little wren, wings folded, sitting inside a triple knot. My rag stops. "Where did you get this?" My voice comes out level. I'm proud of that. "Off a dead man, if you must know." She taps the wren. "The seller said the navigator who drew it vanished years ago. Dead, probably. But here's the thing." She leans in, dropping under the jukebox. "The routes are still true. *Current.* Somebody updates them. Somebody who knows the deep passages through this Belt — the ones that don't exist on any licensed chart." "Maybe the dead man had a student." "Maybe." She drains the glass and slides it toward me. Wordless, I pour the second half. "The people this was stolen from want it back. They're called the Tallymen. They don't send messages. They send visits. I'm two days ahead. Three, if the mag-runs hold." My hands are wiping again. Same spot. Thirteen. "And you came *here*." "I came here because of the wren." Her tendrils go still — all of them at once, which I've never seen a drift-native do. "The routes lead here. All of them. Every quiet passage in the Belt threads through this rock like it's a knot in the middle of everything. Somebody drew this station into the map on purpose. Somebody *wanted* to be findable." The jukebox changes songs. Harlan laughs at something. Somewhere in the moss wall, the irrigation line ticks. "Help me," Vesper says. Quiet. Not begging — she's past begging, into something flatter and harder. "Get me out quiet, and I leave the chart with you and the Tallymen with me." "And if I don't?" "Then I keep running, they keep following, and your slow little bar stays lucky for exactly as long as it takes them to notice the knot in the middle of everything." I look at the wren in the triple knot. I drew that mark a thousand times, in a life I folded up and buried under a bar on the far rim of nowhere. Nobody's updated those routes. Nobody *could*. Except somebody has. The comm behind the bar crackles. Docking control, bored, tinny: *"Outpost, unscheduled arrival, berth four. Vessel Pale Magpie, transponder... verifying. They're asking for the keeper."* My rag stops for real this time. "By name?" I ask the comm. A pause. Paper rustling. *"Asking for someone called the Wren."* Vesper's rings click as every tendril turns toward me. Fourteen.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the cozy sci-fi atmosphere requested. The author successfully establishes Nettle as a compelling narrator with a mysterious past, using her bartending role as an effective lens through which to observe the story's unfolding tension. The dialogue feels natural and purposeful, comprising roughly the requested 60% of the text. Each character has a distinct voice - Vesper's weary desperation contrasts well with Nettle's cautious professionalism. The conversation reveals information organically while building tension toward the climactic revelation. The world-building is economical but evocative. Details like the moss wall, grow-lamps, and drift-natives with their mood-indicating rings create a lived-in feeling without overwhelming exposition. The author skillfully weaves technical elements (mag-runs, shock-batons, transponders) into the narrative without breaking immersion. The central mystery unfolds well - the hand-drawn chart with its significant wren symbol creates intrigue that pays off when Nettle's past identity is revealed. The arrival of the "Pale Magpie" asking for "the Wren" provides an excellent cliffhanger that raises stakes without resolving the conflict. The prose maintains consistent quality with some particularly strong moments, like Vesper folding "onto the stool like her strings were cut" and the description of her holding the whisky glass "like a small animal she's keeping warm." The recurring motif of Nettle wiping the same spot on the bar effectively shows her growing anxiety. However, some elements feel slightly underdeveloped. The Tallymen as antagonists remain somewhat generic, and while Vesper's desperation is clear, her character could use more distinctive traits beyond her obvious distress. The pacing occasionally slows during exposition about the chart and navigation routes. The piece successfully avoids common pitfalls - there's no purple prose, no unearned emotional beats, and the tension builds naturally. The ending maintains appropriate darkness for the situation while preserving the cozy atmosphere through the bar's familiar rhythms continuing in the background. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 88.7
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Gone South — Chapter Two: Where the River Keeps Going** New Orleans smells like somebody spilled a beer on a church and then lit a cigarette. It's nine in the morning and men in rubber boots are hosing off Bourbon Street, sin running pink into the gutters, and I'm standing on Rampart with eighty-four dollars and a dead phone, watching the taillights of the guy who drove me here merge into traffic without looking back. Can't blame him. I said Nashville. He said New Orleans was as far as he went. I said fine. Everything I've said in the last thirty hours has been some version of *fine*. The strap on my backpack slides off my shoulder. It's been doing that since Murfreesboro. I shove it back up. Everything I own is in this bag, and it won't even hold on to me. Two days ago Mom sat at the kitchen table and said, "You'll always be my little girl," and she said it like a eulogy. Like Taylor died and left her a body to bury. Dad went out to the garage and ran the table saw for an hour. Nothing got sawed. Maddie, who's nine and wiser than the whole house, slid a granola bar under my door at midnight without a word. I still have it. Can't eat it, can't throw it away. It's riding in my jacket pocket like a sacred object. Ms. Hargrove, the school counselor, told Mom I had "concerning behavioral patterns." Ha. Wait till she hears about this one. I'll be a whole case study. Anyway. Past-tense Taylor was an idiot. Present-tense Taylor is hungry, and that's the situation. I walk. Decatur Street, Jackson Square, tarot tables unfolding, palm fronds hissing, a brass band warming up somewhere — the whole city tuning up like it knows something's coming. My stomach is doing a solo of its own. "You lost, young blood?" He's got sneakers so clean they're practically a warning label. Gold tooth. Smile like a door opening onto a room with no floor. "A little," I say, because apparently I left my survival instincts in Tennessee too. "Everybody's a little lost here. That's why they come." He steps closer. "I know a spot. Got food, got couches. Kids your age all the time. You hungry?" I am so hungry that for one full second his mouth sounds like a good idea. That's the thing nobody tells you about being hungry — it talks. It says *sure, a stranger's couch, why not.* The strap slides off my shoulder again, and before I can catch it, a hand grabs my arm. "There you are!" A girl, maybe five feet of army jacket in ninety-degree heat, buzzed hair growing out, sunburn peeling on her nose. "Auntie been blowing up my phone about you, wandering off like that." She glares at the guy. "Marquis." "You know this ain't over, Dez," he says, but flat, like a vending machine that's run out of whatever it sells. "It's a little over." She steers me away fast, doesn't let go until we're two blocks down, and then she stops and looks at me properly. "Congratulations. You were forty-five seconds from being somebody's Tuesday revenue." "I was going to say no." "You were going to say *okay*. I watched your mouth getting ready." She sighs. "Rules. Rule one: nobody out here helps you for free, including me. I just helped you because Marquis is a roach and I hate him, so now you owe me a favor. Fair?" "Terrifyingly fair." "Rule two: you got money? Don't tell me. Don't tell anybody. Count it in a bathroom stall like a person with shame." She starts walking. "Rule three: cops ask your name, you give 'em a boring one and a boring story. Boring is invisible." "What do I go by?" she asks, casual, like it's nothing. Like it's weather. "Taylor." "Cool. Taylor." That's it. No third degree, no *but what's it short for*, no tilted head. Two syllables and I almost lose it right there on the sidewalk. *Do not cry in front of the locals.* I bite the inside of my cheek and say, "Cool," back, like my whole chest isn't ringing. Her name is Dez, she says. Nineteen, she says, though her sneakers are little-kid sized and I'd bet they came out of a church bin. On her wrist there's a paper hospital band, chewed to lace, most of the letters gone. All I can read is *—RE*. "What's the bracelet?" "Fashion." "It says St. Something." "That's the fashion." A cop on horseback clops past and Dez goes still, then walks different for a whole block — shoulders down, eyes ahead, invisible. I don't ask. She didn't ask me either. That's maybe rule four, unspoken: everybody out here is carrying a locked door, and you don't rattle the knobs. She takes me to a café on a corner where a woman the size of a hug says, "Dez! And who's this?" — except she calls her *Shanice*, and Dez answers to it smooth as syrup, doesn't even blink. "Miss Odette thinks my name is Shanice," she says after, handing me a paper bag of day-old beignets. Miss Odette called me *baby* twice, the way she'd call anybody baby, and I liked it more than I can say out loud. "Long story?" I ask. "It's not okay, but okay." We eat on the Moonwalk as the light goes bronze. The Mississippi is down there, huge and brown and indifferent, hauling everything toward the Gulf. Somewhere five hundred miles north, Mom has either called the police or hasn't, and I honestly don't know which would hurt worse. The strap slides off my shoulder one more time. Dez digs in her jacket and comes out with a zip tie — "never travel without zip ties and a lighter" — cinches the strap shorter, snugs it flat. "There," she says. "Now it'll quit trying to escape." "Thanks." "You owe me," she says, but soft, looking at the river. Tomorrow I'll figure out food, money, the rest of my life. Tonight the strap stays on my shoulder, Maddie's granola bar sits over my heart, and the city is loud enough to drown out Tennessee. That'll do. That'll do for one day.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional authenticity in portraying a transgender teen runaway's first day in New Orleans. The writing successfully captures Taylor's voice through a blend of vulnerability and defensive humor, with internal monologue that feels genuine rather than forced. The characterization is particularly strong. Taylor emerges as a complex protagonist - hurt but not self-pitying, naive but learning quickly, carrying both trauma and resilience. The backstory is woven in naturally through memory fragments rather than exposition dumps. Dez is equally well-developed, with her own mysterious background hinted at through details like the hospital bracelet and multiple names, creating intrigue without over-explaining. The dialogue feels authentic to the characters and setting. Dez's street-smart voice contrasts effectively with Taylor's more introspective narration, and the "rules" she provides serve both character development and world-building. The interaction with Marquis, though brief, establishes threat without melodrama. The prose style is confident and distinctive, mixing poetic imagery ("New Orleans smells like somebody spilled a beer on a church and then lit a cigarette") with grounded, conversational observations. The mixed tense approach works well, creating immediacy while allowing for reflection. Sensory details effectively establish the New Orleans setting without falling into cliché. The emotional complexity is handled with particular skill. Taylor's conflicted feelings about family, identity, and survival are layered throughout without becoming heavy-handed. The granola bar from sister Maddie serves as an effective symbolic anchor, representing both loss and love. The pacing moves naturally from disorientation through danger to tentative stability, following a believable arc for someone in Taylor's situation. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - not falsely optimistic but offering genuine hope earned through Taylor's resourcefulness and Dez's pragmatic kindness. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the prose occasionally reaches for effect ("sin running pink into the gutters") and the encounter with Marquis, while serving its purpose, feels somewhat predictable in its execution. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 76.8
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The end of the world had settled into a routine, which was more than could be said for Midas. He'd been named Midas in the optimism of his parents. The name delivered on everything but the material: everything he touched turned to trouble, which is like gold, only heavier and on fire. Morning inventory at home base — a collapsed branch library where books were valued by thickness and burnability — revealed one tin labelled MEAT-STYLE PRODUCT,* a jar of pickled onions of uncertain vintage, and enough acorn coffee to stun a horse. "We could eat the coffee," said Midas. "Have a break," said Chewy. Chewy was an animatronic koala from the before time: forty centimetres of synthetic fur and ancient circuitry, one glass eye, and the calm of a sage who has seen everything and been unimpressed by it. At random intervals he emitted slogans of the lost civilization. Midas had long ago decided this was oracular wisdom rather than a failing speech chip, because the alternative was admitting he took orders from a malfunctioning toy. "Good thinking," said Midas. "We'll break into the Galleria." The Meadowbrook Galleria stood two miles east, a cathedral of the ancients whose great signs — EVERYTHING MUST GO — had turned out, in hindsight, to be prophecy.** The mission was pet food. Like all Midas's plans, it was clever right up until it met Midas. Nobody looted pet food; survivors are a proud people, and pride, apparently, is not a nutrient. Dog food, Midas had reasoned, was nutritionally complete. So, in a way, was humility. They set off at dawn, Chewy riding in the rucksack with his head poking out like a furry periscope. "Taste the rainbow," said Chewy, as they crested the ridge. "Right you are," said Midas. The Galleria's parking lot belonged to the feral trolleys, who grazed on litter in herds and had long ago thrown off the tyranny of the coin.*** Midas gave them a wide berth, as one does with wildlife. Mostly. Inside, the mall was a temple. Dust hung in the light shafts like incense. Mannequins watched from the shopfronts with the smugness of a priesthood that has outlived its gods. Somewhere, water dripped with liturgical patience. The pet food aisle was intact: row upon row of tins — dog, cat, and something called ILLUSTRIOUS FERRET — gleaming like treasure. For perhaps the first time in his life, nothing went wrong. Midas filled the rucksack. He turned to go. That was when he saw the runt. It was a trolley with one squeaking wheel, standing apart from the herd and looking — as much as a wireframe cart can look — at Midas with devotion. It followed him out of the aisle. It followed him past the fountain. It followed him into the atrium, squeaking what could only be love songs. It was also, unfortunately, sacred. "The Chariots of the Checkout move only for the Coin," hissed a voice, and Midas turned to find himself ringed by the Congregation of the Final Markdown: robed figures in ceremonial hi-vis vests, their high priest brandishing a laminated sign reading NO REFUNDS. "You have no Coin. Yet the Chariot walks with you. Blasphemy!" "Now with twenty percent more," said Chewy, from the rucksack. "IT SPEAKS THE OLD TONGUE!" screamed the congregation, and fell down, and was briefly torn between worship and murder, and chose murder, as faiths do when caught off guard. What followed was less an escape than a structural survey conducted at speed. Midas ran. The floor, meeting Midas, did what floors did around Midas and gave way, dropping him through the food court ceiling into the ancient ball pit, which was mercifully soft and unmercifully inhabited by things he chose not to identify. The runt trolley leapt the gap after him, scattering cultists. Chewy, launched from the rucksack, sailed over the fountain crying "Fly the friendly skies!" and went down like the ancients' civilization: suddenly, and with a splash. There was no time to fish him out. Midas would feel guilty about that for years. Chewy, being a koala, would never mention it. Midas surfaced, spat out a ball, seized the trolley, and ran for the loading dock with the high priest bellowing that the Manager would hear of this. Out the doors, down the ramp, along the canal towpath, until the Galleria was a smudge on the horizon and his lungs had filed for resignation. The trolley trundled to a stop beside him and squeaked adoringly. "Don't look at me like that," Midas panted. "We're not keeping you." --- He got home in the late afternoon, by the road: wet, singed in a manner involving votive candles that would take too long to explain, one boot poorer, and the bearer of a religious vendetta. That was the first way home. The second way home was Chewy, who arrived an hour later through the storm drain, bobbing out of the canal outflow like a message from a civilization that had finally learned to swim. He had lost an ear and gained a great deal of fountain. His voice now played at half speed and an octave lower, like a demon reading a greetings card. "Beeecaaauuuse yoooou're wooorth iiiit," Chewy rumbled, by way of hello. "You too, buddy," said Midas, and meant it. The third way home arrived at dawn. Midas woke to a familiar squeaking and found the runt trolley outside the library, having followed them eleven miles in the dark, tins aboard — including, somehow, tins that had never been aboard at all. It had a dented dignity. It had clearly fought a raccoon and won. Midas looked at it a long time and sighed the sigh of a man adopting eleven miles of squeaky wheel. "You'd better come in," he said. "Bargain. That's your name now." Bargain squeaked. In the dark of the stacks, Chewy's eye glowed. "It keeps going," said Chewy slowly, "and going, and going..." And then, for the first time in two hundred years, he stopped. Midas sat bolt upright — but it was only the batteries. It was only ever the batteries. He found the last two at the bottom of the rucksack and pushed them in. There was a click, a whirr, and a small smell of ozone, which was Chewy clearing his throat. His eye lit up. His remaining ear twitched. "Where's the beef?" said Chewy. "On the doorstep," said Midas. "In a tin. And this time, buddy, we've got plenty." --- \* The ancients felt the need to put the word MEAT in inverted commas, which tells you everything about their honesty and, frankly, their meat. \*\* Scholars of the after time debate whether EVERYTHING MUST GO was a warning, a promise, or the last honest sentence anyone ever wrote. \*\*\* Zoologists of the after time classify the feral trolley as a pack animal with abandonment issues.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, successfully capturing his dry wit, footnote humor, and philosophical observations wrapped in absurdist scenarios. The author effectively creates a post-apocalyptic world where the mundane becomes sacred and the ridiculous becomes routine. The characterization is particularly well-executed. Midas is established as a hapless protagonist whose very name becomes a clever inversion - everything he touches turns to trouble rather than gold. This central conceit drives both plot and humor effectively. Chewy, the animatronic koala, serves as an excellent foil, dispensing corporate slogans that Midas interprets as wisdom, creating layers of irony that feel authentically Pratchettesque. The world-building is economical yet vivid. The collapsed library valued for "thickness and burnability," the feral shopping trolleys, and the Congregation of the Final Markdown all feel like natural extensions of Pratchett's satirical approach to human institutions. The footnotes particularly shine, offering the kind of wry observations about civilization that made Pratchett's work memorable. The plot structure adheres well to the prompt's requirements, beginning with deliberation, proceeding through inevitable complications, and returning the characters home "in multiple ways, worse for wear." The three-part return (Midas, then Chewy, then Bargain the trolley) is cleverly structured and emotionally satisfying. However, the piece occasionally strains for effect. Some metaphors feel forced ("dust hung in the light shafts like incense"), and certain passages become slightly overwrought in their attempt to maintain the Pratchett voice. The dialogue, while functional, lacks the sharp wit that characterizes the best of Pratchett's character interactions. The ending achieves genuine warmth without sacrificing the established tone, though the transformation of the group into a found family happens somewhat quickly. The emotional beats are earned through the shared adversity and Midas's genuine care for his companions, but could have been developed more gradually. The prose generally flows well, with strong sentence-level craft and effective pacing. The humor lands consistently, and the piece maintains reader engagement throughout. While not quite reaching the heights of its inspiration, it represents a solid pastiche that captures the essential spirit of Pratchett's work while telling its own coherent story. Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Model Output:
# Chapter Three: The Sign's a Liar The bell above the door jangled hard, and a man came through it backwards, hauling it shut behind him like he was bolting a hatch. "We're closed," Carys said, not looking up from the books she was pricing. "Your sign says open." "The sign's a liar." "Shut's perfect, actually. Shut's exactly what I need." He pressed his face to the window, breath fogging the glass. Two men with cameras were crossing the square at speed. "There they are. Followed me from the film set up the coast. I've been doing laps of the churchyard like a fox." Outside, the rain came sideways off the sea, the way it did on the Llŷn nine months of the year. He turned round and gave her the smile. She'd seen that smile before — on the side of a bus, above the word UNMISSABLE. "You don't mind if I—" "It's your puddle. It's my carpet." He looked down at the puddle, then up, delighted. "She bites," he informed the empty shop. "I like her already." He laughed at his own joke, too readily, like a man who'd learned young that laughing at things was charming. "I'm Rafe, by the way. Rafe Vaughan." Nothing. She kept pricing. "Rafe Vaughan," he said again, a shade louder. "The pirate," she said at last, squinting. "Off the lunchbox." "You've seen the films?" "My nephew's got the lunchbox. And the sword. The sword's a health hazard — Mam had to confiscate it." "I do other work. Serious work. *The Outcast* — I was nominated—" "Never saw it." "Four stars. The Times." "I read the backs of cereal packets." He flinched. Small, quickly smoothed — but she saw it, and something in her sat up and paid attention, the way you do when a big dog turns out to be frightened of thunder. "People like me," he said, and for once it wasn't a line. "I'm a likeable man. Ask anyone." "I'd have to find anyone. We're shut." "Lovely shop, though." He drifted along the shelves, touching spines like a man counting his own money. "Smells of—" "Damp." "History." "Damp." He stopped at the front table. Picked up a battered orange paperback — *A Swimmer's Coast: Coves and Currents of the Llŷn* — fifty years out of date and still the best there was. "You swim?" she said, before she could stop herself. "Every morning I can." And his voice changed — dropped the matinee warmth, went somewhere quieter. "Serpentine, mostly, when I'm in London. Did the Christmas Day race once. The Peter Pan Cup." "You did not." "Hand on heart. Water like being slapped by a bishop." "I do the one here. Christmas morning. Santa hat. Every year since I was nine." "You're one of those." "One of what?" "Cold-water lunatics." "The Morons, formally. Môr — sea. We're not clever, we just like it." He laughed then — a real one, head back, no audience in it — and she caught herself smiling at the poetry shelf and stopped. "How cold?" he asked. "Six degrees in June. You stop minding. Then you start needing it." "Six," he breathed, reverent as a prayer. "Thursdays, seven, slipway at Porthdinllaen, by the old herring sheds," she heard herself say. "Bring a bobble hat. You lose most heat from your head, and you've not got much to spare. There's tea after, from a flask. Sometimes cake." "Cake," he repeated, hand to heart. "Is that an invitation?" "It's an instruction." "I look devastating in a bobble hat." "You'll look like everyone else." He paused at that. "That," he said, "is the appeal." "Can I buy this?" "Four fifty." He produced a twenty and told her to keep the change. She counted his change into his palm, coin by coin — starting twice, because the first time she made it sixteen — because they were not a charity, and their fingers did not touch at all, which both of them managed with visible effort. "You know," he said, pocketing it, "you're the first person in a decade who's wanted me somewhere for reasons entirely unconnected to—" he waved a hand at his own face. "We want you for your tolerance of cold water. Nothing else." "That's genuinely the nicest thing anyone's said to me all year," he said, and the terrible thing was that he meant it. She checked the window for him. "They've gone up towards the castle. You can slip out the front now." He didn't move. "You honestly didn't know me. Before the lunchbox." "I don't get to the pictures much." "That's refreshing," he said, in the voice of a man receiving refreshing news at a funeral. "The pirate one had decent waves in, mind. My dad watched it every Christmas till he died." He went very still. "Did he like it?" "Twice, some years." He looked, for a second, like she'd handed him a trophy. She looked away first and busied herself with a till roll that needed no busying. "Why d'you swim?" he asked. "Properly — why you." "Head goes quiet. Everything does. Just the cold and the breathing." "Yes," he said. "That. Exactly that." Then she watched the charm come back online like a lighthouse — watched him aim it — "You've got — there's dust, on your—" he gestured vaguely at her face — "nowhere. Sorry. I don't know what that was. That was nothing." "Right," she said. "Right." "Thursday, then. Seven. Slipway." "Bobble hat." "Bobble hat." He got the door open, bell jangling. "Carys." She'd never told him her name. He tipped his chin at the card propped on the till. "Practising," he said. "For Thursday." And then, God help her, with the bell still ringing: "Don't be late, bach." The door shut. Through the window she watched him cross the square, checking twice — she counted — back at the shop. The cat, Dylan, stared at her from the window seat with open judgment. "Don't," she said. Then she went back to her shelving and found she'd filed Dylan Thomas under Gardening, and she left him there a good half-hour, because a woman with hot ears is allowed one small thing.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested romantic tension and character dynamics. The author successfully creates two distinct voices - Rafe's performative charm masking insecurity, and Carys's dry, deflating wit that conceals her own attraction. The dialogue crackles with authentic Welsh sensibility, particularly in Carys's economical responses and the natural use of "bach" at the end. The setting feels genuinely Welsh rather than generically British, with specific details like the Llŷn Peninsula, Porthdinllaen, and the sideways rain off the sea. The bookstore setting is well-utilized, with books serving as both props and metaphors for the characters' relationship to stories and performance. The character work is particularly strong. Rafe's fragile ego is shown through small moments - his flinch when dismissed, his repeated attempts to get recognition, his genuine pleasure at being wanted for something other than fame. Carys's immunity to his charm is believable because it's not complete immunity - she catches herself smiling, stumbles over making change, and ultimately extends the swimming invitation. The swimming motif works well as both a literal connection point and a metaphor for stripping away pretense. The cold water represents the kind of authentic experience Rafe craves, where "you look like everyone else." This feels earned rather than forced. The prose is generally elegant with some particularly nice turns of phrase ("laughing at things was charming," "the way you do when a big dog turns out to be frightened of thunder"). The pacing moves well between banter and more vulnerable moments. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the metaphors feel slightly overworked, and the ending, while charming, edges toward being a bit too neat. The Dylan Thomas filing mistake is cute but perhaps pushes the whimsy slightly too far. The piece successfully fulfills the prompt requirements while creating genuine chemistry and emotional complexity. Both characters feel real and their attraction develops naturally through their interaction rather than being simply stated. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 86.8
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door gave with a sigh of salt-swollen wood, and the underhold breathed cold up the stair to meet them — old brine, spermaceti, and beneath both something coppery, like a coin held under the tongue too long. Aya descended first, hem gathered, slippers finding each step by memory. The underhold had been raised inside the ribcage of the Old Bull, the leviathan whose bones formed the guildhall's rafters; down here the ribs arched overhead like the nave of a drowned cathedral, strung with spermaceti lamps. Every lamp was lit. "Someone's been at the wicks," Simeon whispered. In his waistcoat, his pocket watch ticked on, absurdly loud, marking each second like a heart shut in a casket. At the far end, upon a plinth of whale vertebrae, stood the reliquary: black iron, and across its face a lattice of silver script drawn fine as spider silk. Aya knew that hand. She had traced those characters as a child, fingertip following her mother's ink across vellum — before the ink, the vellum, and the woman were all carted to the gallows yard at Wrenfield Cross. *Mother*, she thought, *what did you seal for these people?* "You're late, little gulls." A match flared to the left of the plinth. Lamplight found a whalebone chair, and in it — comfortable as a widow at a funeral — sat Mother Morska, carving scrimshaw with a flensing knife, as though the morning's arrest were a rumour she'd heard third-hand. Behind her, two shapes. The big one, Cull, was winding the mainspring of a clockwork bolt-thrower, harpoon-darts gleaming in a chest-rack. The lean one, a grey woman called Grieve, lifted a scripture-lamp. Its light was thin and white and somehow *singing*, and Aya felt the immateria recoil behind the world — whimpering, shut out like a dog in the rain. Katra's knife was half-drawn before Aya's hand closed on her wrist. "Don't," Aya breathed. "Not for this." "Smart girl," said Morska. "Cull, dear — mind the floor. It's only just been scrubbed." There was no fight in it. There was nothing to fight with. Cull took Katra's blades away with hands like dock-cranes; Grieve bound their wrists with tarred cord, humming a hymn through her teeth. "Eleven-turn mainspring on that thrower," Simeon muttered, watching Cull work. "Overwound. It'll jam by the third dart." Cull paused, frowning at the weapon. Grieve cuffed Simeon's ear. Morska rose — joints cracking like ship's timbers — crossed the floor, and hooked one blubber-oil thumb beneath the edge of Aya's mask. She peeled it away with the tenderness of a woman skinning a rabbit. Lamplight fell on Aya's bare face. "Well," said Morska, and showed brown teeth. "Bless the Deep. Harbourmaster Hallowell's girl." The silence that followed had a texture. It settled on Aya's skin like ash. *They hanged my mother at Wrenfield Cross*, she thought, with a strange, floating calm. *They sold tickets. The broadsheets called her the Widow of Wharf Lane for a week, then forgot her. Now her daughter will hang beside her on the same cheap wood.* "Someone say something," Simeon whispered. Then, faintly, to no one: "Forty-one seconds. We've been down here forty-one seconds." "You know what the Office does to witches' get, girl?" Morska said, tapping the flensing knife against her palm. "They don't hang you quick, like your mother. They *examine* you first. Very thorough gentlemen. Very patient." "Then we're agreed on the stakes," said Aya, quietly proud that her voice did not shake. "Which is why you'll hear my offer before Grieve trusses us for the brine rooms." Morska's eyebrows climbed. "An *offer*. From the hostage." "From the asset. A corpse buys you nothing, Mother Morska. Alive, I am worth a fortune in paper. My father is Harbourmaster. Every manifest, every customs seal, every patrol chart in this harbour crosses his desk. Blind eyes at the water-gates. Patrol schedules written a week in advance. Dead, I'm worth a public holiday and a bonfire." "Witches fetch a fine price too. The Inquisitors pay by the ounce." "They pay — and then they *stay*." Aya stepped forward, cord biting her wrists. "The Office of Thaumaturgic Affairs does not leave a quarter clean. Hang me, and they'll put the whole Rookery to the torch tracing where I learned my craft. Your ledgers. Your vats. Your tame sergeants, dredged up like offal. I am worth a great deal more to you unexamined." Silence, but for the watch. Tick. Tick. Tick. "And there is the small matter of the case behind you," Aya went on, softer now. "Twelve years under your roof, and never once opened. Because those wards don't answer brass, or oil, or steel. They answer blood and script. My mother drew them. I traced them before I could write my own name. I can open that case — and Grieve's pretty lamp cannot, and Cull's darts cannot. Kill me, and you'll grow old squinting at silver scribbles." "Aya," Katra said, low and rough. "Don't give the bilge-hag anything." "Mind your tongue," said Morska, without looking at her, "or Cull will mind it for you." She turned the scrimshaw over in her fingers. "You know there was no raid, little gull. Or rather — I was the bait in it. I let the constables take me, to see which of my birds would come pecking at the case the moment my back was turned." She smiled. "The tide was generous. It brought me three." "Then it brought you three of use," said Aya. "The tide keeps what the tide keeps — isn't that your proverb? Keep us." For a long moment Morska studied her the way a flenser studies a carcass, deciding where the first cut goes. "Brine rooms," she said at last. "All three. Let them think on the smell of preserved failure." She leaned close, breath of ambergris and rot. "Tomorrow, rested and fed, you'll open that case for me, Harbourmaster's girl. And if the relic bites you —" she shrugged — "well. That saves me the price of rope." They were marched toward the dark, Grieve's hymn rising behind them. And as Aya passed the reliquary, the thing within it — that curved black crescent, half scythe and half tooth — gave out one low hum, like something vast turning over in its sleep. For a moment, it kept time with Simeon's watch. Tick for hum. Hum for tick. As though somewhere far beneath the world, something had begun, patiently, to count along.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional craft in worldbuilding and atmospheric writing. The author successfully creates a vivid "whalepunk" setting with the underhold built within a leviathan's ribcage, establishing an immediately immersive and unique environment. The Victorian gothic aesthetic is well-executed through both dialogue ("Bless the Deep," "little gulls") and imagery (spermaceti lamps, flensing knives, scripture-lamps). The adherence to instructions is nearly flawless - all story beats are hit organically, the confrontation unfolds as requested without devolving into action, and the word count appears appropriate. The characterization is particularly strong, with each character having a distinct voice: Aya's aristocratic intelligence, Simeon's mechanical obsessions and nervous time-counting, Katra's rough loyalty, and Morska's calculating menace. The dialogue feels authentic to the world and characters, avoiding modern speech patterns while remaining accessible. Morska's revelation that she orchestrated her own "arrest" as a trap is a clever twist that adds layers to her character. Aya's negotiation strategy - leveraging her value as both political hostage and magical key - demonstrates her intelligence and desperation convincingly. The prose strikes an excellent balance between rich description and narrative momentum. Phrases like "silence that followed had a texture" and the description of the scripture-lamp's light as "singing" create atmosphere without becoming overwrought. The mechanical details (eleven-turn mainspring, clockwork bolt-thrower) effectively reinforce the steampunk elements. The ending maintains appropriate tension while setting up future developments. The synchronization between Simeon's watch and the artifact's humming creates an ominous note that suggests larger forces at work. However, some metaphors occasionally border on purple prose ("like a heart shut in a casket"), though they generally serve the gothic atmosphere well. The emotional complexity is well-handled, particularly Aya's internal struggle with her inevitable exposure and the weight of her mother's legacy. The piece successfully balances multiple character perspectives and motivations without losing focus.
