+ Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gunpowder Rendezvous The Yellow Flag smells like mildew, gun oil, and decisions nobody survives on purpose. Rain hammers Roanapur sideways. Spike Spiegel makes his last whiskey last, because his last woolong bought it and his stomach has been filing complaints since Tuesday. Three stools down, a woman drinks Bacardi straight from the bottle. Dragon tattoo coiled down her right arm. Shoulder rig. Two pistol grips worn shiny in the shape of her hands. She watches him in the mirror behind the bottles. He watches her back, because the mirror is the polite way. "The fuck are you looking at?" she says. "In this town, staring gets people buried." "You've counted the exits twice," Spike says. "In this town, that means you're working." Her mouth twitches — not quite a smile. She takes the stool beside him, lifts his lighter off the bar, and flicks it. A ring of rust blooms around the base, orange as an old wound. "Your lighter's been swimming." "Twice. Maybe three. I lose count." "Sloppy." "Lucky." He leans into her flame. "Water's softer than bullets. I drowned once. Didn't take." Something moves behind her eyes. Interest — the dangerous kind. "You're one of those guys who thinks he's already dead." "Knows it. It just hasn't caught up with me yet." She laughs, low and sandpapered, and refills his glass without asking, which in Roanapur is practically a proposal. "Revy." "Spike." "What are you, Spike? Bounty hunter? Mercenary?" "Bounty hunter. You?" "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." He nods like that's the sanest thing anyone's said all week. She slides a photo onto the bar. Thin man, bad skin, a ledger-shaped bulge under his jacket. "Aldous Wren. Lifted something off the Triad and ran. My client wants the book back and the thief in a dumpster." "My client wants him breathing. Eight million woolong. Alive only." Revy whistles. "That's a problem." "For one of us." They smile at the same time. It is not a nice smile, and they share it anyway, like a lit fuse. Behind the bar, Bao starts quietly moving the good bottles off the back shelf. Then the back booth unloads. Wren sees two professionals look at him at once and does the worst thing available: he runs. "So it's like that," Revy says, already moving. "It's usually like that." The alley is rain and neon. Two bodyguards wait at its mouth, and Revy solves them the way she solves everything — both Cutlasses out, muzzle flash strobing the puddles, a laugh in it that Spike files away under *don't*. The third man rushes him, and Spike is water finding the low ground: a heel, an elbow, the Jericho speaking once, politely. Then they're running side by side, and then not side by side, because a bounty is a bounty. He takes the fire escape because it's there. She takes the stairs because she isn't afraid of anything, including gravity. The Sunrise Motel rents rooms by the hour and asks no questions, which is its only amenity. Revy kicks in the door of Room 9, both guns up, and finds Aldous Wren taped to a chair — and Spike Spiegel sitting on the bed eating minibar peanuts, because he hasn't eaten since Tuesday and eight million woolong doesn't feed anyone in advance. "Took you long enough," he says. "The clerk wanted a bribe. I gave him a warning." She aims at his center mass, casual as weather. "Here's the thing. A dead man's lighter to carry than a live one, and my client doesn't do refunds." "Alive is the whole job for me." "Then we've got a conflict of interest." "We've had one since the bar. I was hoping you'd drink enough to reconsider." She crosses the room like she's daring him to be stupid and puts her barrel under his jaw. He raises the Jericho without hurry — muzzle against her ribs — and neither of them blinks. This is the closest either has been to another person in months, not counting the ones trying to kill them. Her breath is Bacardi and cordite. His is cheap tobacco and patience. The dragon on her arm watches him too. "You're not going to shoot me," Spike says. "You'd have done it in the alley. Cleaner." "You're not shooting me either. You had the window, the door, and the peanuts. You waited." "I'm hungry, not rude." "Your eyes don't track together." "One's a souvenir. It remembers things the other would rather forget." Something crosses her face then — quick, gone — the look of someone who can't remember the last time anybody stood this close without flinching. It makes her angry, which makes her press the muzzle closer, which isn't what either of them means by it. The standoff has stopped being about the bounty. Neither of them mentions it. Somewhere off the bay, thunder rolls in, and neither of them hears it. That's when Wren, who has spent ten minutes working one hand free, gets a derringer out of his boot. Neither of them looks at him. Two shots, so close together they're one sound. Wren goes over sideways, chair and all. The derringer clatters under the TV. A long beat. "There goes eight million woolong," Spike says. "My client pays for the ledger, not the corpse." She crouches, goes through the dead man's jacket, comes up with a fat, water-stained book. "I'm still rich." "Whatever happens, happens." "Don't quote fortune cookies at me, you lanky bastard." She stands. Neither of them has holstered. In Roanapur, that's what trust looks like — a gun still in hand, held by someone who's decided twice now not to use it. "There's a place downstairs," she says. "Does eggs at dawn. You look like you haven't eaten in a week." "Since Tuesday." She snorts, lights a cigarette off his lighter — the rusted one, still sparking, still working — and drops it into her pocket. "Hey. That's mine." "Come get it." She walks out and leaves the door open. Spike looks at the dead man, at the empty peanut packet, at the rain. Then he follows, gun loose in his hand, into the gray edge of morning — because whatever happens, happens, and because she still has his lighter, and a man doesn't let a thing like that go.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and character understanding. The author captures both Spike and Revy's voices authentically - Spike's fatalistic philosophy and laid-back demeanor contrasts effectively with Revy's aggressive, profane directness. The dialogue feels natural and character-appropriate, with memorable exchanges that reveal personality through subtext rather than exposition. The prose style is notably strong, employing a noir-influenced voice that suits both source materials. Descriptions are economical but evocative - "The Yellow Flag smells like mildew, gun oil, and decisions nobody survives on purpose" immediately establishes atmosphere. The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining literary quality through precise word choice and rhythm. The plot structure works well, moving from the bar meeting through the chase to the motel standoff as requested. The sexual tension builds naturally through proximity and shared danger rather than forced romantic beats. The standoff scene effectively captures the requested unresolved tension - two professionals who recognize something in each other but remain guarded. Character actions feel believable throughout. Spike's patience and Revy's aggression align with their established personalities, and their mutual recognition of professional competence rings true. The moment where neither shoots the other works because it's earned through their earlier interactions. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - not overly positive but suggesting possibility. Revy taking the lighter and Spike following maintains the tension while providing forward momentum. The resolution of the bounty situation (both clients satisfied through Wren's death) is clever and avoids forced conflict. Some minor weaknesses include occasional reliance on familiar noir tropes and a few moments where the prose becomes slightly self-conscious in its stylishness. The pacing occasionally slows during descriptive passages, though not severely. The piece could have pushed the emotional complexity slightly deeper, particularly regarding both characters' trust issues. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 86.6
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Útiseta I was fifteen the autumn my father's employer transferred him north, and I spent the first month in the village hating everything: the pulp-mill smell that got into your hair, the way my classmates said *Stockholm* like a diagnosis, the dark that came down by four in the afternoon. Then Astrid sat down beside me on the school bus and asked whether I wanted to know what our teacher kept locked in her desk drawer. I did. That was the trouble. Her grandmother, Astrid said, had been a *klok gumma*, a wise woman; people came to her from three parishes away, and what she knew had come down from her own mother, and hers, back past the church, past the records. Before she died she taught Astrid things. Not superstitions, Astrid said, with the flat certainty of someone quoting scripture—methods. That autumn she showed me a few. A mirror game for seeing your future. A way of writing a boy's name that made him notice you inside nine days. I told myself it was nonsense even as it kept working, in small ways, like a watch you don't trust that keeps being right. In October she said we were ready for útiseta. Sitting out. She said the old word like she'd been born with it in her mouth. She issued instructions across one week, matter-of-fact as homework. Wear wool, only wool. Nothing with iron in it—no zips, no keys, nothing with a motor, so my Walkman stayed home. Nothing that had ever been blessed. Fast from sundown; if I had to eat, salt fish and cold water. And don't tell anyone your name that night. "Not even you?" "Especially not me." She would bring the offering. Her father's flask. We went on a Friday; my parents believed we were watching videos at her place. Her moped carried us as far as the crossroads below Nygårds, and from there everything with a motor or a blessing stayed behind. We walked the last kilometre past the chapel and into the clear-cut, where the pines gave out and the stars got suddenly enormous. Wind moved through the trees behind us, a long rush that sounded almost like whispering, the way a crowd murmurs outside a church door. Astrid didn't look back, so I didn't either. We reached the mound a little before midnight. It stood at the edge of the cut like a green whale beached among the stumps—Kungshögen, the King's Mound. Astrid said there was a man under it, a chief or something older, and that he had been sitting there a very long time, and that he was not patient. She laid her grandmother's sheepskin on the top, smelling of lanolin and smoke. We walked three times around the mound with the sun, though there was no sun, only frost and stars. Then she poured brännvin on the grass—"for him"—rapped three times on the frozen ground with her knuckles, and said: "Vakna. We sit. We don't sleep." Her grandmother's version, she told me later, had been longer; she'd forgotten the middle and didn't suppose it mattered. She was sixteen. She thought it was a game with better rules than the others. The rules were these: ask plainly, don't lie, don't laugh, don't say thank you. If you hear your name, don't answer. The first hour was only cold. My feet went numb; the flask went round once, which Astrid said wasn't breaking a rule, only manners. She asked her questions—about a boy called Stefan, about whether she would ever get out of the village—then cocked her head at the wind and said, "There. Did you hear that?" I heard pine needles, frost settling, my own pulse. I said so, and she smiled like I was the one going deaf. Then I noticed the warmth. The grass around the sheepskin was rimed white, but beneath me the ground was warm as a stomach, and I could feel it, very faintly, rising and falling. I decided it was decomposition. I said so out loud, to make her laugh. She didn't. I asked mine then. My grandmother in Stockholm had been sick since spring; I asked—plainly, as instructed—whether she would get better. The wind stopped. Not died down; stopped, mid-rush, the way a tape stops. The silence had a pressure to it, like a held breath, and into it something said one word. I didn't hear it with my ears. It arrived the way you know your own name in the dark. *Soon.* The wind was still stopped when Astrid gripped my wrist. Her face had gone the grey of the frost. "It's saying my name," she whispered. "It's been saying it all night, under the wind. Did you tell it yours?" I hadn't. She stood, dragging the sheepskin. "We go. Walk. Don't run, don't look back, don't speak till the stream." We walked. Behind us the whispering started up again in the pines, keeping pace, politely, like someone seeing you out. It followed us the length of the clear-cut, past the chapel, down towards the water, and I felt it wanting me to turn—I wanted to turn, the way you want to worry a loose tooth—and I understood that Astrid had never once looked back on any of our walks. She had known something all along and called it a game anyway. At the stream we crossed on the plank bridge, and the sound stopped at the water like a door closing. "Grandmother would have whipped me," Astrid said on the far bank. It was the first thing either of us had said. "She told me these weren't games. The dead don't play. You can borrow from them—" she looked at the black water "—but they keep the interest." My grandmother died in February. She had been sick for two years; the doctors had said months. I have done the arithmetic many times since—cold makes warmth, fear makes voices, two girls breathing hard in the dark can hear anything at all—and the arithmetic is good. But I never told Astrid that after the sound stopped at the water, in the silence on the far bank, I heard one word more, and that it was my name. I have never said thank you since, not once, not to anyone, in thirty years. And on autumn nights, when the wind moves through the pines and sounds almost like whispering, I catch myself listening for it again. I never answer.

The author successfully captures the voice of an adult Linnea reflecting on teenage events, maintaining the requested transparency of the framing device while allowing subtle hints of present-day perspective to enhance the narrative's weight. The characterization is particularly effective. Astrid emerges as a compelling figure—confident in her inherited knowledge yet dangerously naive about its implications. Her matter-of-fact delivery of ritual instructions feels authentic to both teenage rebellion and genuine folk tradition. Linnea's voice convincingly captures adolescent psychology: the desire to belong, skepticism warring with curiosity, and the retrospective understanding of having crossed dangerous lines. The prose quality is consistently high, with elegant turns of phrase like "stars got suddenly enormous" and "a green whale beached among the stumps." The author demonstrates restraint, avoiding overwrought descriptions while maintaining atmospheric tension. The pacing builds effectively from mundane preparation through mounting unease to genuine terror. The ambiguity between supernatural and psychological explanations is expertly maintained. The warming ground could be decomposition, the voices could be wind and imagination, yet the specificity of details—the wind stopping mid-rush, the precise timing of the grandmother's death—creates genuine uncertainty. This ambiguity serves the folk horror genre perfectly. The cultural elements feel researched and authentic rather than appropriative. The Swedish setting is established through specific details (pulp-mill smell, *klok gumma*, brännvin) without becoming a tourist brochure. The ritual elements blend believable folk practice with teenage improvisation. The ending is particularly strong, with Linnea's thirty-year refusal to say "thank you" providing a haunting coda that suggests lasting psychological impact regardless of supernatural reality. This detail transforms what could have been a simple scary story into something more psychologically complex. Minor weaknesses include some exposition that edges toward telling rather than showing, particularly in establishing the Stockholm-to-village transition. The dialogue, while functional, occasionally lacks the distinct voice that might further differentiate the characters. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 90.0
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Therapeutic Boundaries The sessions are mandatory—my settlement says so, as if attendance could prove I want this body back. So on Thursdays I lie prone on the plinth with my right ankle propped on a rolled towel, and Mara wheels her stool to the foot of the table and takes my heel in one hand the way you'd hold a bird. Her sleeves are the old ones. Teal and violet, the splatter print from the year we both made the final in Eugene, Lycra gone soft at the cuffs. She wears them like the flag of a country that no longer exists, and I can't decide whether that's tact or cruelty. Twenty-two weeks ago my Achilles let go two steps out of the blocks. A sound like a cap gun, a kick to the back of the leg from nobody. I finished the thought I was mid-sprint on—dinner, absurdly—and looked down to find the leg already someone else's. She retired whole, on a quiet Tuesday, walked out of the sport on her own feet and into a classroom, and came back with Latin names for everything we used to do stupidly to ourselves. I came back with a scar and a calf two sizes wrong. She's still built the way she ran: everything forward, nothing wasted. "Breathe, Voss," she says. Surname, six weeks running. It's armor. We both wear it. She lets my foot fall into plantarflexion to slack the tendon, then pinches the repaired cord between thumb and two fingers and rolls it side to side over the heel bone. It's meant to glide like rope through a block. Mine drags. When she finds an adhesion she leans her weight in and holds, and the pain climbs a register, and my whole leg kicks off the towel. She absorbs it without comment, one hand riding my shin until it settles. My toes curl without asking me. Goosebumps sweep up the calf under her fingers; she pretends not to notice, which is its own kind of noticing. Her thumb rests on the worst adhesion a beat too long—not working, just resting—then she's clinical again. My tissue has no pride. It stopped guarding against her hands years ago, back when we traded partner stretches on the warm-up track and argued about music. Then the wall. Two steps from the plinth, I stand facing it, palms flat at shoulder height, right foot flat, left leg staggered behind. She kneels at my right side—left hand cupping my heel so the movement can't cheat through the arch, right hand just below the kneecap—and rocks my shin toward the baseboard. The tape on the floor says my toes are seven centimeters out. The left foot does eleven without trying. "We'll take a centimeter a month," she says. I used to measure my life in hundredths of a second. Now it's centimeters and weeks, and I hate her plurals—*we*—as if it drafts me onto a team I never chose. She hunts the edge of the pain like a distance runner hunts a pace: right up against it, never through it. At the ceiling of the stretch she asks for a number out of ten, as if I've ever reported honestly in my life. "Six," I say, which means eight. She knows it means eight. Her face, tilted up at mine from the floor, is still water. The stillness is the tell. Then the step. Forefeet on the edge, heels hanging in space. Both feet up onto the toes, weight across to the right, left foot clear, and lower—three seconds down, heel dropping below the platform. "Eccentrics," she says. "The tendon rebuilds on the lengthening." Fifteen with the knee straight, fifteen bent—gastrocnemius, then soleus—naming the debt as if naming makes it fair. She stands behind me, hands hovering an inch off my hips, spotting me like a barbell. At rep eleven my calf starts to judder, a tremor I can feel in my teeth, and her fingers finally land—four points of contact on my hip bones, steady, impersonal, nothing impersonal about them at all. She counts the last four reps in the cadence she used to call my splits from the 200. Some metronomes live in a person. When I step down, her hands lift away a half-second later than spotting requires. Neither of us mentions it. We finish on the mat. Right knee down, left foot forward, and she kneels behind my right hip, palm flat on my sacrum. "Tail under," she says, pressing down and forward while her other hand rests light against my sternum, lifting. Months of limping wound me forward like a clock; now the hip flexor opens like a drawer painted shut. Her knuckles press my spine through her palm. Her breath is at my shoulder. In the far mirror I can see us both pretending, and I watch her eyes drop to my back, catch themselves, come back up. There's a moment—there's always a moment—when the stretch reaches its end and she holds me there, and pain and something else crest together, and I make a sound I can't file under either. Her thumb moves on my sacrum. A millimeter, maybe less. Neither of us breathes. Then she eases me out with the punctuality of a train conductor. "Good," she says. "That's the end feel we want." Only Mara could hand me a word like that and expect it not to be a metaphor. She writes *7 cm* and *3×15* in my chart and pulls her sleeves down over her knuckles—a tell I've catalogued. "Same time Thursday, Eli—" and stops, and it's "Voss" again before the name can land. "We'll get you running." Running. They keep promising my body back in installments—first walking, then jogging—as if the 400 were a jog. I don't want to be good at rehab. I was good at something else. But in a drawer in my apartment I have the matching pair of sleeves, same splatter print, unworn since Eugene. Tonight I'll dig them out, or I'll burn them. I haven't decided which one counts as recovery.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional craft in nearly every aspect. The narrative successfully fulfills the complex prompt requirements, delivering a first-person account of a former athlete in mandatory physical therapy with a former training partner who became their physiotherapist. The sexual tension is palpable yet tastefully handled, never crossing into gratuitous territory. The anatomical precision is remarkable - every therapeutic technique is described with clinical accuracy while maintaining narrative flow. The wall stretch with specific measurements, the eccentric heel drops with proper muscle group identification (gastrocnemius vs. soleus), and the hip flexor stretch are all technically sound and spatially coherent. The author clearly understands both athletic training and physical therapy protocols. The prose style is sophisticated and controlled, employing athletic metaphors that feel organic rather than forced. Phrases like "pain and something else crest together" and "she hunts the edge of the pain like a distance runner hunts a pace" demonstrate elegant integration of the protagonist's athletic background into their current reality. The voice remains consistently bitter yet vulnerable throughout. Character development is nuanced - both protagonists maintain professional boundaries while their shared history creates inevitable tension. The detail of matching team sleeves serves as a powerful symbol of their divergent paths. Mara's clinical professionalism with subtle lapses (the thumb movement, hands lingering) feels authentic, as does Eli's resistance to recovery. The sensory details are vivid without being overwrought. The description of the Achilles rupture ("a sound like a cap gun") and the physical sensations during therapy create an immersive experience. The emotional complexity - resentment toward recovery, attraction complicated by professional boundaries, grief for lost identity - is handled with sophistication. The ending avoids false positivity while suggesting potential movement forward through the metaphor of the matching sleeves. This feels earned rather than artificially hopeful. The piece maintains tension throughout without resolution, which suits the subject matter. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose borders on being slightly precious, though it never fully crosses into purple territory. The piece could have benefited from slightly more direct dialogue to break up the internal monologue, though the existing dialogue serves its purpose effectively. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Coffin Wood *Canton, January 1839* The cough woke me before the factory bell, as it had every morning for a month, and it left its coin on my tongue — copper, always copper, as though I'd been sucking a farthing in my sleep. Loxley, the captain's clerk, came up the loft ladder at half past seven with the day's orders folded in his clean hands. "Survey of the gun-room stores at Whampoa by the noon gun, sir. The captain's particular about it." "Tell him the wind's against me." I coughed again, longer, and had to take hold of the bedpost. "That's an ugly chest, sir." "Sea air. It gets into a man this season." I found a worn Carolus — good King Carlos's face rubbed to a ghost — and folded it into his palm. "Say I took the morning tide downriver and the wind delayed me." "He'll want it in writing, sir." "Then write it. You've a fair hand." "It fails you regular, sir," he said, and pocketed the dollar along with whatever he'd been about to think. Through the shutter slats the factory flags hung slack in the damp — England's, the Dutch, the Swede's, the American's stripes gone grey with soot. Ah-Po's sampan waited at the factory steps. It was January, the trading season, the river loud with shipping, the dawn sky the colour of a fish's belly. The water smelled of fish sauce, wet hemp, tar, and the forty thousand souls who used it as a drain; duck feathers stuck to oars, gunwales, and my sleeve like a snowfall gone wrong. Temple gongs knocked somewhere in the fog. Pigs complained under hatches. "Where today, Red-hair?" said Ah-Po, ninety years old and waterproof. "Coffin Street, Grandmother." "Other officer man go Whampoa, count rope, count cannonball." She spat over the side. "You thin. Wind blow, you fly away — no need coffin." I coughed into my fist. Copper. "Husband cough like that," she said, working the scull. "Now husband burn paper money." "Sea air." She laughed until the boat rocked. "This river, foolish fanqui. Not sea." The coffin-maker's lane off Junk Street smelled of camphor and fresh pine shavings — the sweetest smell in Canton, which tells you something about Canton. Coffins stood stacked to the rafters like tea chests. At the back, behind his scales, sat Ah-Sum. "Patna gone up," he said before I'd shut the door. "Four dollar, one tael." "It was three at Christmas." "Christmas long time ago. Soldiers burn den in Namhoi last week. Mandarin take two head at execution ground Tuesday — dealer head. Trouble coming down from Pekin, people say. New commissioner, very fierce." His abacus ran, beads clicking like insect feet. "You want how much?" "Two dollars and a fistful of cash." "Then you get half tael." He watched my hands on the counter, doing their small weather. "Unless." "Unless what?" "You do Dalgleish job, Thursday. Then maybe I trust you Friday. Dollar he give you Thursday, you pay me Friday — same dollar come back to me twice already. Dollar go round and round." He weighed me with the same eye he weighed opium. "Only you go down. Every day now, Lieutenant. Last month, two time one week. Long time you smoke pipe. Now pipe smoke you." "Half tael now, the rest Friday. And I keep the dirk." "Dirk stay here. Good knife. Somebody buy." He was right. The telescope had gone in October, my father's watch in November. The dirk would see me to the end of January. Dalgleish waited in the Follies, on the Danes' garden walk above the water, red-faced beneath a drizzle that never quite committed to rain. Camellias stood in the wet like lit candles. "Merrick," he said. "You've the colour of a man they've fished out for the inquest." "It's a poor morning to be out." "It's a fine morning to be useful, and useful pays." He dropped his voice. "Thursday. Tide serves at dusk. The Hoppo's cruisers will sweep the reach above the Bocca — on your cutter's own times, mind, which you sold me fair, and I'll not insult you by pretending otherwise. I've a fast crab coming up on the ebb, forty chests. I need a King's coat at the customs station, hailing their boat about a passport irregularity. Official. Slow. Very English. Ten minutes, and my crab crosses behind them." "You want me to be the irregularity." "I want you to be magnificent. You were, once — I've seen your name in the dispatches. Eight dollars, and a ball of Patna on account." "Twelve, and the Patna." "Eight, or I ask Mr. Kier, who'll do it for six and a bottle of Hollands." He said it gently, the way Ah-Sum prices coffins. "Besides, your hands could ring the factory bell." The cough took me then, deep, and I tasted the coin again. "That chest sounds like a ship's pumps." "Sea air." "Aye," he said, mild as milk. "That'll be why it's worst when you're ashore. They say Pekin means it this time, by the way." "They always mean it." "Not like this. A mandarin who can't be bought is an inconvenience to the whole trade. Yours included." The boy Soy brought the lamp at noon: a squat brass sun with a wick like a tongue. He knelt to trim it with a pin, unhurried, a priest with one god and one worshipper. The couch was rattan, the walls papered, the pipe older than my commission. Ah-Sum cooked the pill over the flame — chandu, black and glossy as a beetle's back — and the smell rose off it, burnt sugar and scorched roses, and my whole body swung toward it like a compass needle finding north. "Feed him quick," Ah-Sum told the boy. "Dragon hungry today." Somewhere downriver they'd be striking eight bells over the stores I was meant to be surveying. The first draw went down soft. The cough came up with the smoke, and the copper came with the cough. "Sea air," I told the lamp. Nobody had asked. It gets into a man.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric writing, successfully creating an immersive portrait of a British naval officer's descent into opium addiction in 1830s Canton. The author shows excellent command of period detail and voice, creating authentic dialogue that captures both the colonial dynamics and the protagonist's deteriorating condition. The characterization of Lieutenant Merrick is particularly well-executed. His addiction is portrayed with nuance - neither romanticized nor overly melodramatic. The recurring motif of the copper taste and his repeated excuse of "sea air" for his obvious illness creates effective dramatic irony. The supporting characters, from the pragmatic Ah-Po to the calculating Ah-Sum, feel authentic and serve specific narrative functions beyond mere exposition. The dialogue is consistently strong, revealing character relationships and power dynamics efficiently. Ah-Po's blunt observations, Ah-Sum's business-like manipulation, and Dalgleish's casual exploitation all ring true to their respective positions in this colonial underworld. The conversations advance both plot and character development naturally. The sensory details are particularly impressive - the copper taste, the smell of camphor and pine shavings, the visual of duck feathers stuck to everything like "snowfall gone wrong." These details create vivid atmosphere without becoming overwrought. The author successfully avoids orientalist clichés while still establishing the foreign setting convincingly. The structure follows Merrick's degraded daily routine effectively, showing his systematic abandonment of duty in favor of feeding his addiction. The pacing builds appropriately toward the opium den scene, which serves as both climax and inevitable conclusion. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the period voice feels slightly forced, and the ending, while thematically appropriate, lacks a strong final image or revelation. The piece also could have pushed deeper into Merrick's internal conflict about his situation, though the external focus works well for the chosen approach. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.

# Sisyphus Gives Advice The hill had no name, which suited it fine. It was simply the Hill, the way some dogs are simply Dog, and it had been Sisyphus's address for a very long time. The boulder waited at the bottom, radiating patience. It was granite, and approached life accordingly. Sisyphus wiped his hands and held out an arm. Crow landed on it like a customs official and produced the morning's letters from wherever birds keep things, which is nowhere, and yet, somehow, everywhere.\* \* *The column ran in the Thebes Evening Herald under the byline "A. Stone." Nobody had ever questioned this. The Herald's readers assumed A. Stone was a retired schoolteacher with firm views, and in all the ways that mattered, they were correct.* *Dear Sisyphus — When I ask my wife what's wrong, she says "nothing." Something is wrong. It is a large something. It has been wrong since Tuesday. — Besieged, Argos* "Dear Besieged — 'Nothing' means 'I don't have the words yet.' Don't cross-examine her; you're her husband, not the magistrate. Make the tea, sit in the same room, and be pleasantly interested in existing near her. When the words come, be holding the tea, not a defense. And ask yourself what happened on Tuesday. You know what happened on Tuesday." He set his shoulder to the boulder and dictated on the push. Three thousand years of practice had taught him to breathe in paragraphs. *Dear Sisyphus — I am a clerk in the records office. Last night I dreamed of filing. In the dream the files were out of order. I woke relieved it was only a dream, then remembered it was also my life. — Tired, Thebes* "Dear Tired — You've stopped being a person who works and become work that occasionally walks home. Take an evening off, properly: feet up, no guilt. Guilt is overtime you do for free. The records will keep — that's the trouble with records, and also their one virtue. The work will still be there tomorrow. I do my best thinking on the way down." The boulder reached the top, considered its options, and came down. It did this without malice or enthusiasm. It had the emotional life of a landmark. *Dear Sisyphus — My husband has suggested we "spice things up." He has bought a saddle. He will not say for whom. — Anon, Corinth* Crow took this one down at a slight distance. "Dear Anon — A saddle is a question, not an instruction. Ask him what he actually wants; it's rarely the tack. A want like this is usually just the wish to be wanted, in fancy dress. If it turns out he means it literally — well, you're married. Marriage has survived stranger things, several of them in Corinth." *Dear Sisyphus — My mother-in-law criticizes my cooking, my gods, and my posture. Yesterday she corrected my posture while I was praying to her son. — Stooped, Delphi* "Dear Stooped — You can't fix her. You can only decide how much of her you'll let live in your head, and at those rates she should be paying rent. Serve her the same stew twice. If she complains in exactly the same words both times, she isn't reviewing the stew; she's rehearsing. And stand up straight out of spite. Properly maintained, spite is a load-bearing emotion." He saved the last letter for the walk down. He always did. The walk down was for the ones that mattered. *Dear Sisyphus — I am twenty-two and I don't know my purpose. Everyone else seems to know theirs. — Lost, Athens* "Dear Lost — Nobody knows. Some people have confidence, and you're mistaking it for a plan. Purpose isn't found like a coin in the road. It's built, out of small useful days, until one morning you look back and there's a path, and you're the one who built it, which is better. You're twenty-two. Be bad at several things first. That's how the good ones get found." He folded the reply into a crack in the boulder, where he kept the ones that mattered. The boulder didn't mind. The boulder didn't mind anything. At this point the air at the foot of the hill went thick with candle-smoke and old honey, and a small god appeared in the middle of it, wearing a toga two sizes too important. "Melitodes," said Sisyphus pleasantly. "God of the Honey That Won't Leave the Jar." "You know of me." The god preened. "Everyone knows you. Nobody thanks you." Melitodes deflated slightly, then rallied. "That is not why I am here. I am here about this — *column*. There are standards for the damned, you know. Bitterness. Gnashing. A certain *quality* of despair. Nowhere in your sentencing does it mention correspondence. Have you filed a Form Twelve-B? There is a department. There is always a department." "Would you like to sit?" "I don't sit on granite. It's common." The god looked about for something to criticize. "Also, the bird's handwriting slants." "He's a crow. Everything about him slants." "You're supposed to be *suffering*." "I did suffer," said Sisyphus, "for the first few hundred years. Very thoroughly. I don't like to brag, but I was quite good at it." Melitodes glared at the boulder, at Crow, at the view, which was the same view as everywhere else down here. "It sets a bad example," he said. "The dead will talk." "They do talk. Some of them write in." The god muttered something about standards and vanished in a smell of breakfast.\*\* \*\* *Melitodes had attained godhood through accumulated irritation: every curse ever aimed at a stubborn jar was, technically, a prayer. He received four million of these a day and was thanked never. It is a common career arc.* Crow returned at dawn with the mail, and on top of the mail was a letter smelling faintly of candlewax. *Dear Sisyphus — How does one get people to appreciate small services? Asking for a friend. — Sticky, Olympia* Sisyphus smiled, settled his shoulder against the boulder, and dictated. "Dear Sticky — You won't be thanked. Your people aren't built for it; they're built for toast. Do the job for the doing. But know this: somewhere this morning, someone will get the honey loose on the first try and feel, briefly, like a hero. You're the hero's entire secret. — S." Crow fixed him with one eye, the way crows do, and flew off toward the Herald. The boulder went up. It would come down. There would be letters. On the whole, he recommended it.

The advice itself is genuinely insightful and practical, avoiding clichéd boulder metaphors while sneaking in one subtle reference as requested. The Pratchettesque elements are well-executed: the footnotes feel authentic, the dry observational humor ("The boulder didn't mind. Prompt:
Lost & Found in Osaka Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 1000 words.

# Lost & Found in Osaka ### *Scene One: First Connection* The guitar found her before she found it. Aoi was three junk shops deep into Den Den Town, clutching a bag with a secondhand MIDI cable she had absolutely no use for, when the sound came slicing down the street: clean, then distorted, then a run of notes she recognized before she could name it. By the game center entrance, a girl in a cropped leather jacket stood over a battery-powered amp, hammering "A Cruel Angel's Thesis" like it had insulted her family. Dented Telecaster. Orange Boss pedal. Guitar case full of coins. Behind her, the arcade roared with crane machines. A small crowd, mostly filming. Aoi stopped. She stayed through the whole song. Then the one after it. When the crowd scattered back into the noise, the girl looked straight at her. "You've been there since the first chorus. So either you're a fan, or you're collecting evidence." "S-sorry. I'll—" "Whoa, whoa. Stay. I'm messing with you." The girl slung a towel around her neck. "That's the most anyone's looked at me all week. Everyone else points a phone and leaves." "It was... good. The arrangement. You changed the bridge." "The bridge is boring as written. Needed teeth." A tilt of the head. "You play?" "Not— not guitar. Synthesizers." "Synthesizers, *plural*. Fancy." "It's mostly one. A used one. And a broken one I'm fixing. So... technically plural." The girl laughed, loud and unembarrassed. "I like you. You're funny and you don't know it yet." She toed the pedal at her feet. "Okay, engineer. Tell me something I don't know about my own rig." Aoi's mouth moved before her caution could catch it. "Your delay. On the fast section you pulled the repeats back. The original has longer trails, but live that's— that's smarter. With that much distortion, the trails would just turn to mud." The girl stared at her for a long second. "Name?" "...Aoi." "Aoi. I'm Riko. I've played that song two hundred times on that corner, and you're the first person who heard the delay." She was already crouching, winding cable around her fist. "You don't talk much, but you hear everything. Dangerous combination. I'm starving, and coins count as food money in this economy. Kaitenzushi around the corner. Consider it payment for the consultation." "You don't have to—" "I know I don't have to. That's the fun part." *** They took two stools at the counter. The belt hummed past, the tea taps hissed, and Riko stacked plates like she was building a tower. "Itadakimasu! Fair warning, I eat like I've been rescued from an island." "How much is too much?" "If the tower falls over, we stop." She nodded at the belt. "Fun fact: they invented this in Osaka. Everything good gets invented here when people get impatient." Aoi took one plate of tamago. Riko took four of everything. "So. Synth girl. What have you actually got?" "Analog. Mono. A Volca Bass, and a Monotribe I'm rebuilding — someone sold it for parts, but the VCO's fine, it was just the ribbon controller, so if I can find the flex cable then—" She heard herself and stopped. "Sorry. That was... a lot." "Don't apologize. That's the most alive you've sounded all day. Keep going. What's a VCO?" "The part that makes the raw sound. Everything after it is just... shaping it." Riko chewed that over with her salmon. "Huh. Like a guitar string. Everything after the string is just shaping it." Aoi blinked. "...Yes. Exactly that." "See? Same instrument, different clothes." Chopsticks pointed. "What year are you, anyway?" "Second... second year. High school." "Uni second-year, myself. Music major. The 'major' is doing a lot of work there." The chopsticks swung back. "So what do you play on these synths?" "Soundtracks. Mostly anime. By ear." Aoi turned her teacup in her hands, then made herself say it. "Do you know... *Serial Experiments Lain*?" Riko's chopsticks stopped halfway to her mouth. "The Wired? *Lain of the Wired?*" "You know it?" "'Present day, present time—'" "'—ahaha.'" Aoi finished it before she could be shy about it. Riko slapped the counter. "Two years! Two years I've tried to arrange 'Duvet' for one guitar, and there's a hole in it, I can *hear* the hole—" "The pad. There's a synth pad under everything. You don't notice it until you take it out, and then the whole song sounds empty." "*Yes.* The hole! I knew there was a hole and I didn't know why!" "It's all over the Cyberia soundtrack too, the club scenes, the way they layer the—" Aoi caught Riko's grin and realized she was grinning back. "Nobody knows this show," Riko said. "I made my best friend watch it. She thought Lain was a phone company." "People at school think I'm..." Aoi studied her tea. "The way Lain is. At school." Riko looked at her for a moment, and there was nothing teasing in it. "Lain's the one who figures out the whole thing, though. Everyone else is just logged on." Something in Aoi's chest went quiet and warm. She hid it behind a bite of tamago. "Okay. Listen." Riko leaned in, plates forgotten. "Sunday, I'm back on that corner. Bring the Volca. Bring the broken one too, I want to see it. We find out if 'Duvet' survives the two of us." "I've never played with anyone. Like... *with*. Anyone." "Busking doesn't count as playing with people. It's playing *at* them." Riko nudged the last salmon plate across. "First time for everything." "...Okay." She said it again, steadier. "Okay." "There it is." Riko pulled out her phone. "Give me your LINE. If you ghost me, I have your face and an entire electronics district of witnesses." Aoi recited her ID, watched the friend request land, then did something she'd never done before: grabbed a plate off the belt without hesitating and set it on Riko's tower. "Egg. It's... good, after the spicy." Riko looked at the plate, then at her, and grinned like the whole day had been aimed here. "Look at you. Ordering for me already." "You did say if the tower falls—" "I know what I said." Riko raised her teacup. "Hey, Aoi. No matter where you go..." Aoi lifted hers, the words arriving like a hand finding a switch. "...everyone's connected." "See?" Riko clinked her cup against Aoi's. "We're going to be insufferable together." The belt kept turning. Neither of them watched it anymore.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully creates two distinct character voices - Aoi's hesitant, knowledge-rich interiority contrasts effectively with Riko's confident, playful directness. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple functions: character development, world-building, and plot advancement. The setting is well-established through specific details (Den Den Town, kaitenzushi, specific music equipment) that ground the story in authentic Japanese culture without feeling forced or touristy. The music knowledge displayed is accurate and serves the characterization well - both characters' expertise feels genuine rather than superficial. The pacing works effectively, moving from initial observation through awkward first contact to genuine connection. The transition feels earned rather than rushed, built on shared interests and mutual respect for each other's knowledge. The Serial Experiments Lain reference serves as an effective bonding moment that feels organic to both characters. However, there are some minor weaknesses. The opening line "The guitar found her before she found it" attempts poeticism but feels slightly forced. Some descriptions veer toward the precious ("something in Aoi's chest went quiet and warm"). The transformation from shy to confident, while generally well-handled, happens quite rapidly. The dialogue is the piece's strongest element - each character maintains a distinct voice throughout, and their conversation flows naturally while revealing character depth. Riko's casual confidence ("I like you. You're funny and you don't know it yet") contrasts nicely with Aoi's technical precision and growing comfort. The ending strikes an appropriate note of cautious optimism without overselling the connection. The Lain quote exchange provides a satisfying callback while the final image of the ignored conveyor belt suggests their focus has genuinely shifted to each other. Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. Model Output:
# REWIND ### Chapter Seven The watch was free. That should have been my first warning. It came from Grandpa Warren's estate sale, in a velvet box with no brand name and no instructions, in a plastic bin marked FREE — TAKE. The woman running the sale said, "He'd want someone to have it. Warren always called it his little time-saver." Here's the thing about Grandpa Warren: he died at fifty-eight, but in the casket he looked about a hundred. Nobody in my family ever talked about that. The watch looked like a smartwatch, if smartwatches came from a hundred years ago. The clasp snapped shut the second it touched my wrist — I figured I fumbled it — and the dark screen lit up. 4:12 p.m. Correct time. Then it flickered, just for a second, and showed something else. The number 4. Step counter, I told myself. Probably a step counter. Two days later, Dana Suarez watched me trip over Marcus Reyes's backpack in the cafeteria, launch my tray like an Olympic event, and wear an entire kiwi smoothie home. Head to waist. The whole lunchroom laughed. By sixth period, everyone in seventh grade knew me as Smoothie Boy. In the hallway, I slammed my locker, and my hand slipped. The watch's bezel spun backward under my fingers. Click. Click. Click. The world hiccuped. Lockers un-slammed. Kids moonwalked backward down the hall. In the cafeteria, my smoothie rose off my shirt, poured itself up into the cup, and my tray glided back into my hands. Laughter played in reverse, like a tape unspooling. Then time snapped forward, and I was standing at the start of the lunch line, heart pounding, smoothie unspilled. I stepped over the backpack. No disaster. No nickname. Dana smiled at me. *At me.* The watch buzzed. The screen flickered: **3**. That night my voice cracked so hard my mom dropped a dinner plate. "You're growing so fast," she marveled, like I was a time-lapse video of a beanstalk. There was a pimple on my chin the size of a meteor. I was almost positive it hadn't existed at breakfast. Monday, Mr. Halloran sprang a pop quiz on pre-algebra. I stared at problem one until the numbers swam. When I saw my inevitable F, I clicked the bezel back three times. The quiz un-happened. This time I knew every answer. (Yes. Cheating. Tell it to my GPA.) The aging hit Tuesday like a freight train. I woke up and my pajama pants were floods. Four inches in a week, my mom said, marking the door frame and scheduling a doctor's appointment. My voice came out of me like a radio announcer's. There was actual fuzz on my upper lip, and acne marching across my forehead in formation. I was going through puberty at highway speed. Ms. Petrucci stopped me in the hall: "Sorry — are you the new student aide from the high school?" A sixth grader called me *sir*. SIR. And Dana — Dana, who had never once noticed me — asked if I'd be at her sister's high school party. It should have felt like winning the lottery. It felt like shoplifting my own life. The watch flickered: **2**. I decided to quit cold turkey. Except the clasp wouldn't open. I pulled until my wrist was raw and stinging. The band was warm. Warm like something with a pulse. Saturday morning, my little sister June kicked her ball over the hedge and chased it into Miller Road — right as the delivery truck came around the corner doing forty. I was half a block away. Too far. I screamed her name. The horn blared— I cranked the bezel with both hands. Too hard. Too many clicks. The world smeared backward. The truck un-arrived, reversing around the corner at impossible speed. Birds flew tail-first. The sun slid backward up the sky. I'd overshot by three whole hours. And I felt every minute of it. Bones stretching. Shoulders widening. My jaw squaring out, stubble itching my lip like ants marching. When time lurched forward again, I was staring down at my own sneakers from roughly a mile up. This time I hid the ball. This time June watched cartoons. This time, no truck. I walked home rehearsing explanations. My mom opened the door, screamed, and slammed it in my face. "MA! IT'S ME! IT'S THEO!" Biscuit — our dog, who has loved me since he was a puppy — barked at me through the window like I was a burglar. Because I was. Sort of. That's when I saw the poster on the telephone pole. Sun-bleached. Curling at the corners. MISSING: THEODORE MARSH, AGE 12. LAST SEEN JUNE 4TH. My stomach dropped through the sidewalk. June 4th. The day of the estate sale. The day I first turned the bezel. The world hadn't just changed. It had *corrected itself.* Somewhere in the rewrite, twelve-year-old Theo Marsh had vanished — three years ago, judging by that faded paper — and some too-tall stranger had wandered in wearing his life. Through the window, I could see June, alive, eating cereal, laughing at cartoons. That was the trade. My family got to keep her. And lost me. The watch flickered: **1**. Then the screen did something new. A timer, counting down. 00:47:33. 00:47:32. Whatever was left of the real timeline was draining away like bathwater. When it hit zero, I had a feeling this nightmare would be permanent. One rewind left. One chance to get back to June 4th, to before I ever strapped this thing on. But rewinding three years would cost me three more years — maybe more. Maybe I'd come back a grown-up. Maybe I'd come back looking like Grandpa Warren in his casket: fifty-eight years old, wearing a hundred-year-old face. Maybe I wouldn't come back at all. I looked at the MISSING poster. I looked through the window at my mom, crying over a son who was standing ten feet from her porch. For June. For Mom. For me. I grabbed the bezel and twisted. The streetlights stretched backward like taffy. Cars un-drove. The poster un-yellowed, un-curled, and peeled itself off the pole. I felt the years grinding onto me — spine popping taller, hands roughening, hair creeping down my forearms — and I held on anyway, clicking, clicking, back toward June 4th, back toward twelve years old, back toward me. The screen flickered one last time. It wasn't a number anymore. **HELLO, WARREN.** The last thing I heard, as the whole world unraveled like a rewinding tape, was ticking. Tick. Tock.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Goosebumps-style teen horror prompt, effectively incorporating all required elements: a middle schooler discovering a time-rewinding smartwatch, physical aging consequences, timeline disruption, and the need for one final rewind to fix everything. The writing maintains an appropriately youthful voice throughout while building genuine tension and horror. The character of Theo feels authentic as a middle school protagonist - his motivations (avoiding embarrassment, cheating on tests, impressing Dana) ring true for his age. His escalating panic as he realizes the consequences of his actions creates believable character development. The physical transformations are well-earned through the established rules of the watch's magic system. The prose strikes an effective balance between accessible teen-friendly language and genuinely creepy imagery. Phrases like "I felt every minute of it. Bones stretching. Shoulders widening" and "The world hadn't just changed. It had corrected itself" create visceral horror without becoming overwrought. The pacing builds tension methodically from minor embarrassment to existential crisis. The story's internal logic remains consistent throughout. The watch's countdown system, the physical aging, and the timeline corrections all follow established rules. The revelation that Theo has been erased from his family's timeline is a genuinely chilling twist that recontextualizes everything that came before. The ending avoids false positivity while maintaining the ambiguous, unsettling tone appropriate for the genre. The final revelation "HELLO, WARREN" suggests Theo may be trapped in the same cycle that consumed his grandfather, which is both creative and thematically resonant. Some minor weaknesses include occasional telling rather than showing (particularly in exposition about the family's reaction to Grandpa Warren's appearance), and a few moments where the dialogue feels slightly stilted. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness of the piece. The writing demonstrates sophisticated understanding of horror pacing, building from small stakes to cosmic ones while maintaining the protagonist's relatable teenage perspective throughout. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The tin ducks went by on their chain and nobody shot at them. The gallery stood at the quiet end of the boardwalk, past the fortune-teller's shuttered booth, where the crowd thinned from baby carriages to men in shirtsleeves who watched the water as though it owed them money. He was there, of course. Racking rifles, his back to her, the last daylight sitting on his shoulders. The lights along the boardwalk buzzed on one by one, like a jury coming to a verdict. She could have turned around. The Wonder Wheel turned its slow, lawful circle behind her, and no one would have known. *His locks.* The phrase came again, uninvited, the way it had come all week. She'd found the verse at thirteen, buried in the good book like a knife in a drawer — *bushy, and black as a raven* — and read it standing up in the parlor with one ear tuned for her mother's footsteps. It had simply waited all these years for a head of black curls at a shooting gallery. The smell of cotton candy drifted over — burnt sugar, warm paper — and snagged on something old. A hand on her shoulder. A voice, laughing low behind her. She had been small, and the sweetness had gone out of the world like a match pinched. She could not place it. She was not sure she wanted to. "You came back." He had turned without turning, the way he did everything, as though the world ran a half-step behind him. "I was passing." "No one passes this end of the boardwalk. They come on purpose or they're lost." "Perhaps I'm lost." "Lost people ask directions. You've been standing there ten minutes, deciding." He set the last rifle in its slot. "Which are you, Mrs. Marsh?" The name landed like a hand on the back of her neck. She had not told it to him. She was nearly certain. "You talked a great deal last Tuesday," he said, reading her face with what looked like apology and was not. "You were doing the giving. I was doing the taking. That's the trade I'm in." "I don't remember giving you my name." "You gave me more than that. You were generous." He said it the way another man might say a number. And the trouble was she could not remember what she had told him. That was the thing about him — he was easy to talk to the way a deep porch is easy to fall off of. An hour had gone by like a warm bath, and when she climbed out she could not have repeated one sentence of her own. "You keep rifles," she said. "You don't keep confidences." "I keep whatever's left on the counter." He lifted a rifle, checked it, held it out. "You owe the ducks a rematch." "I missed every one last week." "You flinched. Flinching is honest. Come." She came. "Why do you do this? Rent out guns to strangers?" "Somebody has to arm the unhappy." The rifle was heavier than it looked and smelled of oil and pennies. He stood behind her — not touching, an inch of July air between his hand and her waist — and she was aware of that inch the way you're aware of a lit match. "Elbow," he said, and did not correct it. "You're not going to fix it?" "You'd like that." She would. That was the annoyance of him. "I'd like to hit something." "That's the spirit of the age. Squeeze, don't pull. It only wants what you point it at." She squeezed. The report cracked the dusk; a tin duck rattled past untouched. Her second shot clipped one, and it went down with a clang like a dropped saucepan, absurd and glorious, and she laughed before she could stop. He reached past her to rack the rifle, and for one second his arm was a gate she had walked through. From under the counter he brought a small prize: a pocket mirror in a tin frame. "For the markswoman." "I only hit one." "One's enough. I don't like to be owed." "And if I refuse it?" "Then you'll owe me. And I collect." He put it in her hand and closed her fingers over it, his hand warm, staying a half-second past manners. "Every woman should carry one of these." "To fix my face?" "To see what's coming up behind you." The Wheel turned its slow circle. Somewhere behind them a barker promised the unbelievable — inside, inside only. "Is something coming up behind me?" she asked. "Not yet." He looked at her the way he'd checked the rifle — briefly, expertly, for what it would do. "But you're the sort things happen to. You've been happening since you stepped off the train." "You don't know anything about me." "I know you took off your ring." He tipped his chin at her left hand, light as a doctor. "There's a stripe on your finger where the sun couldn't get in." She put the hand behind her back, which was childish, which acknowledged everything. "That's not your business." "Nothing here is my business. I only rent out rifles." He smiled then, the first full one, and it was worse than the small ones, because it had dimples, because dimples were trustworthy, because nothing else about him was. "You never told me your name," she said. "Joseph," he said, and the ease with which he gave it up told her it wasn't his. "Next Friday. Dusk. The ducks will miss you." "You're very sure I'll come." "Mrs. Marsh." He turned back to his counter and began wiping it down, unhurried, a man closing up. "I'm in the repeat business. I know what it looks like." She walked toward the lights with the mirror in her fist. The cotton candy smell rose again, sweet and scorched, and the memory came up with it, close enough to touch — a voice saying *don't wander, don't wander off* — and sank before she could catch it. Well. She had wandered. Her thumb found the pale stripe on her finger. The ring was at home in the drawer of her jewel box, and she had taken it off — she knew she had taken it off — but she could not remember whether that had been before Tuesday, or after.

+ Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**2.** That night the lodge felt almost normal, and JT clung to that almost the way a drowning man clings to driftwood. Dad fried steaks off the first caribou in the black skillet, butter spitting, and the three of them sat at the plank table under the hiss of the propane lamp. Mike shuffled cards without playing anything—shuffled, cut, shuffled—and Dad hummed under his breath. That was the first wrong thing, or the first one JT let himself notice: Dad never hummed. And it wasn't a tune. It was low and droning and went nowhere, a hymn with the notes flattened out, and after a while JT realized Mike was humming it too, the two of them in unison without knowing it. The steaks came out gray. Not browned—gray, all the way through, and there'd been almost no blood in the pan. JT thought about the field dressing three days back: how Mike had opened the animal up and how little had come out. He'd told himself the knife went in clean. He kept telling himself that. Nobody ate much. Dad said he was full up from the cold. JT was starving—fourteen years old and a full day of muskeg behind him—and he couldn't make his hand do it. "Radio's out again," Dad said, to nobody. Last October the little transistor had pulled in the hockey game every night. Now it was static from one end of the dial to the other, a soft steady wash, like the whole world broadcasting from underwater. "Atmospherics," Dad said, and smiled at his plate. Dad had never in his life used a word like *atmospherics*. Emile hadn't come up for supper. That had never happened, not once in all JT's autumns here—the old guide ate at their table and talked until Dad finally said let's get some sleep, stories about the winter of '63 and the moose that chased him into the lake. Tonight his window across the yard stayed dark, and nobody mentioned it, which was somehow worse than mentioning it. JT found him behind his cabin at dusk, and his stomach dropped before Emile said a word, because Emile's truck was running and the bed was loaded—a steamer trunk, tarps roped down, a dog cage with a blanket thrown over it. Empty. "Where's Napoleon?" Pause. "Took him to my sister's. Down south." "You going somewhere?" "Getting wood." "There's wood." JT nodded at the pile, six cords, split and stacked. Emile looked at him then, and up close his eyes were wet and too bright. "Boy. Does your fadder know the moon comes full Thursday?" "It's just the moon." "Not up here." Emile stepped close, voice dropping. "Fifty years my family's guided this ground. Caribou run. That's all they are—running with legs on. Spook one at four hundred yards, it's gone." His breath came in little clouds. "These ones don't run. These ones *wait*. And a thing that waits for the rifle ain't giving itself, boy. Nothing gives itself to a rifle. It's trading." His jaw worked. "I don't know for what. I'm not staying to find out. Tell your fadder—portage road, south, before Wednesday dark. Don't drive at night. If something's standing in the road—" He stopped, and JT watched him decide not to finish. "Just don't stop." "You're scaring me." "Good," Emile said, climbing in. "Scared's the only thing driving me south tonight." He ran dark until the first bend. JT stood listening to the engine fade, then to the silence closing back in around him like water. He'd half-convinced himself he'd imagined the clearing that afternoon. Emile's face had just un-imagined it. He told Dad at the sink, low, while Mike dealt himself solitaire, flipping cards he didn't look at. Dad dried his hands slow. "Emile's getting old. His brother went the same way. Nerves." "Dad. He said the moon—" "JT." Dad turned around. His face was calm. His eyes were dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle, and it was a long, horrible moment before he remembered where he'd seen eyes like that before. "You saw them today, didn't you. In the clearing." Not a question. JT's mouth went dry. "There's nothing out there but meat," Dad said, gentle as explaining to a small child, and the gentleness was the worst thing yet. "We paid for the week." His head tilted, listening to something JT couldn't hear. "We're not leaving before it's time." At the table, Mike had stopped dealing. He was watching them both, smiling faintly, and JT couldn't have said how long he'd been smiling. JT washed his cup and went to bed. There was nobody left to tell. That was the whole of it. Nobody left in the world. *** He woke at quarter to three without knowing what had woken him. Then he knew: the humming. Faint, coming up through the floorboards. The flattened hymn. The front room below was silver. The moon wasn't full yet, but close enough to lay the yard out white as bone. Dad stood at the big window in his long johns, barefoot on the cold boards. Mike stood beside him. Neither of them turned around. Beyond the yard, at the treeline, the caribou stood in rows in the moonlight. Still. All of them facing the lodge. JT counted nineteen. He counted again and got twenty-three, and not one of them had moved. "Dad," he whispered. "Go back to bed, JT." Soft. Dreamy. Dad's hand was raised, fingertips resting against the cold glass, trembling a little. "It's polite, isn't it," Dad said—to the window, to the herd, to whatever was listening. "How they wait." Out at the treeline, the big buck stepped once out of the rows. Just once. Its ears flicked, lazy and patient. JT backed up the stairs. Nobody stopped him. Nobody even turned around. He lay with the covers pulled to his chin like a little kid, listening to the humming rise and fall beneath the floor, and he understood with a cold, sinking certainty that the herd was not counting the days to Thursday the way he was. He thought of Emile's word—*trading, nothing gives itself to a rifle, it's trading*—and lay awake in the last of the dark, wondering what his family had already agreed to pay.
