+ Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-6288 **Object Class:** Pending **Document Type:** Personal statement of Dr. Ada Reyes, Senior Researcher, Site-17. Submitted at researcher's insistence for joint review by the Temporal Anomalies Department and the Memetics and Infohazards Division. Handwriting on all thirty-one (31) recovered notes has been positively matched to Dr. Reyes. --- I found the first note on March 3rd, tucked under my coffee mug. Standard Foundation memo paper — the cream stock every desk on site is issued. > *Check the seals in Cold Storage before Thursday. Don't put it off.* I assumed I'd written it myself and forgotten. We all do it. I checked the seals anyway. Two were degraded past tolerance; scheduled inspection wasn't until Friday. I told myself it was a coincidence, and for two days I believed it. The second note was in my coat pocket. > *You almost didn't check. I felt you almost not checking. He gets out through the cracks you don't look at.* The handwriting was mine. Document analysis confirmed it: my letterforms, my pressure, but with microtremors consistent with extreme stress or prolonged sleep deprivation. There was no "he" in Cold Storage. There was nothing in Cold Storage but tissue samples and three low-risk containment units. I reported it. That was when Site-17 stopped being mine. Memetics screened me for cognitohazard exposure. Clean. Psych eval: clean, aside from "situational anxiety consistent with reported events." Temporal Anomalies collected copies of everything and then went quiet in the particular way they do. The review board split down the middle. Half believed the notes were genuinely retrocausal — a future version of me pushing warnings backward through the one medium guaranteed to reach me. The other half believed SCP-████ was responsible. It is housed four floors below my old lab: persuasive, patient, fluent in whatever a person most needs to hear. It has talked three researchers into opening its cell over the years, and it has never used the same voice twice. If the notes were real, I had to follow them. If they were forged, following them was precisely what something wanted. Both theories fit the evidence perfectly. That was the worst part. I kept waiting for the fact that would break the tie, and every fact that arrived fit both. I surrendered every sheet of memo paper I owned. Director Okafor locked it in his office safe, changed the combination, and did not tell me the new one. I was moved to quarters containing a cot and a recorder and nothing else. On the morning of March 19th I woke with a note folded inside my fist. > *You can't lock away all the paper. There's always more paper. There is paper inside the walls.* The safe was still sealed. The stack inside was short one sheet. They put a camera on me while I slept. Seven hours of footage: motionless, hands above the blanket, palms open. At 03:12 the image degrades for a quarter of a second. The technicians called it a compression artifact. When the picture clears, my left hand is closed. The note was in it. > *It's not static. Watch the static. — A.R.* After that, coherence left. I want to be precise about what "worse" means, because the early notes were frightening but sane. > *March 47th. The breach happens March 47th. Why does nobody else have that calendar.* > *Tell Marcus the transfer worked. He's waiting in the atrium.* Marcus Halloran died at Site-17 in 2019. I attended the funeral. I still have the program. I checked it four times that night. > *Site-17 was decommissioned in 2004. Why are you still there. Why are you all still there.* > *i have stopped writing these notes i need you to understand that i stopped writing these notes six of them ago and they keep coming* Temporal's final assessment described "factual content irreconcilable with the current timeline, consistent with either genuine divergence or deliberate disorientation." That is a very expensive way of saying they didn't know. The last note came on March 30th. It was on my pillow. The camera showed nothing entering the room, nothing leaving, and me, asleep, both hands visible. > *Don't file the report. Every time you write it down it gets closer to being true. I am begging you. I am begging you in your own handwriting because it is the only hand I have left.* I filed this report anyway. You are reading it, so you know that I did. I needed someone outside my own skull to hold this thing, because I can no longer tell which version of myself to trust. The psych staff call that insight. At night it feels simpler than that: if a future me exists, then somewhere I am desperate enough to beg. And if SCP-████ is doing this, then it knows exactly how to make me beg, and it is watching me decide, right now, whether to believe in myself. There is a fresh sheet of memo paper on my desk. I did not put it there. It is blank. I am afraid to write on it. I am more afraid of who will. --- **Addendum:** The following annotation was appended by Records and Information Security Administration during routine verification: *No personnel file exists for "Marcus Halloran." Site-17 employment records contain no employee by that name. No funeral program was recovered among Dr. Reyes's effects.* *Dr. Reyes has requested that the funeral program — which she maintains is in her nightstand — be submitted for handwriting analysis against her own hand.* *Request status: pending.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP report demonstrates strong technical execution and creative understanding of the SCP Foundation format. The author successfully captures the clinical, bureaucratic tone characteristic of SCP documentation while weaving in the personal narrative of Dr. Reyes. The format choice—presenting this as a personal statement within an SCP framework—is clever and allows for the required first-person perspective while maintaining genre authenticity. The central concept is genuinely unsettling: notes from a future self that may or may not be real, creating an impossible epistemological trap. The author skillfully builds tension through escalating incoherence in the notes, from practical warnings to reality-breaking statements like "March 47th" and references to a decommissioned site that's still operational. The ambiguity between temporal anomaly and memetic manipulation is well-maintained throughout. Character work is solid but not exceptional. Dr. Reyes feels believable as a researcher caught in an impossible situation, and her growing desperation comes through clearly. However, the character remains somewhat archetypal—the rational scientist facing the irrational—without deeper psychological complexity or distinctive voice beyond the situation's demands. The prose is clean and effective, avoiding purple language while maintaining atmospheric tension. The author shows restraint in not over-explaining the horror, letting the implications speak for themselves. The progression from mundane notes to increasingly disturbing content is well-paced. The ending is particularly strong, with the blank paper representing both threat and temptation. The addendum about Marcus Halloran adds another layer of uncertainty about Dr. Reyes's reliability as narrator. This creates genuine ambiguity about whether she's experiencing a temporal anomaly or psychological breakdown. Some weaknesses include limited emotional range—the piece maintains one note of mounting dread without much variation. The supporting characters (Director Okafor, the review board) remain functional rather than memorable. The middle section, while maintaining tension, doesn't develop the central mystery as dynamically as it could. The piece succeeds as both SCP fiction and psychological horror, demonstrating solid craft and creative understanding of the prompt's requirements. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Item #: SCP-7294 **Object Class:** Euclid **Special Containment Procedures:** Foundation assets monitor registries of derelict properties for manifestations of SCP-7294-1. Host structures are acquired through intermediaries and placed under continuous observation; doors are to remain closed. Entry into SCP-7294-2 requires Level 4 authorization, psychological clearance, and is permitted once per personnel lifetime. All recovered material is quarantined at Site-41. **Description:** SCP-7294 designates 31 identical doors (SCP-7294-1) manifesting without pattern in abandoned buildings across six continents. Instances are unmarked, grey-lacquered, unlocked, and set into walls with no corresponding opening on the opposite side. Each bears four parallel scratches around the doorknob, gouged upward from below. The scratches are not merely similar across instances: they are identical at every scale of magnification, as if copied from a single original. Opening any instance grants access to SCP-7294-2, an archive of impossible extent — shelf-stacks receding beyond sight in every direction including overhead, walkways without supports, constant sourceless amber light, no dust. Interior volume vastly exceeds host structures and shows no curvature consistent with a planetary surface. Recovered documents, written in extinct, unknown, and modern scripts, describe a global civilization administered by a body called **the Curatorium**, which collected dangerous phenomena in facilities analogous to Foundation Sites. All texts terminate in references to an unspecified containment failure — "the Sundering" — after which the civilization's records simply stop. Of 214 Curatorium personnel files recovered to date, 61 correspond to current Foundation employees: matching names, photographs, and handwriting, all dated between 1651 and 1791. > *Let this stand as the final record. Our Holdings were secure. Each was secure. What failed was not any Holding but the record of them, and what is unrecorded is uncontained. We are sealing the stacks and clearing the shelves so that nothing may be read back into the world. We kept, so the light need not notice. Do not open the doors from the inside.* --- ## Exploration Log 7294-12 **Team:** MTF Iota-9 ("Stack Rats") — Agent D. Halloran (lead), Agents Okafor and Brandt, Dr. Reyes (archival consultant). **Entry point:** SCP-7294-1, derelict printworks, Lyon, France. Third-person summary compiled from helmet footage. **00:03** — The door opens onto a rotunda. Card catalogues the size of townhouses; aisles radiate outward and upward. Reyes remarks the air smells of "paper that refuses to burn." **00:19** — The team follows an aisle labeled in an unknown script. Brandt photographs a shelf placard reading *RECONSTITUTION — SUBLEVEL 9*. **00:41** — Rhythmic impacts ahead. The team observes six entities in bulky, deteriorated suits resembling hazmat gear — charcoal-grey, faceplates blank. Each carries an entire shelf-section overhead. Where they pass, aisles are left with clean gaps, like pulled teeth. Behind them, a corridor folds closed without visible motion. **00:44** — Halloran calls out. The entities freeze. One turns its faceplate toward the team; there are no features behind the glass. All six flee, moving in a manner analysts describe as "wrong, and then fast." One drops a folder. **00:46** — Okafor recovers the folder: a personnel file on Curatorium letterhead. > **CURATORIUM — PERSONNEL RECORD** > **NAME:** HALLORAN, D. > **APPOINTMENT:** Field Warden, Third Shelf > **ENLISTED:** 1768 > **TERMINATION:** Expunged — the Sundering > **STATUS:** Reconstituted. Pending. Halloran reads it twice, says nothing, and orders the team onward. **01:12** — The team enters a wing being actively cleared. Dozens of entities dismantle stacks in silence. In a gap where shelves have been removed, a free-standing door — identical to SCP-7294-1 — waits alone. An entity approaches it, drags four gloved fingers once around the knob, and flees at the team's approach. Brandt circles the door: it is one centimeter thick. There is no other side. **01:30** — Reyes finds a lectern bearing a ledger titled *REGISTER OF READERS*. Most entries are centuries old. Three are written in ballpoint pen. Handwriting analysis matches sitting members of the O5 Council. Foundation site logs show no authorized visits to the Lyon instance. The most recent entry, dated nine days prior, reads: > *The removal crews are doing necessary work. Do not interrupt them again. Stop looking for the cause; mind the doors. — 7* **01:33** — Halloran orders withdrawal. As the team crosses the rotunda, every catalogue drawer opens simultaneously. Nothing emerges. The team exits at 01:41. The door closes and locks itself behind them. --- ## Addendum 7294-C Follow-up entry attempts through the Lyon door have failed; it now opens onto a bricked wall. Requests for comment submitted to O5 Command regarding the *REGISTER* entries were returned unopened, accompanied by a memorandum revoking MTF Iota-9's clearance for SCP-7294 and reassigning Halloran to Site-41's records annex — the same annex housing the Curatorium files. Halloran's Foundation personnel file was subsequently reviewed. It begins in 1998. It has always begun in 1998. Four new doors have manifested since Exploration 7294-12. All bore fresh scratches.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This SCP entry demonstrates strong adherence to the Foundation's clinical documentation style while weaving a compelling narrative of temporal paradox and institutional horror. The piece successfully fulfills all prompt requirements: doors in abandoned buildings, an impossible archive, references to a previous civilization's containment failure, personnel files matching current staff, exploration logs with fleeing hazmat entities, and evidence of unauthorized O5 visits. The writing maintains the characteristic SCP tone throughout - clinical, detached, yet building dread through implication rather than explicit horror. The author shows sophisticated understanding of SCP conventions, from containment procedures to exploration log formatting. The concept of "the Curatorium" as a predecessor organization creates effective parallel structure, while the detail of identical scratches across all doors adds unsettling precision. Character actions feel authentic within the SCP universe. Halloran's measured response to discovering his own personnel file, the team's professional conduct during anomalous encounters, and the O5 Council's secretive behavior all ring true to established Foundation culture. The exploration team members, while not deeply developed, serve their functional roles effectively. The prose strikes an appropriate balance between clinical documentation and evocative description. Phrases like "paper that refuses to burn," "like pulled teeth," and "wrong, and then fast" provide memorable imagery without breaking the clinical voice. The writing flows naturally, with each section building tension toward the revelation of temporal loops and institutional conspiracy. The piece excels at "show don't tell" - the horror emerges through accumulated details rather than exposition. The scratches, the fleeing entities, the locked door, Halloran's reassignment, and the final revelation about his personnel file create mounting unease. The ending avoids false positivity, maintaining the SCP universe's characteristic bleakness. Some elements could be stronger. The characters, while believable, lack emotional depth beyond professional competence. The concept, while well-executed, follows familiar SCP patterns of temporal anomalies and Foundation conspiracies. The piece doesn't quite achieve the emotional complexity or surprise factor of the most memorable SCPs. The technical execution is solid throughout, with natural sentence flow and consistent formatting. The integration of different document types (containment procedures, exploration logs, recovered documents) creates authentic Foundation documentation style. Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). # The Stolen Light The gifts had been presented, admired, catalogued, and presented again. Four hours into the Ninth Reception, Envoy Orie noticed that no one was watching her, and did what no envoy of the Accord is trained to do. She went out the low door behind the musicians and let the city take her in. It was her first posting. She was twenty-three. Othan is cut downward rather than built upward: a city of stairs and shafts sunk into the limestone of the escarpment, tier below tier, lit by mirrors that carry the noon sun forty levels down to pools of gold on the floors. Beside every light-well the first carvers had set the thief's mark — a man, a flame, a broken chain. Prometheus. *The stolen light. We are grateful thieves,* said the stone. She went down. On the fourth tier the cistern wall ran with carving: a tall woman holding wheat, a girl descending into a cleft of rock, the girl ascending again, wheat again. Demeter. Persephone. The Descent was the founding story — the first generations underground in the bad years, and the coming-up. Every child of Tem learned it before speech, the briefs said. The briefs said a great deal. The market on the sixth tier smelled of wet stone, sheep-fat, frying bread, and a pepper grown on the upland terraces. The money-changer had hung his stall beneath a carved oar and a coin in a skeletal hand: Charon, ferryman of the dead, patron of exchange. A joke three centuries old, and still good. The briefs described four stable morphs, subspecies fixed by adaptation and by the Lineage Laws of the first century: the shel of the stone city, pale, slow, wide-eyed; the duru of the uplands, deep-chested for the thin air; the vei of the terraces; the coastfolk. They did not intermarry, the briefs said. The genetics were closed, the castes rigid, the society frozen. At a tea stall a shel woman poured for her daughter, a girl of fourteen who stood a head above her mother and would be duru-tall at twenty, laughing with a herder boy over the cups. On the wall behind them, names newly cut: children grafted that week into lineages not their blood. Lineage here was a house, not a chain. When Orie asked the price of tea in careful old speech, the woman corrected one vowel, gently, as one straightens a guest's collar, and charged her half of nothing. The bread was cheap. The undercity was supposed to be hungry, sullen, near revolt. The bread was cheap, two women argued happily about the Festival of Mirrors, an old man slept in a sun-pool with his mouth open, and no one looked twice at the stranger. She had come to observe, and was being observed, she began to suspect, with better manners. She was gone four hours. She knew it before she reached her door. The reprimand was delivered in person, which meant Command considered it serious. Chief Envoy Silla stood, which was itself the sentence. "You were dark to your escort for four hours in a foreign city. If you had died, we would have learned nothing and lost the treaty." A pause. "The Ministry noticed, of course. They noticed before you left the citadel. You were let out, Orie. That should frighten you more than anything on this world." "I'm sorry. I needed—" "You needed. Yes. That is what they count on." Silla's face was tired rather than angry. "The Minister of Science has asked for you. Tomorrow. Alone. Odai holds the portfolio because her family holds the water. Her science is genealogy; her laboratory, the registry. Do not mistake the eyes for weakness. Do not mistake anything for anything." The Minister of Science received her at the head of a light-shaft, in a room where noon arrived by mirrors and a small fire kept tea. She was shel: small, pale, with great dark eyes that made her look like a child until she used them. She looked thirty. She was, by the registry she governed, seventy-one. "Read the lintel," she said, without greeting. Orie read. A man walking up out of the dark, leading a woman by the hand; at the last light he turns; she is going back into the stone. "Orpheus," she said. "He looked back." "Why?" "Because he was human. Because he could not believe in what he had been given." Odai poured tea. "Your Command turned the same way, forty years ago. They had the treaty in hand at the last conference, and they looked back — at their fear, at their budgets — and it dissolved. So now they send me a child." She sat. "Your briefs say we do not intermarry. That four percent of Othan is of mixed lineage." "Three percent, by our figures," Orie said. "Eleven, by yours." The great eyes widened a very little, and were pleased. "So the offworlder reads two books. Why did you leave the reception?" Orie considered lying and had no time to build a good one. "Because I had read four hundred pages about your people and never met one." "Wrong answer," said Odai, and let the silence stand. Orie rose halfway to go, and then did not, and sat again, and let the silence spend itself. "No," the Minister said at last. "The only answer. Listen, then. Your Accord offers us genetic services. Correction, you call it. We did not ask to be corrected, Envoy. We asked to be visited. The tension your briefs fear is not shel against duru. It is Tem against the map of Tem — and your people keep redrawing the map and calling it the country." She set down the pot. "You will come again. Not as envoy. As the girl who reads walls. Her I will talk to. Now go, and tell your Chief you were tested and failed, and see whether she believes you." Orie went out through the mirror-light. On the cistern wall the girl went down into the earth, and the earth kept her, and in its season she came up. The stone did not promise she came up unchanged. Only that she came up.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of Ursula K. Le Guin's literary style, successfully capturing her anthropological approach to science fiction, her measured prose rhythm, and her focus on cultural observation over action. The author creates a believable alien society in Othan, with its underground city, light-shaft architecture, and complex social structures that feel lived-in rather than constructed for plot convenience. The characterization is particularly strong. Orie emerges as a credible young diplomat - curious, somewhat naive, but intelligent enough to recognize the gaps between official briefings and reality. Her decision to leave the reception feels authentic to her character and age. Minister Odai is expertly crafted as a seasoned political operator, using silence and misdirection as weapons while revealing genuine depth in her concerns about cultural autonomy versus outside "correction." The world-building excels through specific, concrete details: the thief's mark beside light-wells, the carved mythological figures, the tea stall interaction, and especially the revelation that lineage adoption contradicts the official briefings. These details serve both atmospheric and thematic purposes, supporting the central tension between perception and reality. The dialogue feels natural and purposeful, particularly Odai's testing of Orie through the Orpheus reference and her final dismissal that is simultaneously a invitation. The conversation crackles with subtext and political maneuvering while remaining accessible. The prose maintains Le Guin's characteristic restraint and precision. Sentences like "Lineage here was a house, not a chain" demonstrate the author's ability to convey complex social concepts economically. The mythological framework (Prometheus, Persephone, Orpheus, Charon) provides thematic coherence without feeling forced. However, some elements feel slightly underdeveloped. The physical descriptions of the different morphs could be more vivid, and the political stakes, while present, could use more concrete grounding. The ending, while thematically appropriate, leaves perhaps too many threads unresolved for a complete chapter experience. The piece successfully avoids common science fiction pitfalls - no exposition dumps, no overwrought descriptions of technology, no simplistic cultural conflicts. Instead, it focuses on the subtle complexities of intercultural contact and the limitations of bureaucratic understanding. Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Eleven: Amplicon The solar rig coughed at two in the afternoon—thirteen volts sagging to eleven—and the thermocycler beeped its one flat note of complaint. "Pin." Suture didn't look up from the gel she was casting. "Clouds?" "Ash bank, coming off the ridge." The boy sat cross-legged before the multimeter, watching the needle like it owed him money. "Riding the caps. Six minutes." Six minutes of grace from the defibrillator capacitors she'd gutted and wired in parallel behind the bench. After that, the bicycle. The thermocycler was the heart of the lab and its most patient liar. She'd hauled it from a flooded Providence Agrigenics depot two winters back, power board green with corrosion, and rebuilt it around a scooter controller with firmware she'd burned by hand. The heated lid was a hair straightener. The block held temperature within half a degree if you didn't rush it, and if the sun held, and if the caps held, and if the world held. Cycle twenty-two of thirty-five. Inside the tubes: DNA from a Granary potato leaf, primers she'd dried onto filter paper five years ago, and the last corporate Taq in the territory, riding a cellar thermos packed with mountain ice. Eight hundred and forty base pairs. The length of the lock. Five years since the Fallow—the spring the world's engineered fields came up green and set no seed, and every contract outlived its courts. Providence had sold forty percent of the calories on Earth, and sold them with a license: one generation, then buy again. Then there was nobody left to buy from. Ossuary had come at dawn with the fog, a lean man in a coat too good for the road, and set a steel case on her bench. Two hundred reactions of freeze-dried polymerase, corporate stock, expiry date printed in a year that no longer meant anything. Beneath the foam: a sleeve of primers, a charge controller still in shrink wrap, antibiotics thick as a hymnal. "The Provost's terms," he said. "The Granary's Prov-7 line. Excise the HarvestLock cassette. Deliver cuttings that breed true. Payment on verification of a second generation." "Verification takes a season." "The Provost plans in generations. It's why she's still feeding people." A pause, courteous as a knife laid flat. "And why Halstead isn't." Halstead had refused the tithe. The Granary had burned it to its footings and salted the ash with herbicide. Everyone at the Terraces remembered. She'd signed anyway. Her tomatoes were browning in vitro for want of enzyme, and the seed vault was a dream with a deadline. The contract wanted her thumbprint; she pressed the pad and left a blank smear. The Graft had taken her fingerprints years ago, along with everything else Providence had ever given anybody. The Graft. Three years ago, coughing blood into a rag, she'd dosed herself with a salvaged pulmonary vector—wrong blood type, never trialed past Phase One—to rebuild lungs scarred by the Blight's spore-fall. It worked. It also ran her body at thirty-nine degrees, so she saved incubator power by strapping culture vials to her forearms overnight and letting the fever do the work. Her skin healed in half the time it should; last week's burn from the ninety-five-degree block was already a pink rumor across her knuckles. The blight fungus couldn't colonize her at all. The price was nightsweats that soaked the mattress, graft-lines that itched like solder, a tremor when it flared. And the vector was fading—somatic by design. One body. One lifetime. No inheritance. Providence had written the same license into her lungs they'd written into the world's wheat: it would die with her, and her children, if she had them, would be born owing. At cycle twenty-nine the ash bank swallowed the sun and the caps bled dry. Pin was already on the bicycle, hammering, the needle quivering at every annealing drop. "Ninety-four point six," Suture read. "Hold it, hold it—" The block sagged toward the eighties and the controller clawed it back. At cycle thirty-three the boy's legs went rubbery, and she took the seat without a word, pedaling through the flare that lit her forearms up like filaments, sweat sheeting, hands steady through sheer spite. Three years ago that effort would have drowned her in her own chest. Her rebuilt lungs took it like bellows. She held seventy-two degrees through the final extension and did not get off the bike until the machine chimed done. She loaded the gel with an insulin syringe scored in microliters—agarose from the university stash, running buffer mixed from laundry borax and battery acid—and ran it in a food container threaded with platinum wire pulled from a catalytic converter. Ethidium bromide, the carcinogen she'd inherited: one more thing that wouldn't live long enough to kill her. Under the germicidal wand in its plywood box, viewed through a welding filter, the bands glowed clean and bright. Eight hundred forty base pairs. The lock, amplified, mapped, ready to cut. While Ossuary's man waited at the gate, she loaded one more lane. Terrace tomato DNA, same primers. Providence had used one lock everywhere, the way cheap companies do, and whatever edit she built for the Granary's potatoes would open her own tomatoes like a door. The contract said all products of the run belonged to the Provost. The gel said otherwise. She photographed nothing. She dried the amplicon onto filter paper and slid it into her primer book, between the sequences, where the dead company's handwriting lived. At dusk the panels went dark for good and Ossuary left with his guards and his half of a handshake, believing what he'd been told. Suture stood in the cooling lab, fever ticking down, fingertips raw where the prints used to be. Providence had engineered the ending into everything—seeds, lungs, futures—and called it a license. Fine. Let the Granary own this generation. She was already working on the next one.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This biopunk chapter demonstrates strong technical writing and worldbuilding within the specified parameters. The author creates a convincing post-apocalyptic setting where corporate genetic engineering with built-in obsolescence has led to societal collapse, and follows biohacker "Suture" as she works to circumvent genetic locks in crops. The technical aspects are particularly well-executed. The author displays genuine understanding of PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) processes, using accurate terminology like "thermocycler," "primers," "Taq polymerase," and "base pairs." The jury-rigged equipment feels authentic - a thermocycler rebuilt with a scooter controller, a hair straightener for a heated lid, and a bicycle generator for power. These details create believable improvisation without feeling forced. The worldbuilding is economical but effective. The "Fallow" event, Providence Agrigenics' licensing model, and the political dynamics between settlements like the Granary and Halstead are established through context rather than exposition. The protagonist's "Graft" - her self-administered genetic modification that rebuilt her lungs but runs her body hot - serves both plot and character functions while illustrating the story's themes about genetic modification's costs and benefits. Suture emerges as a compelling character through her actions and circumstances rather than explicit characterization. Her missing fingerprints, her calculated risk-taking, and her quiet defiance of the contract terms reveal personality efficiently. The supporting characters like Pin and Ossuary are sketched minimally but serve their functions well. The prose maintains a consistent, clinical tone that matches the scientific setting while incorporating evocative imagery. Phrases like "the needle quivering at every annealing drop" and "fever that lit her forearms up like filaments" blend technical precision with poetic language effectively. The chapter's structure builds tension through the PCR process itself, using the technical procedure as a dramatic framework. The power failures, the physical demands of maintaining temperature, and the race against time create genuine suspense from mundane laboratory work. However, the piece has some weaknesses. The ending, while thematically appropriate, feels somewhat predictable - the clever protagonist outwitting the corporate power structure. Some of the technical language, while accurate, may alienate readers unfamiliar with molecular biology. The emotional stakes, while present, could be more deeply developed to create stronger reader investment. The dialogue is minimal but functional, though it lacks distinctive character voices. Pin's sparse technical updates and Ossuary's formal threats serve their purposes without being particularly memorable. Overall, this is sophisticated genre fiction that successfully fulfills its prompt requirements while demonstrating strong technical knowledge and worldbuilding skills. The integration of real science with speculative elements is particularly well-handled. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Seven: The Honored Guest For the third time in as many minutes, Arthur Neegan adjusted his collar, and for the third time it refused to sit properly against his throat. The tunic was Earth-cut, of stiff recyclate-linen, and it had been waiting for him in a sealed garment bag aboard the shuttle before anyone had told him he would need a garment bag, or a shuttle, or that six polite men with sidearms would arrive at his habitat at dawn and address him as *sir*. Through the ferry's viewport, Mars was shrinking to a rust-colored coin. Arthur watched it go and tried to assemble the morning into something sensible. He was a mining engineer. He owned four hundred hectares of regolith and a broken spectrometer. Eleven days ago he had dug a trench for a water line and found Azra glittering in the wall of it like frost. Now he wore a dead man's collar aboard a vessel he hadn't been told the name of, flying toward a meeting he hadn't been told the purpose of, wearing insignia he hadn't been invited to identify. The insignia was a silver wreath and stars. He had looked it up in the ferry's slim shipboard library: Antares diplomatic corps. Diplomatic, Arthur thought, in the way a trench knife was cutlery. "The Undersecretary prefers punctuality," said the lieutenant who had introduced herself only as Maren. She stood by the airlock with her hands folded, as though armed courtesy were a posture one could hold indefinitely. "Who is the Undersecretary?" "You'll be briefed, sir." "Will I be told where I'm going?" The ferry's atomic jets sighed through their turnover burn. Maren smiled with professional warmth and said nothing at all. The *Meridian* was three kilometers of gray hull, and inside it was wood. Actual wood — paneling, a desk, a floor that creaked. Arthur had never stood on a creaking floor in his life. The cost of hauling one board of it from Earth would have kept his habitat in oxygen for a year, and he said so. "Two years," said the woman behind the desk, without looking up from her papers. Actual papers. "Cedar is light. Please sit, Mr. Neegan. You've been fidgeting with that collar since you came aboard the ferry. I watched you on the cabin feed. It doesn't fit because it wasn't cut for you. Very little aboard this ship was cut for you, so let us dispense with pretense early and save time." She was perhaps fifty, gray at the temples, with the kind of stillness that Arthur associated with deep rock — the certainty that everything above her would eventually settle. She poured tea from a bulb-decanter. Real tea. He could smell it from the chair. "I'm Undersecretary Voss. Antares Compact, External Affairs. You know what Azra does?" "Folklore says it makes radium go quiet. I've seen a sample fog a film badge across a sealed room, and I've seen a reactor-fed assay lamp burn nine years of fuel in a week. So it doesn't make anything quiet. It makes everything *fast*." "Then you know more than the Terran Directorate's public position, which is that Azra doesn't exist, and slightly less than their private position, which is that no one else must be allowed to have it. Consider the arithmetic, Mr. Neegan. A fistful of Azra in the right place idles a battleship's pile. A ton of it takes a ship to Antares in four months instead of four centuries. It is simultaneously the end of atomic weapons and the beginning of interstellar empire. Every power in the system has done this arithmetic. Several have done it about you specifically." "Because of my trench." "Because your four hundred hectares sit on a vein the survey now estimates at greater mass than every corporate claim in the Tharsis leaseholds combined. The Combine companies have spent nine years stripping Mars with indentured labor to get one percent of what you tripped over digging a water line. There is a certain comedy in that which I hope you appreciate, because no one else in the system will be permitted to." Arthur set down his teacup. "Then why am I drinking tea instead of disappearing? The Combine lost a prospector at Elysium last year. Seal failure, the report said." "Seal failures are remarkably common wherever Azra is found. Which is why you are drinking tea with *us*, Mr. Neegan. Under the Martian Homestead Act, a first-generation claim cannot be transferred to any non-colonial entity. The Directorate would simply seize you under the Lunar Accords — exotic minerals are strategic state property, they say. The Combine would lease you, indenture you, and let a seal fail. We propose something old-fashioned." She slid a document across the cedar desk. Paper, printed, with a signature line. "You remain owner of record. The Compact operates extraction through the *Neegan Extraction Concern* — a company consisting of yourself, a rubber stamp, and eventually several thousand of our employees. You receive an annuity of two hundred thousand credits per year, colonial citizenship, and our protection." "In exchange for the vein." "In exchange for your name on a lease. The law is the only thing currently preventing open war over your trench, Mr. Neegan. Whoever breaks the law first unites everyone else against them. We prefer not to be first. We intend, in fact, to be *legal*, and legality on Mars wears your face." Arthur looked at the document without touching it. "And what does the Compact want Azra for? Roads?" "Azra is a weapon that makes weapons useless. Whoever holds it decides whether anyone else's atomics function at all. We would prefer that holder be us. Second best — that it be a reasonable man." She folded her hands. "You have until the Terran cruiser *Resolute* reaches orbit. Thirty-one hours. After that, your options narrow considerably." Arthur looked at the silver wreath on her breast for a long moment. "One question. Your insignia has eleven stars." "The Compact charter has nine." "So it does." Voss's expression didn't change, but something behind it did — approval, or appetite. "You count, Mr. Neegan. Good. A man who counts survives longer in this system. Think on the arithmetic." The tea went cold between them. Neither poured more. Through the viewport behind her, Mars hung like a bent coin, and Arthur thought of his four hundred hectares of quiet red dirt, which were quiet no longer, and never would be again.

The characterization is solid, particularly Undersecretary Voss, who embodies the calculating, politically astute figures common in Asimov's work. Her dialogue feels natural and reveals character through subtext - her casual mention of watching Arthur on cabin feeds and her measured responses to his questions establish her as someone accustomed to control. Arthur's reactions are believable for someone thrust into circumstances beyond his understanding, though he could be slightly more developed. The prose is elegant and restrained, avoiding purple language while maintaining vivid imagery. However, the piece has some minor weaknesses. The political intrigue, while well-established, follows somewhat predictable patterns - the powerful entity making an offer the protagonist can't refuse is a familiar trope. Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations I'm good at knowing what I want. Ask anyone—my professors, my exes, the guy at the paint counter who tried to talk me out of cadmium red. I walk into rooms like I built them. So it's strange, being in this one, twelve square feet of blackout curtain and vinegar-smelling air, not knowing anything at all. Third night in the darkroom with Elliot. Our final project is due Friday and we're behind, which is technically his fault—he's a perfectionist about negatives—but I haven't minded. I haven't minded at all. He works with his head down, chipped black polish, silver rings clicking against the tray edges. Nu-goth by way of the thrift store on Fifth: lace cuffs over a band tee, boots that cost him eight dollars and look like a threat. He's nineteen and quiet in a way that isn't shy, exactly. More like he's saving his words for something worth them. I'm used to being the loudest thing in a room. Around him, I keep ending up quiet too. "Test strip," he says, sliding the paper under the enlarger. I set the timer. We've got a rhythm now, hands passing tongs, no eye contact necessary—which is good, because the safelight turns everything the color of a secret and I've stopped trusting what my face does under it. The strip goes into the developer. Ten seconds. Fifteen. Grays bloom up out of nothing. That's the thing about this place that gets me. The paper is never blank. It's full the second the light hits it—holding an entire image, invisible, patient—until the chemistry calls it forward. Latent, they call it. I used to think that was the saddest word. Now I'm not sure it isn't the most hopeful one. "Elliot." He's been holding a negative sleeve for ten minutes without taking anything out. "You're hovering." "I'm not." He is. His hands are shaking slightly, the way prints shake when the wash runs too cold. He's six years younger than me and some old instinct wants to stand between him and anything sharp. But he's not fragile. He's developing. "Do you ever," he says, and stops. Starts again. "Shoot something you don't want anyone to see?" "Constantly. That's what the shoebox under my bed is for." Half a laugh out of him. He slides one negative free and holds it against the safelight like he's deciding whether to burn it. "I've been thinking about the word *pretty*," he says, to the negative, not to me. "Not about anyone. About me. Whether it would fit." A pause. "I bought eyeliner first because that seemed easy. Then it wasn't enough, and I don't know what that means. I don't know what I am, Dani. I keep trying to figure out if that's a question I'm even allowed to ask." Every instinct I have is a fire alarm. I want to say *of course you're allowed*, and here's a reading list, and here's the good vintage store, and I'll fight anyone who looks at you wrong. I want to make it a campaign. "You should—" I start, and hear myself, the whole machinery of Dani gearing up to fix him. He waits. He's used to people finishing his sentences, I realize. I close my mouth. Try again. "What does it feel like? When you try the word on." He looks up like I've handed him something. "Like a photo before the developer. Like it's there and I can't see it yet." I don't have a follow-up. Dani, twenty-five, professionally opinionated, does not have a follow-up. Because here's the thing I've been not-thinking about all semester: I like people who are finished sentences. Women who dress like they could rebuild an engine. Men with a whole aesthetic and a thesis about it. I like knowing what I'm looking at. It's tidy. It's hot. It has never once felt like this. "Can I show you something," he says—not a question, the way he says it. He sets the negative in the enlarger, focuses, and I feed the paper in without being asked. We're a machine now. The image comes up in the tray between us. Him, in a slip he must have gotten from somewhere, lace at the shoulders, face turned three-quarters to the camera with an expression I've never seen him wear in daylight—like he's daring the photo to laugh at him. Soft and severe at once. The red light makes his eyeliner look like candlelight. It is, objectively, the best thing he's ever shot. My phone buzzes against my thigh—once, twice, insistent. Marcus, probably, wanting to know if I'm coming out, wanting the version of me that has answers about everything. I let it die in my pocket. "You look like you mean it," I say. "That's the whole trick of a portrait. Most people never do." He lets out a breath he's been holding since Tuesday. Maybe longer. His shoulder is against mine now; I don't remember when that happened. The print needs the fixer. Neither of us moves. "Does it change anything?" he asks, quiet. "For you. I've seen how you look at people. People who know what they are." There it is—the question I've been asking myself in the dark for weeks. I don't know how to say that I've never watched anyone become anything before, and it turns out that's the whole show. That the not-knowing, on him, is the most defined thing in this room. "I'm figuring out what I'm looking at," I say. "But I haven't looked away once." The fixer timer chirps. He reaches for the tongs and his hand lands over mine—half accident, half not—and stays. "Same time tomorrow?" he says. "I'll bring the good paper." I don't move my hand either. Some things you don't rush. You leave them in the chemicals long enough to hold.

Her self-awareness about her usual patterns ("the whole machinery of Dani gearing up to fix him") demonstrates psychological depth. The prose strikes an effective balance between literary sophistication and accessibility. Phrases like "I walk into rooms like I built them" and "hands passing tongs, no eye contact necessary" are memorable without being overwrought. The photography metaphors enhance rather than overwhelm the narrative. The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes—revealing character, advancing plot, and exploring themes. Elliot's tentative sharing about gender identity avoids both clinical exposition and melodrama. Dani's responses show her learning to listen rather than immediately problem-solve. The pacing builds tension effectively through the three darkroom sessions, culminating in Elliot sharing his self-portrait. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the metaphorical language borders on being too neat (the latent image comparison, while effective, is somewhat predictable given the setting). Prompt:

This will form the beginning of a larger story. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Model Output:
# Stolen Moments in Roma The guidebook was to blame, Ben decided later — he had stepped off the kerb backwards, pencil in the margin, mid-correction. (The book credited Bernini with the Trevi. It was Salvi's fountain; Bernini had only sketched it, and someone ought to say so.) Brakes shrieked. The world tilted. A motorcycle shuddered to a halt close enough that he smelled hot rubber, citrus, cigarettes. "*Ma sei scemo?!*" The rider wrenched off her helmet. Dark hair, incandescent eyes. "*Ti sembra il posto di camminare all'indietro?! In mezzo alla strada!*" "I'm so sorry — *mi dispiace* — terribly — *moltissimo*—" She stared. "*Moltissimo*," she repeated, tasting it. "You apologize like a man losing a fight with weather." "It's the guidebook's fault," Ben said. "It's wrong about the fountain." She snatched it from his hands and read his pencilled marginalia, eyebrows climbing. "You correct your guidebook. In pencil." "It was wrong." "Nobody corrects Rome." "Someone ought to." Something happened to her mouth — a laugh escaping custody. She looked at him the way one looks at a stray dog that has just performed arithmetic. Then, briskly, she patted his shoulders and chest, ostensibly checking for damage. "You have plans today?" "A walking tour. Baroque churches—" "You have different plans now." She held out a spare helmet. "Alessandra. Get on." "I haven't — that is — insurance-wise—" "Professore." She'd read the flyleaf; his name was in it. "Get on the bike." *** Rome at forty kilometres an hour was the same city finally telling the truth. Alessandra's scarred old Ducati threaded gaps Ben would have sworn were optical illusions. She delivered a dress to a tailor off Via del Governo Vecchio, documents to a notary above a butcher's; everywhere, people shouted her name — greeting or warning, in Rome the same word. She took a one-way street the wrong way, one-handed, gesturing for Ben to stop praying. In Trastevere she bought two coffees at the bar and, while the barista's back was turned, pocketed a lighter off the counter. "You don't smoke," Ben said. "Not today." She flicked it, caught it. "It wanted to travel." "Did you pay for—" "I paid for the coffee. The lighter volunteered." He should have said something. He drank his coffee instead, and the silence where his objection should have been felt briefly, alarmingly, like freedom. *** In the afternoon she talked them past a hotel doorman — "*ispezione*," she said solemnly, with the confidence of a woman never once asked *ispezione of what* — and up a service stair to a rooftop where Rome's domes lay steaming like a just-cooked meal. She lifted two glasses of prosecco from a tray and left money for one. "You paid for one glass," Ben observed. "I paid for the idea of both." She handed him one. "Bernini," she added, nodding at the skyline as if the man owed her money. "A show-off." "A genius." "Same thing." Ben heard himself deliver, in Italian of frankly archaeological quality, a defence of the colonnade of St. Peter's — and heard the terrace staff applaud. Alessandra watched him with narrowed, delighted eyes, as though she'd suspected something about him all along and was now being proven right. *** The sky broke at four — Roman rain, warm, sudden, biblical. Tourists stampeded; Alessandra took Ben's wrist and *strolled*, of all things, through the steaming streets, and installed them beneath the striped awning of a gelateria as the gutters ran silver. They stood close, dripping. She wrung out her hair. Then, because rain was "not a reason against gelato — rain is a reason for it," she went in and bought two cones anyway: pistachio for herself, fior di latte for him. "You are a fior di latte man," she informed him. "Am I?" "You are now." At the register her hand drifted across the postcard rack, and a card of the Pantheon vanished into her jacket, smooth as a card trick. Ben saw. She saw him see. She didn't blink, and he looked away first — complicit, his pulse doing something profoundly unscholarly. Under the awning, rain drumming, they ate gelato and watched Rome rinse itself. "Why me?" he asked finally. "Today." She watched the water sheet off the stripes. "This morning you stepped off a curb backwards with your nose in a book. No idea what was behind you." "A motorcycle, as it happens." "A whole city, Professore. You were about to waste it." She licked pistachio off her thumb. "Also — most people never step anywhere without looking first. It was the bravest stupid thing I've seen all week." He turned toward her. She leaned in — close enough that he counted raindrops in her eyelashes — then straightened his collar instead. "Not yet," she said. "You're still deciding whether you're the man who does this." "I'm fairly sure I'm not." "Good," she said. "That's the fun part." *** By dusk the streets had dried to a smell of wet stone and jasmine, and she brought him back where they'd begun, the Trevi floodlit and murmuring to itself. She handed him the spare helmet. "Tuesday. Testaccio market, eight o'clock. You return my helmet, I return your dignity." "Could I — your number, perhaps—" "Numbers are for people with no imagination. Give me a coin." He patted his pockets. Empty. Alessandra held a fifty-cent piece between two fingers, eyes bright with the day's first open mischief. "You had one this morning," she said. "When I checked you for damage." She turned her back to the water and threw it over her shoulder — proper form — and the coin flashed and vanished. "One coin means you return to Rome," she said. "That one was yours." "And two?" "Two is romance. Three is marriage." She swung onto the Ducati and kicked it alive. "Ask me Tuesday." She kissed him then — brief, certain, tasting of pistachio — and was gone, the engine's echo rolling off the travertine long after her taillight had. At his hotel, reaching for his room key, Ben found something in his jacket pocket that had not been there that morning: the postcard of the Pantheon. On the back, in fierce, slanting script: *You never once told me to stop. — A.* He sat down on the edge of the bed with his wet shoes, his stolen postcard, and his heart going like a small engine, and began — for the first time in his careful life — to look forward to a Tuesday.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and creative execution within the contemporary romance genre. The author successfully creates two distinct, compelling characters whose personalities emerge naturally through action and dialogue rather than exposition. Alessandra's kleptomaniac tendencies are woven seamlessly into the narrative through subtle actions (the lighter, the gelato postcard) that reveal character without heavy-handed explanation. The prose style is sophisticated and economical, with particularly strong metaphorical language ("Rome at forty kilometres an hour was the same city finally telling the truth"). The dialogue feels authentic to each character - Alessandra's rapid-fire Italian mixed with sharp English observations contrasts effectively with Ben's flustered academic politeness. The author handles the language barrier naturally, using it to enhance rather than complicate the romantic tension. The structure works well, using short vignette-style scenes that build momentum while revealing character depth. The pacing accelerates appropriately, mirroring Ben's growing comfort with spontaneity. The Rome setting is vividly rendered without becoming touristy or clichéd - the author clearly knows the city and uses specific details effectively. The romantic tension builds believably through small moments and stolen glances rather than forced dramatic gestures. Ben's transformation from cautious academic to willing accomplice feels earned through the accumulation of small boundary-crossings. Alessandra remains appropriately enigmatic while showing enough vulnerability to avoid being a mere manic pixie dream girl archetype. The ending strikes the right note - romantic but not overly saccharine, with the postcard revelation providing a satisfying callback that deepens our understanding of both characters. The coin-throwing scene provides cultural authenticity while serving the romantic plot. Minor weaknesses include some slightly precious moments ("rain is a reason for it") and the occasional overly clever turn of phrase, but these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. The piece successfully establishes the foundation for a longer work while providing satisfying closure to this particular day. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 80.9
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Last Outpost ## Chapter One: Neat The gravity dips at quarter past nine, the way it always does when the recyclers cycle, and every glass on my bar shivers like it knows something. I watch the ring of condensation crawl off Dozer's stout. Third refill tonight. Dozer drinks the way he mines—slow, patient, all shift. Three by nine means something's chewing on him. "Say it," I tell him. "Say what?" He folds hands that could palm an ore crate around the glass like it's a sparrow. "You've rearranged your face six times since you sat down. Rhea's supply run docks Tuesday, and you've been rehearsing something since Thursday. Out with it." Prisha snorts into her fizz from the far end. "He wrote it down. Saw him in the galley, mouthing at a napkin." "It's a draft," Dozer says, with dignity. "It's a napkin." "There are four drafts." "Read me draft four." He mumbles something about how her smile should be classified as a navigational hazard. "That's the one. Give her that." "Out loud? With my mouth?" "Words on paper, Doze. You hand her the napkin, you say *I wrote you something*, and you walk away. Let the napkin be brave for you." "Nets, you're a genius." He toasts me with his stout. "I'm a bartender. Same thing." The gravity hiccups again; the amber in Prisha's glass leans left, then remembers itself. That's the Outpost for you—nothing level, nothing straight, and everyone stays anyway. Including me. Especially me. Dozer pays in ore scrip and folds himself out the door, napkin pressed to his chest like a prayer. Prisha wanders off to argue with her cargo manifest. For a minute it's just me, the hum of the recycler, and Mopsy the fern under her grow light. The quiet is good. So naturally, that's when the door slides open. She's tall-ish, wrapped in a flight coat with no guild patch, and her dreads—a dozen dark tentacles, gene-spliced or alien, I can't tell from here—hang askew, one kinked like a bent hose. You don't see tentacled dreads unkempt. It's like seeing a bird with wet feathers. She takes the stool at the end. The one with sightlines to both the door and the dock readout. She doesn't take off the coat. "Vega whisky, neat." Her voice is sandpaper. "Better make that a double." Vega whisky isn't a drink you enjoy. It's a drink you take like medicine. I pour it, set it down; the gravity wobbles and the whisky shivers, and she watches it like it might be a threat. "You're the bartender," she says. Not a question. "Last one awake, anyway. Rough docking?" "Rough decade." She takes the double like a shot—no savoring, just down—and taps the glass for another. Her eyes flick up to the manifest glowing over my shelf. Reading it. Counting berths. I pour the second. It's a talent of mine, pouring the drink people actually need instead of the one they order. She needs this one slower, so I make it a single and slide it over. She notices. Her dreads flare faintly, then settle. "Cheapskate," she says, but she sips this one. "You keep looking at the dock readout like it owes you money." "Maybe it does." A tentacle curls around her glass—they do that, I've seen it in vids, anchor themselves when the owner's hands aren't steady. Hers aren't. "How many ships come through on a slow night?" "Depends who's asking." "Someone looking for a person." She turns on the stool, and I get the full weight of her attention, tired and sharp at once. "Human, or near enough. Tall. Burn scars up one forearm, like she lost an argument with a still. Used to pour on the Ceres side, then Vega Station, then nowhere. Went by Sparrow. Went by Vesper." Old habit: I clock the exits. Two years at the end of nowhere and I still do it. The glass in my hand doesn't shake. That's the other talent—the lying. The one I never found a shelf for. It pours out of me smooth and cold, no sediment. "Doesn't ring a bell." "Mm." She sips. "Someone told me she'd be tending bar at the ass end of the arm. Said she can't stay away from a barstool and a problem, and this place is nothing but." One dread points, lazily, at me. "You've got a scar's shape under that sleeve. Left arm, though. Maybe she's a lefty now. Maybe she's you." "I'm nobody's anything," I say, and wipe a glass that's already clean. "Who sent you?" "Paid me half up front to find her first." She taps the bar, twice. "The other half is the part that worries me, because the people hunting her don't send warnings. But I was paid to deliver one anyway." She leans in, dreads coiling tight. "Tell her: *they woke Cadmus.*" The name goes through me like a coolant leak. The fern, the hum, Prisha's laugh from the cargo bay—all of it drops away, and I'm twenty-six again, and running. Then the dock chime sounds. One bright note. The manifest refreshes over my shelf. *Berth six: incoming vessel. No transponder. No registry. Requesting atmosphere.* The stranger's dreads go rigid, all twelve, like a hand closing into a fist. "That's them," she says. The gravity dips. Every glass on my bar shivers. This time, I know what.

+ Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 85.9
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.

# Gone South ## Chapter Two: Where Y'at The sprinklers in Jackson Square come on at five a.m. and nobody warns you about that. I woke up soaked to the knees on a bench under an oak tree older than the whole state of Tennessee, while somewhere behind the cathedral a trumpet player warmed up like the world's most aggressive alarm clock. New Orleans in the morning smells like the river—diesel and mud and something sweet underneath. Beignet sugar, maybe. Or jasmine. Or the city just rotting beautifully into itself. This is my life now. I ran away to a place that smells like dessert and decay. Fitting. Habit had me checking my phone before my eyes were all the way open. 12%. Forty-seven texts from Mom. I read three. Mistake. *I'm not angry, just come home.* That one used my name. *Your father didn't mean it, he just needs time.* That one used the other one—the dead one—the name Mom still reaches for when she's scared. *Taylor, I'm calling the police in one hour.* That came eleven hours ago, which means she didn't call, or the police are slow, and I don't know which option drops my stomach harder. Two days ago—only two, though it feels like a whole school year—Dad didn't even yell. That was the worst part. He just went quiet and looked at me like I was a receipt for something he never ordered. Mom cried in the kitchen with the exhaust fan running, like that ever hid anything from anybody. So last night I emptied the shoebox—$211, count it—and got out. Anyway. Present tense. Focus. By nine I was starving in the way that stops being an emotion and becomes a sound, a low hum behind my ribs, walking Decatur with my bag strap across my chest like I'd invented caution. A man with a laminated lanyard and a smile with too much investment in it fell into step beside me. "You lost, sweetheart? You look like you could be somebody. You model?" "I—" I said, brilliantly. "There you *are*." A hand grabbed my sleeve. Small hand, chipped black polish, attached to a person maybe fifteen or maybe nineteen—buzzed hair growing out, army jacket in eighty-five-degree humidity, flip-flops, a nose peeling with sunburn. Eyes that did math on the lanyard guy in half a second. "Been looking *everywhere*. Auntie's gonna kill us." And just like that, towed me down the block while the smile evaporated behind us. "Rule one," my rescuer said once we'd turned the corner. "Nobody out here buys you breakfast for free. Nobody 'scouts' you for free. Free is the most expensive thing there is." "Thanks. I guess." "Don't guess. Know it." A head tilt, reading me like a billboard. "Day one?" "...Day one." "Lord." Almost fond. "What do they call you?" Here it comes, I thought, and braced. "Taylor." "Taylor what?" "Just Taylor." "Okay, Just Taylor. I'm Dez. Off Desire Street." When I looked confused, Dez shrugged. "Named myself off a street sign. Everybody out here picks their name off a map one way or another." *Just Taylor.* No follow-up. No *what's it short for*, no *what did your mama put on your birth certificate*, no eyebrow. Dez didn't ask because Dez didn't care, or because Dez already knew something about names, and either way my chest did something complicated that I filed under *later*. Dez fed me. Not with money—with knowledge, which is apparently the same thing here. The church on Rampart does breakfast at eight sharp and Sister Bernadette doesn't ask questions, just don't cuss in the line. The library on St. Charles has AC and outlets— "Outlets," I said, clutching my phone like a rosary. 10% now. "Ration it. That thing's your lifeline and your leash both. Airplane mode till you need it. Want it to last the week? Treat it like it's already dead." Dez talked in rules and it should've gotten old, but every rule was a door I didn't know existed. Don't sleep in the Quarter after dark. Cops ride horses down here and horses don't have feelings about your rights. Keep your business to yourself; lie small, lie boring. That last one I had covered—I'm an expert liar from a town where everybody invents their own drama. Except Dez lied too. Somewhere between the church and the river, Dez mentioned California—*saving up, heading west, week or two*—and the tone was exactly the one I use on the school counselor, bright and rehearsed, a lie worn smooth from handling. I didn't call it. You don't call somebody's lie on day one of your whole entire new life. And there was the phone. Dead since March, by Dez's own admission, but it rode in the army-jacket pocket like it was alive. I asked why carry it. Dez went still in a way that had nothing to do with the street. "One number in there I ain't figured out how to delete yet." Then a laugh, like we'd been joking, and the subject changed to brass bands, and I let it be changed. We ended the day on the riverfront, the sky going orange behind the cathedral, the Mississippi churning past like chocolate milk with commitment issues. And I felt—this is the part I can't make make sense—I felt more like myself than I ever have, and more like nothing at all. Nobody here knows the name on my birth certificate. Nobody here knows to use it. Dez evaporated around sunset like streetlights were a curfew, leaving me half a granola bar, directions to the library, and a warning about a van. I don't know if Dez was a friend or a recruiter with better manners. Trust is apparently also something you ration. 7%. I opened Mom's thread. Typed *I'm safe.* Deleted it. Typed it again. My thumb hovered over send like it was a cliff. Two words cost me one percent. I hit send and shut the phone off before the reply dots could appear, so whatever Mom said back is sitting behind a black screen until morning, like a present I'm too scared to shake. Day one. I'm still Taylor.
