+ Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# OLD SCHOOL ### Chapter One: No Refunds My thirteenth birthday started out normal. Pancakes. Twenty bucks from Grandma. And one small box with no return address. Inside was a smartwatch. Black band, silver face, no brand name — just a tiny hourglass etched beneath the screen. The card read: **HAPPY BIRTHDAY, DEX. SWIPE LEFT TO GO BACK.** And underneath, in very small print: **NO REFUNDS.** No note about who sent it. Mom guessed Aunt Carla, which tracked, because Aunt Carla once gave me a coupon book for a restaurant that had closed down. The watch did normal watch stuff. Steps. Heart rate. Weather. And a number in the corner of the screen that said **13**. I figured it was the date. It was not the date. The first rewind happened Tuesday at lunch. I was carrying my tray past the eighth-grade table when Marcus Bell stuck out his sneaker. I went down hard. Chili everywhere — my shirt, my hair, the floor. The whole cafeteria laughed. Marcus laughed loudest. I sat there in the chili, ears burning, and did what anyone would do: I slapped my watch and swiped left across the face, like I could flick the moment away. I could. The world went backward. Kids slid backward across the floor. The chili rose off the tiles in red ribbons and flew back onto my tray. Laughter played in reverse — *ha-ha-ha* became *ah-ah-ah*. Marcus's leg un-stuck itself. Then everything snapped forward, normal speed, and I was walking with my tray again, and Marcus's sneaker was sliding out — I stepped over it. Marcus stared like I'd levitated. I walked to my table with my heart slamming and zero chili on me. Here's the weird part. Well — the *first* weird part. Tuesday's lunch was supposed to be sloppy joes. That day it was pizza. Nobody noticed but me. That night my jeans were two inches too short. "Growth spurt," Mom said. On the phone, my voice came out low and croaky, like a stranger borrowing my mouth. Coincidence, I told myself. Thirteen-year-olds grow. The watch said **14** now. You have to understand: I was short, bad at dodgeball, and had once cried at a spelling bee. The watch was the first thing that had ever gone right for me. So I kept swiping. I un-dropped the fly ball in gym. I un-said the thing about Mr. Battaglia's tie. (Any fly could see it was terrible. But still.) Each time, the world hiccupped backward and handed me a do-over. Each time, it took something back. By Friday I was five foot nine. My voice had settled into a news anchor's. Dark fuzz sprouted above my lip. Zits arrived, then brought friends. Mr. Battaglia's tie was blue now. It had been red. Kids I'd known since kindergarten squinted at me. "Dex? You look... different." "You look like a gym teacher," said my best friend Priya. Ms. Alvarez asked if I was the new student aide. A cashier called me "sir." Mom booked a doctor's appointment and kept staring at me across the dinner table, like I might be a stranger wearing her son's face. The watch said **16**. Saturday morning, brushing my teeth, I finally made myself look hard at the bathroom mirror. For half a second — I swear on the sloppy joes — my reflection flickered. Not the tall kid with the mustache fuzz. An older face. *Way* older. Gray stubble. Deep grooves around the eyes. A tired face that had seen too many Tuesdays. Then it flickered back. Just me. Sort of me. I dropped my toothbrush and didn't pick it up for a full minute. That was the day I decided I was done. No more swiping. I'd throw the watch in the lake. I really, truly meant to. But that afternoon, walking home from the library, Priya stepped off the curb staring at her phone, and the 42 bus was coming, and the driver was looking at *his* phone, and I was too far away to — I swiped left. Hard. The bus slid backward. Priya moonwalked up onto the curb. Time snapped forward — and I caught her arm and yanked her back as the bus roared past, close enough to lift my hair. "Dex!" she yelled, shaking me off. "What is your prob—" She stopped. Her eyes went wide. "Wait. Do I know you?" That's when I felt it. The watch had pulled harder this time. Taken a bigger bite. My arm ached. My knees ached. Gray hairs — actual gray hairs — curled out from under the band. And the world had skipped. Our front door was blue. It had been red my whole life. Inside, a man stood in my kitchen. My dad — but older, thinner, grayer, like a photograph of Dad left in the sun. "Buddy," he said carefully, "this is the third time this week. You can't just walk into people's homes." "Dad. It's me. Dex." Mom came in, and I watched her face do something worse than anger. It did *nothing*. "Honey, call someone." I ran upstairs. My room was a home gym. A treadmill stood where my bed should be. And the room next door — Zoe's room, with the glow stars and the hamster — was a sewing room. Had *always* been a sewing room. In the hallway photo albums, every family picture was just Mom, Dad, and nobody. An empty gap where a kid should be, like the camera had blinked. My little sister had never been born. I stood in the sewing room, shaking, in a body that shouldn't exist. My hands were a stranger's hands — veined, spotted, forty years old. The watch said **41**. And underneath, in small gray letters I'd never noticed: **REMAINING REWINDS: 1. RESULTS NOT GUARANTEED.** One swipe left. One swipe to undo the bus, undo the week, undo everything — to get Zoe back. Whatever it cost — ten years, twenty — I'd pay it. What else could I do? Grow old in a world where my sister never existed? I pressed my finger to the glass. "For Zoe," I whispered, and swiped. The world hiccupped. Backward. Backward. Backward. I woke up in my own bed — bed, not treadmill. Downstairs: a red door, pancakes, and Zoe yelling at her hamster. I was thirteen. Short. My voice cracked when I laughed, and it was the best sound I'd ever heard. The watch sat on my nightstand, screen dark. Dead. I'd throw it in the lake that afternoon. I promised. But that night, brushing my teeth, my reflection flickered. The old man was back. Gray stubble. Deep grooves. Tired eyes — eyes that looked like they'd been fighting a very long time. He raised his hand. So did I. Except I didn't. The old man pressed one finger to his lips. *Shhh.* And behind me — from the nightstand, through the walls, everywhere, patient as anything — something had started to tick.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong adherence to the Goosebumps-style teen horror prompt, successfully incorporating all required elements: a middle schooler discovering a time-rewinding smartwatch, physical aging consequences, timeline shifts with disastrous results, and the need for one final rewind to fix things. The author captures the appropriate tone for the genre - accessible yet genuinely unsettling. The narrative structure is well-executed, building tension through escalating consequences. The protagonist's motivations feel authentic for a thirteen-year-old - using the watch to avoid embarrassment and social mishaps before facing the ultimate moral test of saving his sister. The aging progression is handled cleverly, with physical changes that feel realistic and increasingly alarming. The prose demonstrates considerable skill, particularly in the time-reversal sequences. Descriptions like "Kids slid backward across the floor. The chili rose off the tiles in red ribbons" are vivid and original. The author shows strong command of pacing, moving from small-stakes embarrassments to existential horror effectively. Character development is solid within the constraints of the format. Dex's voice remains consistent throughout his physical transformation, and his relationships with family members feel genuine. The supporting characters serve their purposes well, though they remain somewhat archetypal. The horror elements work effectively, particularly the gradual realization that Dex is erasing his own existence and that of his sister. The final twist with the reflection and the ticking sound provides an appropriately ominous conclusion that suggests the story's consequences extend beyond the apparent resolution. Some minor weaknesses include occasional reliance on familiar middle-grade tropes and a few moments where the exposition feels slightly forced. The dialogue, while functional, doesn't particularly distinguish the characters' voices. The ending, while atmospheric, relies somewhat heavily on ambiguity rather than earned complexity. The technical execution is strong throughout, with natural sentence flow and engaging descriptive passages that avoid purple prose while maintaining atmospheric tension. + Noir romance: Carnival of Dangerous Intentions — Score: 87.2
Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The tin ducks paraded their endless arc, and the gallery smelled of gunpowder and oil, mixing with the salt and frying clams until the boardwalk felt like one long held breath. Down the beach the Wonder Wheel turned its slow bright revolution; behind it the Cyclone rattled and screamed and rattled. Every bulb on the avenue buzzing on at once, moths already throwing themselves at the light. She had wrapped the ring in a handkerchief and buried it in her handbag before leaving the house — an act so deliberate it embarrassed her now, the way premeditation always does once the moment arrives. *His locks.* There it was again, a knock at a door she'd told herself she'd locked. Beside the gallery stood the fortune teller's booth, canvas gone the color of weak tea. A banner hung across it bearing an enormous painted hand, its lines inked like a subway map. LINE OF HEART. LINE OF HEAD. THE GIRDLE OF VENUS. And in the corner, small enough to miss: A CROSS UPON THE MOUNT OF VENUS DENOTETH A FATAL ATTACHMENT. The fortune teller sat in her doorway over a cigarette. "You can read the charts for nothing, miss. It's the hands that cost." "I'm meeting someone." "I know." A slow exhale. "I've watched him meet them." "Them?" The old woman looked past her, down the boardwalk. "He's here." And he was. "You came back." He was beside her the way he'd been on Thursday — suddenly, without arriving, as though the crowd had agreed to rearrange itself around him. Obsidian curls, darker eyes, a white shirt too clean for the boardwalk. "I was passing," she said. "Nobody passes Coney Island. It's the end of the line. It isn't on the way to anything." "Then I'm not going anywhere." "That's the first honest thing you've said since Thursday." *Since the Wheel stopped with us at the top,* she thought, and slammed the door on the rest of it. "How did you know I'd come?" "I didn't. I've been here every night since." "That's—" "Honest? Yes. You started it." The barker leaned over his counter. "Three shots for a dime, doll for the lady—" He laid the dime down and offered her the rifle, grip-first. "You strike me as someone who's never held one." "You'd be surprised what I've held." "I hope so." She stripped off her gloves — heard herself do it, the small surrender of the buttons — and set the stock against her shoulder the way her brother had shown her a hundred summers ago. The tin ducks glided. The ocean glided. She pulled. Nothing fell. "You flinch," he said. "The recoil—" "Before the recoil. You close your eyes before you pull the trigger. You decide to miss." He came around behind her, near enough that she felt the heat of him off his shirt. "May I?" She said nothing, which was yes. Two fingers at her elbow, light as a bank teller counting; then her arm, her shoulder, the angle of her chin — each touch brief, administrative, worse for it. "Again." She kept her eyes open. The duck went over backward with a clang, the barker whooped, and something in her chest went over backward too. "There," he said. "You only needed permission." "From you?" "From whoever. Tonight it happened to be me." She set the rifle down before her hands could give anything else away. "Give me your hand." "The fortune teller charges a dime for that." "She reads hands. I read what's on them." He turned her palm up, and she watched her own hand lie in his like a thing that had surrendered separately from the rest of her. "Your head line and heart line begin apart," he said. "Rare. Most people are born tangled. You keep your reasons and your feelings in separate pockets." His thumb crossed the mound of her thumb and stopped. "And here's a line that isn't on any of her charts." The groove where the ring had lived for six years, pale as a scar from some earlier accident. She tried to take her hand back. He didn't hold it. He only didn't give it back. "It fades," she said. "Everything does. Do you want it to?" "What else do you see?" "You don't want the rest." "I've never once been told what I want." "There it is again," he said, pleased. "An island on your line of life. Islands are secrets." "Everyone has secrets." "Yours is small and gold and wrapped in a handkerchief." The boardwalk noise went very far away. "You're guessing." "Look at my face and tell me I'm guessing." She didn't look. That was an answer too. Over his shoulder the banner rippled in the sea wind: A CROSS UPON THE MOUNT OF VENUS DENOTETH A FATAL ATTACHMENT. *His locks are bushy, and black as a raven.* Song of Solomon — the one book of the Bible the minister always skipped. She understood now why he skipped it; had understood, she admitted, since Thursday, at the top of the Wheel, with the whole shining city laid out below like something being offered. "You're smiling," he said. "At what?" "An old song." "Sing it for me sometime." "You wouldn't like it. It's very forward." "I would like it," he said, "very much." She took her hand back herself this time. "I don't know anything about you. I don't even know your name." "You know what matters. Everyone else on this boardwalk looks through you — the way they look through her charts." He smiled, a beautiful smile, the smile of a man showing you a knife because he admires the workmanship. "Is that meant to frighten me?" "It's meant to be true. Frightening is your half." "Then give me one true thing. Your name." "I don't lie to you. That's the only promise I'll make." "That's not a promise. That's a dare." "Yes," he said. "A name is the last thing you take from a person, and we're nowhere near done." The fortune teller stood and began taking her charts in off the wire, one at a time, the way you bring laundry in when you don't trust the weather. She looked at her once — not at him — and shook her head, the slow movement you make at a funeral. "West of Steeplechase the lamps give out," he said, offering his arm like a business arrangement. "It's better in the dark. Come and see, Ruth." She had never told him that. Not Thursday, not in any letter she hadn't written. He'd said it like a thing kept in his pocket all evening. "You never asked my name." "I don't ask," he said. "I find out." She told herself it was only a walk — the same way she'd told herself she was only passing, the same way she'd told herself the handkerchief was because the ring had grown loose. Behind her the fortune teller's lamp went out like a door closing. Ahead, past the last of the lights, the dark held itself out like something being offered. She took his arm.

+ Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**II.** Supper that night was backstrap from the first caribou, fried with onions in the black skillet that had hung on the same nail since before JT was born. His father ate with appetite, tearing meat off his fork, and Mike ate the same way, and the Coleman lantern hissed on the table between them like something patient. JT moved pieces around his plate. It smelled wonderful. It always had. But every bite he swallowed sat in his stomach like a stone. "Eat," his father said, not unkindly. "It's what we came for." *It's what we came for.* JT ate. What else did you do? Afterward the two of them played cribbage while JT washed the skillet. Usually the game was half the fun of the night—Mike accusing Dad of palming cards, Dad calling Mike a crook in the making, both of them laughing like boys. Tonight they played in silence. Pegs clicked. Once in a while one of them said "fifteen two, fifteen four" in a low, careful voice, like men counting a rosary. The propane fridge ticked. The calendar by the door still said August, a girl in a bass boat—had it always? He couldn't remember. Over the door, Grandpa Earl's old caribou mount looked down on all of them, and JT, elbows deep in suds, kept catching the glass eyes in the lantern light. He'd never noticed how dark they were. How flat. How calm. "Dad?" The water had gone cold around his hands. "That buck today. In the clearing." The peg stopped moving. "What buck?" "The big one. You were right up on it. Your rifle was down, you had your hand out, you were about to—" "You were back in the trees tying your boots." His father's voice was mild, pleasant, terribly reasonable. "You didn't see anything, JT." Mike didn't look up from the board. "We hiked. We saw diddly. We came home." He said it evenly, like a boy reciting a catechism he'd been made to memorize. "Long day." JT looked down at his hands in the gray water. He remembered tying his boots. He also remembered his boots already tied, the stiff laces double-knotted, remembered it clearly—but it couldn't be both, could it? One of the memories had to be a lie, and it stood to reason the liar was him. It was always safer to think so. "Right," he said. "Long day." He went to bed early. Nobody stopped him. --- He did not sleep. Or he slept and the dream was exactly like lying awake, which was worse. The woods outside were silent—truly silent, no wind, no porcupine clatter, no owl—and the silence had a listening quality, a held-breath quality, like the moment after a rifle goes off and before the echo comes back. The wind-up clock downstairs said ten past three when JT heard the screen door open. He knew that door. It had shrieked every autumn of his life; his father oiled it every year and it shrieked anyway, a rusty animal sound that meant somebody was up, somebody couldn't sleep, somebody was going out to smoke or look at the stars. Tonight it made no sound at all. Only a turning of cold air through the house, and the floorboards downstairs not quite creaking. JT got up. He didn't decide to. His feet just carried him, the way they had in the clearing, and he crept to the landing window with his heart going like a rabbit's. His father stood on the porch in his union suit, barefoot on the frost-white boards, breath rising off him in slow clouds. Beyond him, the yard was full of caribou. Thirty of them. More. They stood in rows, neat as pews, every one facing the lodge, and their breath rose from all of them together—one great slow cloud, as if the herd were a single enormous animal breathing. The big buck stood out front, one step ahead of the rest. *Waiting for the shot,* JT thought, and the thought came in his father's voice. His father's hand hung out over the rail, trembling exactly as it had in the clearing. His face, in profile, held that same quiet dignity JT had seen in the first caribou as it fell. *As though he wanted nothing more.* "Not this year," his father said. He wasn't speaking to the buck, JT understood that much; he was speaking through it, the way you speak through a screen door to whatever's knocked. "Not him. I'm the one who—" The wind took the rest. Or something wearing the wind did. Then, without turning, without moving anything but his mouth: "Go on back to bed, JT." And every head in the yard turned toward the window at once—smooth and silent as grass bending in a wind JT couldn't feel—thirty pairs of flat dark eyes finding him through the glass. He stepped back. His heel struck the landing board, the one that always groaned, and it didn't make a sound either. When he made himself look again, the yard was empty. The porch was empty. The screen door hung open on its silent hinge, swinging gently, like a thing that had just been used. --- He woke at dawn in his bunk with his socks on. They were soaked through, and they smelled of pine and animal musk, and he had no memory of putting them on. No memory of the stairs, of his bed, of any of it. He lay still a long time, listening to bacon, listening to his father whistling something slow and tuneless downstairs. Outside, the frost lay thick on the yard, and the tracks were there, pressed deep: a half-circle ringing the porch, every track pointed in—toward the steps, toward the door. Not one pointed back at the woods. "Up and at 'em, JT." His father stood at the stove, spatula in hand, smiling in a way that didn't get past the edges of his eyes. "Big day today. They'll come to us this year." "To us," Mike said from the table. He was already dressed, already booted, and he said it agreeably, the way you agree with something you've known a long time. His father set the pan down, bowed his head over the bacon, and—JT could not remember him doing this once since their mother died—said grace. "For what we're about to receive," he said, "we give thanks." Outside, the woods leaned in a little closer.

The author successfully maintains JT's perspective as an unreliable narrator caught between reality and nightmare, creating genuine psychological ambiguity about what's real versus imagined. The atmospheric writing is particularly effective. Details like the Coleman lantern hissing "like something patient" and the calendar stuck on August create an unsettling sense of time distortion. The imagery of caribou arranged "neat as pews" in the moonlit yard is genuinely haunting and original. The author builds tension methodically through small wrongnesses - the silent screen door, JT's wet socks, the inward-pointing tracks. Character actions feel believable within the surreal context. The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining literary quality. The piece builds to genuine payoffs - the midnight scene with the caribou herd and the morning revelation of tracks creates earned horror. The ending with the father's grace and "they'll come to us this year" provides satisfying darkness that feels inevitable rather than forced. Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Hell Is Other Demons The ash began before dawn, which in Hell is less a time than a rumor. It fell in a fine grey drizzle over the spires of Pandemonium, on the just and the unjust alike, though the just were elsewhere. It pasted itself to windows. It pooled in the gutters. Below the kitchen window, the damned on ash-detail shoveled grey drifts from one pile to another, as regulation required, and then back again. Lucifer Morningstar stood barefoot at the counter drinking coffee smuggled up from the living world—his one indulgence since the Fall, if you didn't count the pride—and read the overnight reports. Soul intake: up four percent. Misery index: holding steady. A complaint from the Second Circle alleging ash "in places ash has no business being." He signed it *Noted* and did not look at the note under the magnet on the icebox. Lilith's handwriting, four months old now. *I need space. You have all of it.* They had broken up for the last time, by his count, forty-one times. He fed the hound. The hound had three heads, and each wanted breakfast separately, and this was the sort of thing one learned to manage or died managing. Then he dressed—charcoal grey; everything he owned was the color of ash now, which was either practical or defeatist, depending on the century—and went to work. Mephistopheles was waiting with the clipboard. There were items. There were always items. The Phlegethon's filters were clogged with ash again. The Furies had filed a grievance regarding uncompensated overtime, which was bold, eternity being rather the whole point. A soul in the Fifth Circle had been observed smiling, and Internal Affairs wished to know how. And the Equinox Revel required the founder's seal: the Guild of Succubi did nothing without its mother's mark. "I'll handle it," said Lucifer, too quickly. Mephistopheles wrote something down. It was not what he said aloud. Midday was petitions. A tyrant begged for mercy, citing the hospital wing he had built. Lucifer denied it; the wing had been named after the tyrant, and vanity was not a currency Hell accepted at par. A poet asked for an umbrella. Granted—one umbrella, black, guaranteed until the Third Circle froze over. The poet wept with gratitude. It was the cheapest mercy Lucifer had dispensed in an eon, and he was barely paying attention, because he was wondering about honey. Whether Lilith still took honey in her tea. It was the kind of question that could occupy a morning. It had occupied an epoch. She knocked at four. That was new. Historically she had simply arrived, like weather, like plague. There was ash in her hair, grey against black, worn like a crown she'd refused to have delivered. She held a box. "You left these." "You've had them four months." "I was busy." The box contained, among other things, his copy of *Paradise Lost*. She had annotated the margins. *He never said that. Wrong. He was taller.* "You come off well," she said. "Considering." "Considering what?" "Everything." She had also, she said, come about the Equinox seal, which was a lie so transparent they let it stand in the doorway with them, dripping ash. He made tea. He put honey in her cup without asking, and she looked at the cup for a long moment, and drank. It was the most romantic thing to happen in Hell since the Fall, and they both pretended not to notice. "You're letting the ash pile up," she said. "It piles." "That's no way to live." "It's an excellent way to be damned." She told him the Ninth Circle was running cold and he was an icicle with delusions of grandeur. He told her the apartment was brisk and she was a furnace with opinions. They agreed, as they had for six thousand years, to revisit the thermostat at the end of time. She mentioned Adam—in Heaven these days, apparently; still blaming everyone; some men never learn to apologize, present company excluded, then included, then excluded again. He almost laughed. Ash slid off the eaves outside in a soft grey rush, and for a moment their hands were both on the teapot, and then they weren't. She stayed two hours past the paperwork. When she rose to go, she said she'd oversee the Revel herself. In person. "Tuesday," said Lucifer. There are no Tuesdays in Hell. Time there is a spiral staircase in a burning house; the days are all the same day, wearing different masks. Lilith smiled anyway, which was answer enough, and she left with his umbrella—the raven-handled one, his favorite—and he did not mention it, because you don't mention these things. You count them. In the evening he denied a request for hotter flames on grounds of austerity, approved the Flaying Roster for the nine o'clock slot, and commuted the sentence of a man who had once been kind to a dog, which no one in Accounting would ever notice. The hound ate. The ash fell. The forecast for tomorrow was ash, followed by ash, continuing into eternity, and he found that he minded it slightly less than he had at breakfast. He washed two cups, though he had used one. Then he consulted the calendar Mephistopheles had left on his desk—days of the week had never been necessary before; eternity, etc.—and drew a small, careful circle around a day that had not existed that morning. There had never been Tuesdays in Hell. There were now.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft and sophisticated understanding of the prompt requirements. The author successfully captures Neil Gaiman's distinctive voice through understated irony and the juxtaposition of cosmic/infernal elements with mundane domestic concerns. The central conceit—Hell's bureaucracy mirroring earthly administrative tedium—creates effective dark comedy throughout. The characterization is particularly strong. Lucifer emerges as a complex figure caught between his cosmic role and personal loneliness, while Lilith maintains agency and mystery. Their relationship dynamics feel authentic despite the fantastical setting. The author avoids the trap of making either character purely sympathetic or villainous. The prose style is elegant and controlled, with memorable phrases like "time there is a spiral staircase in a burning house" and "vanity was not a currency Hell accepted at par." The ash motif works both literally and metaphorically, representing the weight of their situation and the passage of time. The story's structure follows a clear arc from morning routine through their reunion, building to the quietly powerful ending where Lucifer creates Tuesday—a day that didn't exist in Hell before. This transformation feels earned through the careful accumulation of small moments and gestures. The dialogue, while limited, serves its purpose effectively. The exchanges between Lucifer and Lilith crackle with history and unspoken understanding. The bureaucratic elements provide appropriate contrast without overwhelming the central relationship. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the Gaiman pastiche becomes slightly too obvious, and a few descriptive passages that edge toward preciousness. However, these don't significantly detract from the overall achievement. The ending strikes an appropriate balance—hopeful without being saccharine, suggesting possibility rather than resolution. The creation of Tuesday represents genuine character growth while maintaining the story's tonal consistency. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 90.9
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Shape of the Blade The Ludus Magnus smelled of oil, iron, and sand. Sand above all — sand in the bread, sand in the wine, sand ground so deep into the creases of my knuckles that no strigil would ever find it. *Harena*, the Romans say, and it is their word for the arena as well. They named the place after its floor, as though nothing above the floor were worth naming. I woke to the armorer's hammer, as I had woken for eleven years. In the yard below, the fighters were already at the rope-wrapped posts, wooden blades cracking, Fuscus the doctor shouting his one word, which was *again*. Beyond the wall, Rome did what Rome does at the first hour: hawkers, hooves, the syrup of an auctioneer poured over everything, threaded with bread-smell from the Subura ovens, garum, and the ammonia stink of the fullers' vats. A million people, each one louder than the last. The new boy was sick behind the water butt. Vitalis — an *auctoratus*, a volunteer; a word for a free man the city has ruined. Nineteen, a baker's son out of the Subura. The rent had eaten the bakery, the debts had eaten the rest, and so he had stood in the lanista Sabinus's tablinum and sworn the oath: to be burned, bound, flogged, and killed by iron. I never swore it. No one asks a horse to swear. Fuscus gave him to me for the afternoon, because in four days, at the Quinquatrus, Vitalis would debut as a murmillo, and murmillos are fed to Thracians. To men like me. So I took up the wooden sica and taught him the geometry of his own death — where it comes from, and how to be elsewhere. "Shield high," I told him. "Small steps. The curved blade does not argue with a shield. It goes around, under, over — it ends the argument. So you make yourself narrow, and you make your wall move." He was quick. That was the pity of it. In one afternoon he learned the feint — high at the helmet, low beneath the rim — and when he caught the trick of it, something in my chest went cold and glad at once. Quick is what the crowd forgives. Quick, they love. He asked if I had been afraid, my first time in the sand. Every time, I told him. He laughed, thinking it a joke. We rested in the shade of the armory wall, and I told him what nobody had told me. The wooden sword we drill with is called a *rudis*. The same word, the same plain stick of wood, given to a man in the sand before the crowd, means freedom. Every morning I hold freedom in my hand, and every morning it is only wood. Then I unwrapped the real one, because a man should see the thing that is hunting him. Shorter than a legionary's gladius, bent in the last third of the blade like a reaper's hook, the grip corded and worn to the exact shape of my hand. Roman iron. Thracian curve. Sabinus's smith forged it in my first month here, and when I first closed my fist on it, I had to turn away, because the shape undid me. It was the one thing Rome had given back. My father's sica had hung above our door to keep the night out. The soldiers took it when they took the village. He used to say that straight iron knocks on the shield, and curved iron comes in through the window. Nineteen men have died under that curve. Not one of them was Rome. Gauls, a Numidian, Syrians, a Cappadocian who cried for his mother in a tongue I understood better than Latin. That is the genius of the arena, though it took me years to see it: Rome does not bleed here. Rome watches. The conquered kill the conquered in the afternoon, after the beasts have had their morning and the condemned their noon, and the city calls it mercy when it lets one of us live. The Quinquatrus would be lavish that year. The Caesar honors Minerva, his gray-eyed patroness, and the games are his gift to the people — the grain fleet had come in from Alexandria, the dole was flowing, and a fed crowd is a loving crowd. Loving crowds grant *missio*. Loving crowds throw palms, coins, and once in a great while a wooden sword. The wind turned, and brought the musk of leopards penned for the hunts. Across the street the amphitheatre sat like a mountain with its throat open, built, they say, from the gold of Jerusalem's burned temple. I believed it. I had watched my own country feed the same appetite — the beasts, the timber, the boys in the yard. Conquest comes to Rome and is ground fine, like everything else, into sand. They paint my name on tavern walls in red — THRAX, with a hooked blade beneath it. Matrons send notes up the hill. A senator once asked my opinion of a horse. Yet in the law I am *infamis*, a thing without a name, which Sabinus rents out at twelve thousand sesterces an afternoon — more than a legionary sees in a lifetime of pay. Hope is another thing the sand gets into. My winnings sit banked with the lanista, and I am patient the way iron is patient. At dusk the city changed its voice. By the old traffic law, carts are forbidden in daylight; only when the lamps were lit did the wheels begin, hundreds of them, groaning over the stones with wine and marble and grain. Rome at night is the sound of the empire being fed. Vitalis found me at the bench, whetting the blade. "Thrax," he said, trying the word. "That is the name they shout." "Then what are you called?" I had not heard it aloud in a long time. "Seuthes." He said it twice, the way a man learns a road, then went in to his barley porridge and the ash Fuscus stirs into it, which knits bones. I sat with the lamp and let the stone sing along the edge until the curve of the blade held the flame the way the Hebrus holds the evening light between its banks. A river far from home. Still running. Four days, and the sand.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a sophisticated piece of historical fiction that demonstrates considerable literary skill and historical knowledge. The author creates an immersive first-person narrative from the perspective of Seuthes, a Thracian gladiator in ancient Rome, successfully avoiding the combat scene as requested while building tension toward an upcoming fight. The prose is consistently elegant and evocative, with particularly strong sensory details that ground the reader in the ancient world. The opening line "The Ludus Magnus smelled of oil, iron, and sand" immediately establishes place and atmosphere. The author demonstrates impressive command of historical detail, from the specific terminology (ludus, harena, auctoratus, missio) to the social and political context (grain dole, traffic laws, the conquest economics of the empire). The characterization of Seuthes is nuanced and compelling. He's neither a stereotypical noble savage nor a broken victim, but a complex individual who maintains his identity while navigating an impossible system. His relationship with the young gladiator Vitalis provides emotional depth without sentimentality. The revelation of his real name at the end is particularly effective. The political and social commentary is woven seamlessly into the narrative rather than feeling didactic. The observation that "Rome does not bleed here. Rome watches. The conquered kill the conquered" encapsulates the imperial system's exploitation with elegant economy. The voice remains consistent throughout - world-weary but not defeated, observant and philosophical without being pretentious. The pacing builds naturally toward the upcoming games, creating tension without requiring action scenes. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose edges toward being overly literary, and a few metaphors that feel slightly forced. The dialogue, while limited, feels authentic to character and period. The ending strikes an appropriate note of resigned determination rather than false hope or despair. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 84.3
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Lighthouse Keeper **Sgeir Bhan Rock Light — 14 September 1957** Dear Ma, Well, I'm here. Sgeir Bhan — the white skerry, though nothing on it's white but the gulls and their opinions. It's a rock the size of the kirkyard at home and half as cheery, with the tower stuck on it like a candle in a clootie dumpling. A hundred and sixty-eight steps to the lamp room and I ken every one by the ache in my legs. There's three of us. Mr Rennie, the principal, does his crossword and speaks when the clock strikes. Young Fraser plays the mouth organ and speaks for the both of them. The light takes paraffin and tending every night. I'm fine for socks. Dinnae send socks. Your Davie --- **14 Bishop Street, Stepps — 2 October 1957** Dear Davie, Socks in the parcel, and the cake. Dinnae eat the cake the one night like the last one. The wool's the good wool; dinnae wear them in the boat, they'll felt. Your father's tally is in the parcel too. I found it in the drawer with the buttons. You'll mind it: the brass oval off his neck, CARDOWAN and his number 1187 stamped in it, the hole at the top where the bootlace went. He wore it every shift doon the pit and rubbed it smooth as a hen's egg waiting on the cage. It came up the day he came up last, and it's lain in a drawer twenty year. It did its waiting doon a pit. Let it do some up a lighthouse. Mrs Boyle's fence is doon again. Eat the greens. Ma --- **Sgeir Bhan — 19 December 1957** Dear Ma, The relief boat's no come. Three weeks now; the swell's too heavy to land the punt. Rennie says he's seen nine weeks and it's nothing, which from Rennie is a sermon. Fraser's mouth organ has started to sound like music to me, which is how I ken it's bad. Thursday the sea hit the tower so hard the paraffin shoogled in the trays. I had your man's tally in my fist the whole night through. I'm no saying I was feared. I'm saying the brass has a thumb-shaped wear in it now that's mine as well as his. A Happy New Year, when it comes. If it comes. Your Davie --- **14 Bishop Street — 26 February 1958** Dear Davie, Your father's tally getting a second wearing — he'd have laughed, and then he'd no have. I've had the cough that's went round the scheme, same as everybody. The doctor wanted me for x-rays. I told him this family's been x-rayed enough for one lifetime. He's an auld wife wi' a stethoscope. The kirk sale made eleven pound. Eat the greens. Ma --- **Sgeir Bhan — 20 April 1958** Dear Ma, Your writing's taken to wandering across the page like a man coming home from the club. Is your hand no right? Write me the truth, and if you cannae write it, get Isobel to. Since I'm asking for truth, I'll pay some. Fraser's transferred away and his replacement is a silent man from Lewis, so it's me and two crosswords now. Some nights at three in the morning, when the light's turning and nothing else in the world is, I stand at the rail and I'd give a year's wage for the sound of a bus. I ken I told you the company was fine. The company is fine. It's the silence after it. Your Davie --- **14 Bishop Street — 7 June 1958** Dear Davie, Isobel's writing this, my hand being tired wi' the knitting for the kirk sale. That's all it is. Here's the truth you asked for, since you asked. I was in the Western Infirmary a fortnight, tests on my chest. Tests, and nothing more, so dinnae greet. The doctor said a word I cannae spell and Isobel won't. I'll tell you why I said nothing, then we're done wi' it. Your father's wage kept a roof on us and killed him by inches in the doing. Yours keeps you in clean air, three hundred mile from the pits and the yards. I wasnae going to be the thing that pulled you back doon. Eat the greens. Ma --- **Telegram — 11 August 1958** WESTERN INFIRMARY STOP OPERATION TUESDAY STOP COME IF THE SEA ALLOWS STOP DONT FASH STOP MA --- **Telegram — same day** COMING STOP HOLD ON STOP DAVIE --- **Sgeir Bhan — 20 August 1958** Ma, I'm writing this so it's ready for the boat, because the boat cannae come. Nine days the gales have held it off the rock. I've stood on the landing watching the weather do its work, and there's nothing a man can do but keep the light going, and last night was the first I ever hated a job for being done right. I sat in the lamp room with the tally roond my neck and talked to him. I asked how he managed it — every shift doon in the dark, twenty year, and never one word of complaint carried home. I ken the answer now. You. You were the reason no to speak. You've been the reason no to speak for twenty year, and it's my turn to say it: speak. Stay. When the sea lets me off this rock I'm coming to the Western, and I'm no leaving till they put you out the front door and no the other one. Your Davie --- **Cloch Point Lighthouse — 2 November 1958** Ma, You ken it all by noo, but the letters should say it too. I got in on the Friday, the tenth day. You were the thin thing in the bed by the window, and you looked at me and said, "You've no shaved," which was how I kent you'd be alright. Here's my news. I've been transferred. Cloch Point, on the Clyde — a shore station, a house, and a garden you'll have opinions about. The rock lights are for the young and the unmarried, Rennie says, and I've stopped arguing. I'll be up Thursdays wi' the messages. The tally sits on the watch-room window ledge. Every seven seconds the beam comes roon and lights it up like a wee coal. Your man spent a hundred years under the ground wi' never a light but the lamp on his bunnet, and noo he gets one every night, regular as the clock. You told me once he never saw the sea. He's seen it every night this year, Ma. Thursday I'll bring him up, and you can see the two of us together. Eat the greens. Your Davie

The author demonstrates strong command of Scottish speech patterns without resorting to heavy-handed phonetic spelling that would impede readability. The story structure follows a clear emotional arc spanning over a year, building from initial adjustment to isolation, through crisis, to resolution. The gradual revelation of the mother's illness creates genuine tension, while the father's mining tally serves as an effective symbolic thread connecting past and present, underground and elevated work, darkness and light. Character development is particularly strong. Davie's voice evolves from somewhat cocky newcomer to someone grappling with profound isolation, then to a man making difficult choices about duty versus family. His mother's voice, even filtered through brief letters, reveals a stoic woman protecting her son while battling her own mortality. The contrast between their communication styles - his increasingly verbose and emotional, hers consistently practical and understated - feels authentic to their relationship and backgrounds. The imagery is consistently strong without becoming overwrought. Descriptions like "a rock the size of the kirkyard at home and half as cheery" and "the tower stuck on it like a candle in a clootie dumpling" are both vivid and character-appropriate. The lighthouse beam illuminating the father's tally creates a powerful recurring image that ties the narrative themes together. The emotional climax builds naturally through escalating isolation, the mother's illness revelation, and Davie's inability to reach her during the storm. The resolution feels earned rather than artificially positive - Davie makes a practical choice to transfer to a shore station, and his mother survives, but the story acknowledges the ongoing reality of her condition. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the symbolic weight of the father's tally feels slightly heavy-handed, and the telegram section, while dramatically effective, breaks the established rhythm somewhat abruptly. The ending, while satisfying, perhaps ties things together a bit too neatly with the symbolic imagery of the tally being illuminated by the lighthouse beam. The prose maintains consistent quality throughout, with natural sentence flow and authentic dialogue that serves character development. The story avoids common pitfalls of forced dialect or melodramatic emotional manipulation. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Vulnerability Disclosure The WiFi password is taped to the register, and I hate that I've already memorized it. *IlPomodoro2019.* Capital I, lowercase l — so half the staff has typo-locked themselves out and reset it to something worse. That's the guest network, and if I had to bet, and my brain always bets, it shares a subnet with the card readers. The router's in the back office next to the mop sink, admin login unchanged since 2019, which is to say: also on the tape. A padlock doesn't count as security when you tape the key to the frame. I'm on a date. I am threat-modeling an Italian restaurant. Be a person. Be a person. Her name is Priya. She got here first, which I respect — early arrival is good tradecraft. She's turning her wineglass by the stem and pretending not to watch the door, and I recognize the pretense because I invented it. We do weather. We do jobs. I say "cybersecurity consultant," the answer that lets people assume I install antivirus. She teaches eighth-grade science. "So you handle threats daily," I say, and she laughs — a real laugh, unforced. No fake laugh deploys that fast. The bread lands. She tears a piece. "Confession: I almost rescheduled. Wednesday is Commander night with my playgroup." Time stops. Somewhere in my chest, a slot machine pays out. "Commander," I say, with the composure of a man who has not just topdecked the exact card he needed. "You play EDH?" What follows is forty minutes of conversation we don't have to fake. She runs Talrand — mono-blue, counterspell tribal, self-described villain of the table. I confess my Meren graveyard value engine and she says, "Oh, so you're *patient.* That's worse." She starts a story with "so it's turn two and this guy drops a Sol Ring" and I am gone, I am in. Somewhere in there I stopped cataloging the dome camera's blind spot by the restrooms. Stopped clocking the waiter's tablet with its default PIN worn shiny into the glass. I am present. I am a normal man discussing the stack with a delightful woman. Then she picks up her phone. "Okay, I have to show you the deck." She wakes the screen. Draws her unlock pattern. Top-left start. A big lazy Z, four nodes, thumb moving with the confidence of ten thousand repetitions. My brain cracks it before her thumb lifts. It's not a challenge; it's a formality. Top-left start is "admin." A Z is "password." Under the right light I could read it out of the finger grease on the glass. The phone is confessing to anyone who bothers to look. "You know that's one of the five most common unlock patterns on the planet, right?" The words are out before I consult anyone. Fork down. Wineglass paused mid-sip. "...You watched me unlock my phone." Intrusion detected. Alarms. Abort. Abort. And here's the ugly part: some sliver of me — the old me, the one who lived in other people's systems like a ghost in the walls — wants to double down. Wants to list it all. *You're left-handed. You pre-decided your order. You've checked the door three times since I sat down.* Burn it down on my terms. Because sabotage is a known outcome; I can plan around rejection. But being observed back — being actually seen mid-attempt — that's the one exploit I never patched. That's a zero-day aimed at *me.* "I'm sorry," I say. "That was — okay. You know how you can't not read a card someone flips, even across the room, even upside down? My entire career is that, except it's everything. Locks. Passwords. Patterns. People. I spent my early twenties being the ghost in other people's machines. Now companies pay me to find the flaws before worse people do. Six years of that, and nobody installs an off switch." Beat. "It's not a flex. It's a tic." She lets the apology sit on the stack a moment. Teachers are good at silence. "What else," she says. "What else did you notice." The fork in the road. I can take the flex — show off the deductions, win the trick, lose the game. Or. "I noticed you laughed at my joke before the punchline, which means you're kind or generous, and I've spent forty minutes hoping it's both. I noticed I rehearsed three conversation topics in the car and you torched all of them in ten minutes. I noticed this is the best date I've had in years, and that terrifies me, because I just told a woman whose job is noticing things that my job is noticing things, and now she's noticing *mine.*" She lets that resolve. Then: "You know what I noticed? You've looked at that register nine times since we sat down." She points her breadstick at the counter. "What's wrong with the password?" I'm compromised. There is no incident response for this. "You counted?" "I teach eighth grade. I notice everything. Mine are people, not packets." She picks up her phone. "Okay, hacker. Fix me." "Longer. Cross the middle. Use all nine points. Don't start in a corner." She draws something elaborate, angling the screen away — respect — then locks it and sets it face down. "Better?" "Statistically." "*Statistically,*" she repeats. But she's smiling. "Now. The password. Talk." So I talk. Subnets, VLANs, the router by the mop sink, a key taped to the outside of the lock. She leans in, chin on her fist, like I'm telling her a story about goblins — and somewhere in the middle of it I realize I've stopped scanning the room entirely. The only system I'm auditing is this conversation, and it contains no vulnerabilities I want to exploit. The password stays taped to the register. Some flaws you report. Some you leave for the next audit. She asks if I want dessert. I check my hand for a response. Nothing. I've been outplayed since the bread. I say yes.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative understanding of the prompt. The author successfully captures the mindset of a reformed hacker through vivid, specific details about security vulnerabilities - from the WiFi password taped to the register to the worn PIN on the waiter's tablet. The internal monologue feels authentic and maintains consistent voice throughout. The Magic: The Gathering connection works well as a believable bonding moment, and the author shows good knowledge of the game's terminology and culture. The central conflict - the protagonist's inability to stop themselves from commenting on the insecure unlock pattern - creates genuine tension and feels true to character. The writing contains several elegant metaphors that enhance rather than distract ("topdecked the exact card he needed," "checking my hand for a response"). The technical details feel researched and authentic without becoming overly dense for general readers. Character development is nuanced - both the protagonist and Priya feel like real people with distinct personalities. Priya's response to the security breach revelation is particularly well-handled; her curiosity rather than immediate offense feels earned given her established character as someone who "notices everything." The emotional arc is well-constructed, moving from anxiety through connection to crisis and tentative resolution. The protagonist's vulnerability about their condition feels genuine, and their choice between "flexing" knowledge versus honest confession creates meaningful internal conflict. Some minor weaknesses include occasional over-explanation of metaphors and a few moments where the technical jargon slightly overwhelms the emotional content. The ending, while satisfying, resolves perhaps a bit too neatly given the severity of the social breach. The prose flows naturally with good rhythm and pacing. The piece maintains reader engagement throughout and successfully balances technical authenticity with emotional resonance. + First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 86.6
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Overthinking It Ms. Herrera claims the lab partners were "randomly selected," which is a lie, because nothing about the way my heart is currently trying to exit through my ribs feels random. It feels targeted. It feels like the universe did research. Eli Nakamura is sitting eighteen inches away, writing his name at the top of our data table, and I have prepared exactly zero of the many things I prepared. That's not true. I've prepared eleven of them. Drafted, edited, and rejected on a rolling basis since Thursday, when Ms. Herrera read the pairs aloud and my entire body turned to static. Eleven openers, like a newspaper nobody will ever print. Opener three was about the cabbage indicator. When she boiled the cabbage yesterday, the whole hallway smelled like a vegetable committing a crime, and everyone complained, so the topic is used up. Openers have expiration dates. You can't comment on a smell from yesterday. Then you're just a person still thinking about yesterday's smell. Did *he* complain about the smell? I think he said something to Marcus. Or Marcus said something and Eli laughed. If I bring up the cabbage, will he know I heard him laugh? Did I hear him laugh? (Yes. Obviously. I can at least admit that to myself.) "Do you want to do the dropper or the recording?" Eli asks. "Recording." It comes out normal. Volume normal, tone normal. I want to replay it seventeen times, but he's already handing me the pencil, so I take it, and our fingers brush—no. There was no contact event. I need to stop. The data table is the one part of this I can do. Columns straight, hypothesis in complete sentences, because neat handwriting is the only variable I fully control. I print pH values like they're evidence for my defense. Opener seven: the color joke. His vinegar just turned hot pink and mine's gone teal, and somewhere in my head there's a perfectly calibrated sentence about our station looking like a salon. But jokes require the other person to laugh, and if he doesn't, I'll have to sit inside the silence of a failed joke, which is worse than ordinary silence. Ordinary silence is ambient. Failed-joke silence has a shape, and the shape is me. So: no jokes. Meanwhile I am manually operating my face. I read online that resting faces look angry even when people feel neutral, so for twenty minutes I've been holding a soft, pleasant, mildly-interested-in-science expression, and my cheeks ache. Where are my eyes supposed to go? His hands are the natural place, but there's a threshold past which watching someone's hands becomes *staring* at someone's hands, and I don't know where the threshold is, so I keep glancing at the clock instead, which makes me look like I can't wait to leave. Great. Now I look like a person who hates him. The exact opposite of the situation. Last Tuesday he said "nice one" when I answered the covalent bond question—unprompted, socially unnecessary—and I have been photosynthesizing off that comment ever since. Like a plant that got watered once and is making it last. Opener nine involves the pin on his backpack, the one from that game. If I mention it, he'll know I noticed the pin, and noticing is one step from paying attention, which is one step from caring, which is one step from desperate, and desperate girls at this school become cautionary tales. They get a *tone of voice* attached to their name. I've heard the tone of voice. I refuse to have a tone of voice. The problem, the actual structural problem, is that inside my head I'm fluent. In here I'm articulate and warm and I ask excellent follow-up questions and my timing is impeccable. Out there, I have produced three audible words in fifteen minutes—"recording," "yeah," "okay"—while containing entire essays. Ms. Herrera drifts past and says our data table looks "very organized," and I accept the compliment on behalf of my entire nervous system. Opener eleven was going to be something about whether our results counted as real data or just *colors*, and whether he— The smell arrives. Sharp, chemical, stinging the back of my nose so suddenly my eyes water. Ammonia. Unmistakable. The janitor must have mopped during lunch, or the counters got wiped with something industrial, and it ambushes me mid-sentence and my whole draft just—dissolves. Like someone lifted the needle off the record. For one full second my mind is nothing but white and stinging and blank. Then the thought comes back. Different. Better. Ammonia is a *base*. pH around eleven, one of the most famous household bases in existence, and we are sitting here testing dish soap like it's breaking news, and the room itself has been mopped in base. The floor is on our topic. This is the single most relevant thing I have ever had the opportunity to say out loud. New draft: *The janitor mopped with ammonia, and ammonia's a base, so technically the floor is part of our lab.* Trim. *Smell that? Ammonia. The janitor is basically doing our homework.* The "smell that?" is risky—commanding his nose. Analysis: too nerdy? He's in honors science. He corrected Ms. Herrera's typo on the board last week without shame. Nerdy might be legal tender here. But what if my voice does the thing where it comes out too quiet and he says "what" and I have to say it twice, and by then the sentence has been exposed to air and gone stale and I can hear how stupid— He's capping the vinegar. Ten minutes left. After this, the universe re-randomizes and I go back to being a person with a three-word vocabulary. "What" is not fatal, I tell myself. People say "what" forty times a day for purely acoustic reasons. Catastrophizing. That's the word from the article. I am doing the thing. I open my mouth. "The floor smells like our homework." That is not the sentence I drafted. That is not any of the eleven drafts. It comes out at sixty percent volume and is objectively deranged, and Eli looks up with his goggles pushed into his hair. "What?" "The—ammonia. They mopped with ammonia. It's a base. So." *So.* I said *so*. Out loud. Like a person ending a text message. He snorts—an actual snort, not a polite one. "Wait, that's true. The floor is a base. That's kind of great." "It's like a pH of eleven," I say, and it comes out fast and clear, because apparently once the seal breaks, the fluency was right there the whole time, just stuck in the queue. "I'm putting it in the conclusion. 'The floor is a base.' Extra credit for real-world applications." And I laugh. A real laugh, unoperated, my face doing whatever it wants for the first time in forty minutes. Then my brain restarts, because wins have shelf lives too: I need a follow-up before the silence curdles, and I must not mention the eleven drafts, and "kind of great" is a figure of speech, not a confession. But underneath all the noise sits one small fact, next to the ammonia still stinging the air: the catastrophe didn't come. I said a weird sentence, and the world failed to end. The bell rings in four minutes. Draft one:
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional craft in capturing the authentic voice of an anxious 8th-grade girl. The writer successfully maintains the internal monologue format throughout, creating a convincing stream-of-consciousness that feels genuinely adolescent without being condescending. The voice is consistently intelligent yet age-appropriate, with sophisticated observations filtered through teenage concerns. The characterization is particularly strong. The protagonist's anxiety manifests in believable ways - the "eleven openers" she's drafted and rejected, her hyperawareness of every micro-interaction, and her catastrophic thinking patterns all ring true. The gap between her articulate internal voice and her stilted external expression is expertly rendered, especially in moments like "Recording" coming out "normal" while she internally dissects every aspect of the interaction. The prose demonstrates considerable skill with metaphor and imagery. Phrases like "my entire body turned to static," "photosynthesizing off that comment," and "like someone lifted the needle off the record" are fresh and authentic to the character's perspective. The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining vivid, specific details that ground the reader in the experience. The story structure is well-paced, building tension through the protagonist's escalating anxiety before the ammonia moment provides a natural breakthrough. The ending feels earned rather than artificially positive - her small victory is appropriately scaled to the situation and her character growth is minimal but realistic. The adherence to instructions is nearly perfect. The piece maintains the first-person perspective, focuses on the science project setting, captures social anxiety authentically, and stays almost entirely in internal monologue as requested. The word count appears appropriate for the 1000-word target. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose becomes slightly overwrought, and the metaphors, while generally excellent, sometimes pile up in ways that draw attention to the writing itself. However, these are minor issues in an otherwise accomplished piece. Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Rehearsing Rejection** Eight years of friendship. Six weeks of the other thing — her mouth, her kettle, her name in my phone at 2 a.m. Nine days of her going quiet. I know it's nine because I counted, and I counted twice, because the first count made me pathetic and the second made me pathetic with precision. Third shirt. The first said *trying too hard*, the second said *I don't care*, this one says *I always looked like this*. On the way back from the closet the hallway mirror catches me — shoulders up around my ears, one hand strangling the hem — and I turn away fast, before the posture can be entered into evidence. She'll do it gently. That's the worst version, the one I keep casting. *"I think we moved too fast. You're a lot, you know that? You love like a door left open in winter."* And I'll say — I've been saying it all morning — *"Funny. I was going to say the same thing."* Small laugh. Gather the coat. I'm not the one who gets left; I'm the one who was already leaving. The laugh has to be right. Too big and it's bitter, too small and it's wounded. I practice it into the closet dark. On the bus I run the scene again with better lighting. I'm calm. Devastating, but calm. She cries a little and I hand her a napkin, because even in my own nightmare I'm polite. Then the other one: she doesn't come at all, texts an apology with a period in it, and I rehearse my dignity, which is mostly typing *no worries* like a knife. The "ha" she sent Tuesday. Lowercase, no punctuation. A door easing shut. Forty-one messages from me since the ninth; twelve from her. I did the math and hated myself for doing the math, then did it again. I did this with Marcus, and Marcus left, so. The pattern is fluent in me because life taught it the words. That's not catastrophizing, that's history. Priya — my old therapist — would say the fluency is the problem. Priya had a worksheet. I filled it out beautifully: catastrophizing my catastrophizing. Knowing the name of the weather doesn't stop the rain. And the rehearsals are vivid, high definition, every line blocking-perfect, while the real June is soft focus, subject to interpretation. The imagined June I can control. If I've already been left a hundred times in here, the real leaving is just a rerun. That's the theory. It has never once worked. I decide to be cold tonight. Not rude — unavailable. If she's going, she goes from someone already halfway out the door. I practice the shrug against the bus window. My reflection does it better than I do. She's already there. She waves through the glass before I'm through the door — off script immediately; nobody waves in my version. The coldness I practiced doesn't fit anywhere on my face. Corner table. Two drinks. Mine is right: oat milk, half-syrup, the fussy order I always apologize for. "You look like you need this," she says, "and I need to say I'm sorry. Nine days. My mom — they found something on a scan, then more tests, waiting rooms, my sister falling apart, and I kept drafting texts to you and deleting them because they all sounded like I was pulling away when I was just scared. You're the person I most didn't want to disappear on." Say it again. Don't say it again — if she says it again it becomes a thing she's doing because I need it. Relief hits like warm water, my eyes sting, and I study the table because crying is a scene and scenes get remembered against you. She remembered the syrup. People are generous on their way out. No. Stop. Her hand is over mine, thumb moving across my knuckles. Her hand is warm. Her hand will leave in a minute to stir her coffee. It doesn't leave. "You could've texted," I say, and I hear the exact sharpness I rehearsed, except in rehearsal it was cooler. "Anything." "I know." She doesn't defend herself, which is disarming, because defenses I could fight. "I'll be better. Next time I go quiet, it's not you. Ask me. I promise I'll answer." A promise. I'll replay it all night until it wears out, and then I'll decide it was a lie because it wore out. Her phone buzzes — her sister, the hospital — she glances, apologizes, and I think: *escape plan.* Then I hate myself. Then I hate that hating myself doesn't stop the thought, only adds a second voice to it, a Greek chorus with my face. "Nine days," she says. "What did you decide was happening? Tell me which version won." She wants the truth. The truth is a room I don't let people into — forty-one messages and a worksheet and a mirror I turned away from. "I don't remember," I say, which is a lie, and she knows it's a lie, and she lets it go with a small sad smile and squeezes my hand, and even her grace gets processed on the way in: *she's being gentle the way you're gentle with something breakable, and being found breakable is its own rejection* — no. No. She asked. She asked which version won. Who asks that? Someone staying asks that. I make a joke — something small about her mother's radiologist, I don't even know what — and she laughs the real laugh, the snort, the one I could pick out of a thousand laughing people, and for one second there is no version, no count, no script. One second. I try to stand inside it. It's the size of a doorway. Walking home I hold her sentence like a coin warming in my fist. *You're the person I most didn't want to disappear on.* I could live inside it. I want to ask her to say it again and I want to never need it said again, both wants in one breath. And underneath, already, quietly, the next rehearsal is loading: *she was exhausted, anyone would say it; pity wears the same clothes as love; wait until the results come back and she needs someone strong.* I know. I know. I know. Knowing is just watching myself from the front row, unable to reach the stage. The hallway mirror will be waiting when I get home. Maybe tonight I'll look. Maybe I'll see what she saw — someone worth waving at through the glass. Or I'll turn away before it can tell me what I already rehearsed. I'm good at that part. I've practiced.
