+ Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 87.8
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Nine: Annealing The cycler ticked through its thirty-first cycle, patient as a rosary. Vera had built it from the corpse of a 3D printer and three aluminum blocks off a salvaged lathe bed: one held at ninety-four degrees by a kettle element, one at fifty-eight, one at seventy-two, each temperature babysat by a thermostat torn from a clothes iron. The printer's gantry ferried her tube rack between them—denature, anneal, extend—stepper motors counting steps like decades of a devotion. Power came off solar panels bolted above the hearse port of Mullins & Sons, Funerals Since 1954. The mortuary's drawer unit held a steady eleven degrees for reagents. The viewing room, with its X-ray lightbox, made a fine darkroom for reading gels. Her electrophoresis rig was a picture frame and speaker wire. Agar from the last grocery stock east of the river; running buffer mixed from Twenty Mule Team borax; bands stained with methylene blue filched from the aquarium trade. Her micropipette was cracked and recalibrated against weighed drops of water. None of it was clean. All of it worked, which was the only compliment left worth giving. The precious things lived in the canisters—six vacuum-jacketed dry shippers looted off a CERES Agrigen dock in the first winter, holding cold for weeks without power. Under her grease-pencil labels—TAQ, dNTPs, PRIMERS/BEAN—the dead company's font still insisted: LICENSED BIOLOGICAL MATERIAL. PROPAGATION STRICTLY PROHIBITED. Their cold chain had outlived them by nine years. Vera found that funny in a way she never said aloud: the last cold in the world, delivered by the people who burned it down. CERES had never sold seed. It sold seasons. *Generational Rights Management*, the prospectuses said—a renewal cassette tucked into every licensed line, dormant in what you bought, awake in what you saved. Second-generation seed came up green and hopeful for eleven days, then went to paper, chromosomes shredded in the embryo by a toxin under a seed-specific promoter. Buy again. When the towers fell and the vaults burned and no new licenses issued, the world learned that four of every five calories on earth had been rented. They named the second spring after starving. Her craft was a change of tense: leased to owned. She crossed CERES lines against heirloom stock—pre-Collapse, public domain, true-breeding, hoarded like scripture—and screened the children by PCR, hunting the one seedling in four hundred where the cassette had recombined itself out. One leaf punch, two hours, and she'd know. Without the machine she'd be planting whole fields on faith. She had forty microliters of Taq left, amber and cold, worth more than the guards. The bloom had taken her sister in nineteen days, lungs filling like cellars. So when it came through the Terraces—her settlement stacked up a dead parking structure—Vera had dosed herself with a leftover vector, AAV with ends already fraying, carrying a clawed frog's defensin gene: untested, unapproved, unlabeled. The toll kept its ledger. Skin that ran cold at thirty-five degrees. Breath fogging in July. A dull ache where her kidneys were. Cravings for crickets, by the paper cone. A patch on her shoulder gone glassy and pond-colored where the vector had integrated somewhere it shouldn't—and every re-dose a fresh gamble, the ends fraying worse each time. She was, medically speaking, part amphibian now. But she hadn't caught the bloom. Her sweat stopped rot: the children of the Terraces lined up for her thumb pressed to their scrapes, and none had died of a cut in two years. She felt rain coming a day out, in her teeth, like weather living inside her. Small mercies. Strange ones. Ketch came at dusk with two guards who waited politely by the embalming drain, and a steel case, foam-lined, still cold. Five vials of Taq. A desiccated primer library, ninety-six wells. A dNTP set. And at the bottom, wrapped in wax paper, a tin: true barley, a public line out of the old Ethiopian bank, a kilo weight. Seed that bred true forever. The Tollhouse had looted a university vault in year three and had been spending it one temptation at a time. "Tenancy potatoes," Ketch said. "Tubers that won't break dormancy without our primer chemical. Farms on Tollhouse land plant them, and come spring they trade with us or they don't plant." He was a decent man doing indecent arithmetic, the most common profession left. "Nobody's asking you to invent anything, Vera. Just put back what used to be there." What used to be there had starved half the world. She thought it. She didn't say it. The Terraces held nine hundred mouths and forty days of grain, her spring wheat was unscreenable without polymerase, and the barley in that tin could be crossed into her lines in a single season and make them stable forever. She pressed her cold thumb to the contract's line, ink taking the whorls like frost. "Six weeks," she said. "Tell the Tollhouse six weeks." That night she ran her own wheat with their Taq—Tollhouse polymerase amplifying her truth, leaf punches to a billion copies each, the little gantry ticking between its three temperatures. On the lightbox the short bands glowed where they should: cassette-free, true-breeding, owned. And when she built the Tollhouse its lock, she would write a stutter into the promoter. A slipping repeat, four generations deep, that would silence itself quietly, some spring when no one at the Tollhouse was counting. A lock that ate its own keyhole. She set the cycle count to thirty-five and watched the tubes shuttle, hot to cool to warm, the mortuary humming around her. That was all PCR was, in the end: one small true thing, copied until it was too loud to ignore.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a sophisticated piece of biopunk fiction that demonstrates exceptional technical knowledge and literary craft. The author has created a compelling post-apocalyptic world where genetic engineering's built-in obsolescence has led to societal collapse, and follows biohacker Vera as she navigates both scientific challenges and moral compromises. The technical authenticity is remarkable - the detailed descriptions of jury-rigged PCR equipment, electrophoresis rigs, and genetic modification procedures feel genuinely researched rather than hand-waved. The author understands the science well enough to make the improvised laboratory equipment believable, from the 3D printer converted to a thermal cycler to the mortuary repurposed as a lab space. The worldbuilding is economical yet comprehensive. The concept of "Generational Rights Management" and rental calories provides a chilling extrapolation of current corporate practices. The author efficiently establishes the post-collapse world through specific details like "LICENSED BIOLOGICAL MATERIAL. PROPAGATION STRICTLY PROHIBITED" still visible on salvaged equipment. Vera emerges as a complex protagonist whose amphibian modifications serve both practical and symbolic purposes. Her physical transformation - cold skin, weather sensitivity, the need for crickets - creates genuine body horror while also providing tangible benefits to her community. The moral ambiguity of her situation is well-handled; she's simultaneously savior and potential destroyer. The prose style is consistently strong, with memorable phrases like "seasons, not seed" and "the last cold in the world, delivered by the people who burned it down." The technical language is integrated naturally without becoming incomprehensible to lay readers. The black market contract plot provides appropriate tension and moral complexity. Vera's decision to build a genetic "time bomb" into the Tollhouse's crop control system shows her operating in shades of gray rather than simple heroism. Minor weaknesses include some passages that border on overly dense technical description, and Ketch could have been developed slightly more as an antagonist. The ending, while thematically appropriate, feels somewhat predictable in its "clever scientist outsmarts the oppressors" resolution.
